events.event_narrative: Several SNOTEL stations including Farmington, Ben Lomond Peak, Lookout Peak, and Hardscrabble measured 3.8 to 4.1 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 20 to 24 inches of heavy wet snow. In addition, automated weather station recorded wind gusts included 64 mph and 60 mph at SR-30 at Laketown Summit and Logan Summit, respectively.

Alta - Collins recorded 3.12 inches of snow water equivalent, with 17 inches of heavy wet snow reported at the site. In addition, Alta Ski Area and Brighton Resort both received 15 inches of snow, with Park City Mountain Resort receiving 14 inches of snow. A wind gust of 95 mph was recorded by the Alta Mt Baldy automated weather station. Other automated weather station wind gusts included 62 mph at Cardiff Peak, 60 mph at Canyons Lookout, and 58 mph at Reynolds Peak.

Several SNOTEL stations including Trial Lake, Chalk Creek, Brown Duck, Lakefork Basin, and Hayden Fork recorded between 1.6 and 1.9 inches of snow water equivalent, or approxmiately 10 to 12 inches of heavy wet snow. A tornado developed near the summit of US-191 and Argyle Canyon |Road in remote southwestern Duchesne County at about 9200 feet. |Sporadic damage is noted in this area as it moved north over a |ridge line and into a valley adjacent to US-191 along Indian |Canyon.||The tornado then descended down the length of the valley from |about 9200 feet to a creek adjacent to US-191 at an elevation of |about 8500 feet. Over this period, both the strength and and width|of the tornado increased substantially with a continuous damage |path through a mixed aspen and conifer forest. The maximum damage |was found in this area and was significant. Almost all trees over |a large hillside facing the road were violently blown down, |snapped, or topped into a clearly convergent axis. Several tree |tops were desposited along the creek and road with no clear |indicatation as to where they orginated.||The tornado then crossed US-191 and ascended the hillside from |about 8500 feet to another ridge on the northwest side of the road|to an elevation of about 9100 feet. Considerable damage was noted|immediately north of US-191 where numerous trees were snapped or |uprooted, although not to the severe extent noted on the south |side of the road. Damage decreased considerably up the hillside to|the top of the 9100 foot ridge line with more sporadic toppled |trees.||A few toppled trees were noted into the next basin over the ridge|on the north side of the road, marking the last discernible |damage from the tornado, and the end of the 2 mile damage path.

A strong thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall, primarily over the high terrain just east of U.S. Highway 191/U.S. Highway 6 near milepost 292. Radar estimates showed roughly 1 to 2 inches of rain over the course of around an hour to an hour and a half. It was later reported that this led to a family's SUV being washed off of the road, and the family required rescue. No injuries were reported.

The U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground Playa Station mesonet station measured a wind gust of 61 mph at 2:45 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.

The PacifiCorp Aerie mesonet station near Park City measured an initial wind gust of 60 mph at 3:00 pm MST, followed by a peak wind gust of 65 mph at 3:10 pm MST, as a result of strong outflow from nearby convection.
The U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground Lower Cedar Mountain mesonet station measured a wind gust of 65 mph at 3:00 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.
The U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground Dugway 32 mesonet station measured a wind gust of 60 mph at 3:15 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.

The Utah Department of Transportation Johnsons Pass mesonet station measured a peak wind gust of 62 mph at 3:30 pm MST, followed by an additional wind gust of 60 mph at 3:40 pm MST, as a result of strong outflow from nearby convection.
The Utah Department of Transportation I-80 @ Grassey mesonet station measured a wind gust of 69 mph at 3:40 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.
The Utah Department of Transportation I-80 at MP 71 East Delle mesonet station measured a wind gust of 58 mph at 3:50 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.
The Utah Department of Transportation I-80 at MP 79 Timpie mesonet station measured a wind gust of 58 mph at 4:00 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.
The Utah Department of Transportation I-80 at MP 107 mesonet station measured a wind gust of 58 mph at 4:10 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.
The Utah Department of Transportation Legacy Parkway mesonet station measured a wind gust of 59 mph at 4:40 pm MST as a result of convective outflow.

A strong microburst near Erda, UT was observed by a live area webcam. Multiple pictures were later received showing a large tree downed, roof shingles blown off, play structures damaged and/or blown over, fences damaged, a house under construction damaged, and a center pivot damaged. Based on the damage pictures, an estimated wind gust of around 70 mph was determined.

A thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall in the high terrain around the town of Hildale, as well as within the town itself. Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor (MRMS) 1-hour estimates showed around 1 to 2 inches of rainfall with this storm. Light to moderate rain continued for a while thereafter, with 3-hour MRMS estimates exceeding 2 inches of rainfall in spots. This rainfall ran into Short Creek, and resulted in a flow through the town of Hildale, though the flow was not significant enough to overtop any road crossings within town.

A thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall over the course of an hour or so in the high terrain northwest of the town of Leeds, UT. Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor 1-hour estimates show around 1.5 to 2.5 inches of rainfall with this storm. An initial report was received of water over the bridge at Red Cliffs Campground as water flowed out of Water Canyon and through Harrisburg Creek. A short time later, a video was found on Twitter showing water flowing through the campground and overtopping the access bridge.
The Utah Department of Transportation SR-7 at MP 19.5 Sand Hollow mesonet station measured a wind gust of 68 mph at 5:40 pm MST as a result of a nearby microburst's outflow.

Heavy rain in portions of the headwaters region of the Paria River resulted in a flow downstream. The Paria River Near Kanab, Utah gauge indicated a rise from 5 CFS to over 520 CFS in a span of 10 minutes, and peaked at 842 CFS, with a rise of over 2 feet.
Rangers at Zion National Park reported flash flooding in Pine Creek and side canyons off of Bridge Mountain due to excessive rainfall in the region.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall over the high terrain near the town of Hildale over the course of an hour, with Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor 1-hour estimates of around 1 to 1.5 inches of rainfall. Light to moderate rain persisted for 2 to 3 hours thereafter. The rainfall resulted in a strong flow in Short Creek through Hildale and on into Colorado City. Dispatch from Colorado City reported all street crossings across the creek were closed due to flooding, and 3 feet of fast moving water was reported to be flowing across Hildale Street.
The Utah Department of Transportation I-15 @ Plymouth mesonet station measured a wind gust of 68 mph at 9:40 pm MST as a result of outflow from nearby thunderstorms.
The PacifiCorp Crow Mountain mesnonet station measured a wind gust of 59 mph at 8:10 pm MST as a result of nearby thunderstorms.
An Incident Meteorologist deployed to the Dodge Springs Fire reported a mudflow over Gunlock Road south of Gunlock Reservoir.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall north of Brian Head, with 3-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor rainfall estimates of around 1 to 2.5 inches. This resulted in debris flows over state Route 143 between mileposts 11 and 13, and closure of the road. Additional reports from the public and media reported debris was up to 7 feet deep in spots.

Thunderstorms produced heavy precipitation over the Tank Hollow Fire burn scar, with 1-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor estimates of 1.5 to 2.5 inches of rain. Associated with this, the Dispatch Center in the city of Price reported running water and debris along U.S. Highway 6 from mileposts 197 to 198. It was further reported that dirt and mud was a foot deep, with tree trunks and logs 8 to 10 inches in diameter included in the debris.
A tree fell on a church in Springville.
Trees fell onto several hourse in Springville.
Several trees were uprooted or snapped off in Springville Cemetery.
A peak wind gust of 58 mph was recorded at Salt Lake City International Airport.
A peak wind gust of 60 mph was measured at the UDOT SR-85 at SR-201 mesonet site.
A large tree branch fell on a vehicle in Salt Lake City. Time estimated based on radar.
A peak wind gust of 66 mph was measured by the Fremont Island mesonet station.
A peak wind gust of 63 mph was measured by the UDOT SR-201 at I-80 automated weather station.
Emery County dispatch reported state Route 29 was impassible from milepost 9 to Joes Valley Reservoir. Up to a foot of mud and debris was deposited across the road.
Capitol Reef National Park reported flash flooding on Sulphur Creek. Water was several feet deep and came within 2 feet or so from the bottom of the bridge on state Route 24.
A large debris flow originating off of the Dollar Ridge Fire burn scar passed through the Strawberry Pinnacles area.

LANDSPOUT. Location: 40.710, -112.040. A landspout tornado was observed for approximately 8 minutes over undeveloped land on the northwest side of West Valley City. No damage was reported. Location is approximate and based on eyewitness accounts.
A Summit County official reported a foot of water and some gravel spilled out onto Chalk Creek Road.
LANDSPOUT. Location: 37.070N, 113.630W. A video posted to social media showed a landspout tornado near Tonaquint Drive in St. George. No damage was reported. Time estimated from radar.

Moderate to heavy rain fell across Zion National Park and surrounding areas, with 3-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor rainfall estimates of around 0.50 inches. As a result, the North Fork Virgin at Springdale river gauge recorded a rapid rise in stage from around 50 CFS to over 1200 CFS in under 2 hours. Additionally, park rangers at Zion National Park reported flooding in many slot canyons in the park, as well as several observed waterfalls.

Moderate to heavy rainfall from earlier in the day resulted in a flood wave traversing downstream along the Virgin River. The Virgin at Virgin river gauge recorded a flow increase from 333 CFS at 12:15 am MST to a peak of 2020 CFS at 2:00 am MST.
The Sundance Arrowhead mesonet weather station recorded a wind gust of 62 mph.

Bureau of Land Management officials reported a flash flood wave moving down Phipps Wash toward the Escalante River. This is most likely associated with a brief thunderstorm which moved through the area between roughly 11:30 am MST to 12:30 pm MST and produced moderate to heavy rainfall. Event time is based upon report.

Park rangers relayed a report of flash flooding in Capitol Gorge, with floodwaters as much as 4 feet deep. This is associated with showers and thunderstorms which moved through the area between around 12:30 pm MST to 2:00 pm MST and produced around 0.50 inches of rainfall.
The I-80 at MP 68 West Delle weather station recorded a wind gust of 61 mph as a result of a thunderstorm moving over the site.

The Fremont Island - Miller Hill weather station recorded an initial gust of 79 mph at 9:35 pm MST, with a peak gust of 80 mph subsequently recorded at 9:40 pm MST. The weather station then continued to record gusts ranging from 58 mph to 72 mph through 10:10 pm MST. The wind gusts were associated with strong thunderstorms moving through the area.
High flows were reported in the Clear Creek drainage in the southeastern portion of Zion National Park.
Numerous videos and photos from the media and the public showed street flooding in the West Jordan area. One basement was flooded. Time of this report is estimated.
Scenic Drive in Capitol Reef National Park was closed due to flooding in the Grand Wash.
Flash flooding produced a washout on Ophir Canyon Road. Time of the event is estimated based on reports.
Six to eight inches of rapidly flowing water crossed roads in Grand Wash and Capitol Gorge in Capitol Reef National Park.
A wind gust of 64 mph was recorded by the I-15 at Beaver mesonet site.
A flash flood was observed in the Pine Creek Slot Canyon due to earlier heavy rain upstream on Clear Creek.
Flash flooding was reported in Clear Creek within Zion National Park.
A flash flood on Short Creek in Hildale flooded a home.

Flows increased on the North Fork of the Virgin River in Zion National Park. The trail became impassable near the mouth of The Narrows. Flood waters in The Narrows swept some hikers off their feet and isolated others on higher ground. Two people were swept downstream. One was swept a couple of hundred yards and found. The individual survived with minor injuries. The other was reported as missing to Zion National Park officials later that evening, and was found deceased the following Monday. The North Fork Virgin - Springdale river gauge, which is downstream from The Narrows, rose from approximately 75 cfs to 735 cfs, corresponding to a rise of slightly over 2 feet in height.
Flash flooding was reported in Clear Creek, Pine Creek, and Spry Canyon in Zion National Park.
The North Fork Virgin - Springdale, Nr gauge rose from near 50 cfs. to 1160 cfs. A corresponding rise over 3 ft. was recorded on the gauge height.
Social media videos showed flash flooding over roads in and near Hildale.
Flash flooding was reported along Pine Creek near the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel.
Flash flooding was reported in the vicinity of The Narrows in Zion National Park.
The Hildale Dispatch reported two road closures near waterways due to rises from flash flooding.
Grand Wash in Capitol Reef National Park was closed due to flash flooding.
Flash flooding occurred in Grand Wash in Capitol Reef National Park, with 1-2 feet of water flowing over the road.
A video from social media showed significant flows on Alvey Wash, with at least several inches of water and debris flowing across Cedar Wash Road. Location is approximate.
A flash flood was observed in Sulphur Creek near Panorama Point in Capitol Reef National Park.
A debris flow from the Trail Mountain Fire burn scar was observed on Huntington Creek near the Huntington Power Plant.
Flash flooding was reported along Pine Creek within Zion National Park.
Ping pong ball-sized hail fell in Beryl. Location and time are estimated by radar.
A storm produced hail 1 inch in diameter in St. George. The time of the report is estimated.
Horseman Park Drive from River Road to Little Valley Elementary was closed due to flash flooding.
Strong winds blew a roof off a house in Cannonville. The time of the report is estimated.
Flash flooding was reported in Cannonville and Henrieville, with mud and debris on state Route 12 between the towns.
A carport was blown down in Brigham City.
Flash flooding was reported in Isaac Canyon near Court of the Patriarchs.
A wind gust of 64 mph was recorded within the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet.
A wind gust of 73 mph was recorded by Salt Flats mesonet station.
A wind gust of 64 mph was recorded by the Wendover Port of Entry automated weather station.
The Wig Mountain weather station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of a thunderstorm and its associated outflow winds moving over the site.

The Groome weather station recorded an initial peak gust of 66 mph at 5:39 pm MST, with final lesser gusts of 63 mph at 6:05 and 6:06 pm MST. These wind gusts were  associated with a cluster of strong thunderstorms and their associated outflow winds which were moving through the area.

The Camel Back MTN weather station recorded an initial wind gust of 59 mph at 2:20 pm MST in association with nearby thunderstorm outflow winds. After a brief lull with lighter winds, an additional nearby shower resulted in more strong outflow winds which yielded a peak wind gust of 64 mph at 4:40 pm MST, and a final strong wind gust of 60 mph at 4:45 pm MST.
The English Village weather station recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph as a result of a thunderstorm and associated outflow winds moving over the site.
The SR-201 at I-80, weather station recorded a wind gust of 65 mph as a result of a thunderstorm and associated outflow winds moving over the site.
The Beach weather station recorded a wind gust of 77 mph as a result of a thunderstorm and associated outflow winds moving over the site.
The I-80 at MP 107 weather station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of a thunderstorm and associated outflow winds moving over the site.

The Logan Peak weather station recorded an initial peak wind gust of 63 mph at 9:00 pm MST as a result of a thunderstorm and associated outflow winds moving over the site. A second thunderstorm an hour later resulted in a wind gust of 58 mph at 10:00 pm MST.
The Cardiff Peak weather station recorded a peak wind gust of 64 mph as a result of outflow winds from a nearby thunderstorm moving over the site.

Moderate rain moved over portions of Wire Pass and Buckskin Gulch slot canyons, as well as nearby drainages, with 1-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor rainfall estimates up to 0.75 inches. Flash Flooding was reported by the Paria Contact Station at 12:00 pm MST, with reports of several hikers in the area needing to form human chains in three separate locations to escape flood waters. No injuries were noted at the time of report.

A strong thunderstorm moved through portions of the Paria River drainage basin, with widespread 1-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor rainfall estimates of 0.50 to 0.75 inches. This generated a flood wave that propagated downstream, with the Paria near Kanab river gauge rising from 100 CFS around 1:00 pm MST to 1180 CFS at 1:25 pm MST.

Strong thunderstorms moved over the Oquirrh Mountains over the course of an hour or two, resulting in moderate to at times heavy rain over the Jacob City Fire burn scar. Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor 1-hour rainfall estimates were in the 0.50 to 0.75 inch range. This was enough to result in a flow along Soldier Creek, which resulted in the evacuation of one house by State Route 36 and a road closure.

Heavy rain from nearby thunderstorms resulted in 3-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor estimates of around 1 to 2 inches total. Garfield County Dispatch reported flooding in Tropic, Cannonville, and Henrieville. One basement was flooded. Time estimated by radar.

Multiple thunderstorms with moderate to heavy rainfall moved over Bryce Canyon National Park during the late evening hours. Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor 3-hour rainfall estimates showed widespread amounts of 1 to 2 inches, and the Bryce Canyon Airport ASOS recorded nearly 1.5 inches of rain over the span of 3:30 pm MST to 4:30 pm MST. Many trails sustained damage, with some leading to extended trail closures. The Queen's Garden trail suffered a few debris flows with unstable footing and two retaining wall failures. The Peekaboo Loop suffered numerous debris flows and points of trail surface erosion. The Bryce Point Peekaboo Connecting Trail suffered numerous rockfalls and debris flows, two retaining wall failures, and deep incisions of around 1 foot into the trail surface. The Fairyland Loop trail suffered deep incisions of around 1 foot into the trail surface. The Navajo Loop trail had a tree downed on the Two Bridges side. The Wall Street side of the Navajo Loop Trail suffered further debris flows and complete trail erosion in some sections, resulting in an extended trail closure.

Nearby thunderstorms with moderate rainfall resulted in 3-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor accumulation estimates of around 0.25 to 0.75 inches. The Pine Creek near Escalante stream gauge spiked to a peak flow of 228 CFS at 7:15 pm MST.

A thunderstorm moved through portions of the Escalante River drainage basin, producing moderate rainfall, with widespread 3-hour Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor rainfall estimates of 0.50 to 1.00 inches in upstream tributary areas. This generated a flood wave that propagated downstream, resulting in the Escalante near Escalante river gauge spiking to  804 CFS at 9:50 pm MST.
The Grantsville South weather station recorded a wind gust of 69 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The Tower Grid weather station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The Beach weather station recorded an initial wind gust of 66 mph at 6:50 pm MST, with a peak gust of 75 mph at 7:00 pm MST.  These gusts were associated with outflow from clusters of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The Marina weather station recorded an initial wind gust of 60 mph at 6:50 pm MST, with a peak wind gust of 61 mph at 7:20 pm MST. These gusts were associated with outflow from clusters of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The SR-201 at I-80, weather station  recorded an initial peak wind gust of 70 mph at 7:00 pm MST, and a lesser wind gust of 64 mph at 7:20 pm MST. These gusts were associated with outflow from clusters of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The Vernon Hill weather station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The I-80 at MP 81 Dolomite weather station recorded a wind gust of 66 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The Fremont Island - Miller Hill weather station recorded an initial peak wind gust of 61 mph at 8:00 pm MST, and a lesser wind gust of 59 mph at 8:10 pm MST. These gusts were associated with outflow from clusters of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The I-80 at MP 107 weather station recorded an initial wind gust of 59 mph at 7:00 pm MST, and a second wind gust of 59 mph at 7:10 pm MST. These gusts were associated with outflow from clusters of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.

The Snowbasin - Mount Ogden weather station recorded wind gusts of 61 mph at 8:30 pm MST and 8:45 pm MST, and subsequent peak wind gusts of 62 mph at 9:00 pm MST and 9:15 pm MST. These gusts were associated with outflow from clusters of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The Murray's Hill weather station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The Causeway weather station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The SR-65 at Big Mountain Pass weather station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
The Vernon Hill weather station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
Officials from Capitol Reef National Park reported 1 to 2 feet of water flowing through a wash that feeds into the Grand Wash, as well as 1 to 2 feet of water flowing through Grand Wash itself.

Zion National Park officials reported that normally dry washes near Canyon Junction were seeing flash flooding, that there were waterfalls on both sides of Zion Canyon, and that the campground had minor flooding. A thunderstorm which moved through produced an estimated 0.25 to 0.75 inches of rainfall per Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor 1-hour analysis.
The sensor at the Trans-Jordan Landfill recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
Lehi received a maximum wind gust of 70 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Multiple sites in the northwest deserts and mountains received strong wind gusts, including 59 to 61 mph wind gusts at several sites in the Dugway mesonet, and a maximum wind gust of 83 mph at the Wendover Peak sensor.
The Fish Springs sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The Deer Creek Dam Chute sensor, at an altitude of 6,670 feet MSL, received a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
Capitol Reef National Park officials reported flows from Sheets Gulch into Sandy Creek.
Capitol Reef National Park officials relayed a public report of flows across Burr Trail Switchbacks, resulting in the road becoming impassable.
Capitol Reef National Park officials reported flash flooding on Sulphur Creek.

Precipitation amounts includes 2.05 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 20 inches of snow, at the Brian Head SNOTEL, 1.8 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 18 inches of snow, at the Midway Valley SNOTEL, and 1.25 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 12 inches of snow, at the Webster Flat SNOTEL.
The Hans Flat Ranger Station Coop observer reported 5.8 inches of snow.
The Fort Pearce Wash gauge peaked at 789 cfs.
The Escalante at Escalante river gauge peaked at 518 cfs with a flood wave around 7 p.m.
Hail sizes ranged from pea to golf ball. An Anasazi State Park employee noted that hail lasted for 30 minutes in Boulder with 2-6 inches of accumulation. At least one car windshield was broken.
An Anasazi State Park employee reported 1 inch diameter hail at the Anasazi State Park Museum.
A resident reported quarter-sized hail that dented cars in Hanksville.
Pictures from social media shared by broadcast media showed hail damage from Cedar City to Enoch. The largest hail was estimated to be ping pong ball-sized.
An NWS employee recorded 7.0 inches of snow in Tooele.

Precipitation amounts includes 3.24 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 26 inches of snow, at Alta Ski Area and approximately 18 inches of snow reported from an employee at Solitude Mountain Resort.
The US-89 at Park Lane mesonet site recorded a peak wind gust of 69 mph. The Farmington Bench mesonet site recorded a peak wind gust of 64 mph.
The Sherwood Hills automated weather station near Wellsville recorded a peak wind gust of 79 mph.
The Central Wasatch Peaks automated weather station recorded a wind gust of 96 mph.
The Fremont Island - Miller Hill automated weather station recorded a wind gust of 76 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The I-80 @ mp 1 automated weather station recorded a wind gust of 74 mph. Other mesonet site wind gusts included 71 mph by English Village, 62 mph by Hat Island, 62 mph by I-80 @ Grassey, 60 mph by I-80 at MP 40 Knolls, and 58 mph by I-80 at MP 81 Dolomite. Several high profile vehicles were blown over on Interstate 80.
The Junction South automated weather station recorded a wind gust of 64 mph.
The US-6 @ Eureka automated weather station recorded a wind gust of 63 mph. A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded by the Fish Springs mesonet station.

The I-15 at MP 57 Cedar City automated weather station recorded a gust of 63 mph. A peak wind gust of 61 mph was recorded by the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field ASOS. A 58 mph wind gust was recorded by the I-15 at MP 54 Hamiltons Fort mesonet station.
The I-70 at Salina automated weather station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.

Precipitation amounts includes 1.8 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 22 inches of snow, at the Kolob SNOTEL, 1.3 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 16 inches of snow, at the Midway Valley SNOTEL, and 1 inch of snow water equivalent, or approximately 12 inches of snow, at the Lonesome Beaver SNOTEL.
A peak wind gust of 71 mph was recoded by the Logan-Cache Airport ASOS. An additional gust of 66 mph was by the reported by the US-91 at MP 39 Richmond mesonet site.

A peak wind gust of 80 mph was recorded by the I-80 at MP 79 automated weather station. An additional significant wind gust of 75 mph was reported by the SR-201 at I-80 station.  Other strong wind gusts included 68 mph by the I-80 @ mp 78 station, 62 mph by the LAKE POINT I-80 station, and 60 mph by the SR-112 @ MP 6 Utah Avenue station.

A peak wind gust of 77 mph was reported at the Beach mesonet site. An additional wind gust of 69 mph was reported at the Marina mesonet site. Another strong wind gust of 58 mph was reported by the POM North Side mesonet site.

A peak wind gust of 79 mph was recorded by the Ogden Peak mesonet station, with additional wind gusts of 78 mph recorded by the LOGAN PEAK mesonet sensor, and 75 mph by the Crow Mountain mesonet sensor.

A peak wind gust of 72 mph was recorded by the SR-201 at I-80 mesonet station. Other selected strong wind gusts measured around the zone included 69 mph SR-112 @ MP 6 Utah Avenue, and 63 mph at Bolinder Field-Tooele Valley Airport.

Several SNOTEL stations including Bug Lake, Lightning Ridge, and Tony Grove Lake recorded between around 2.1 to 3.1 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 2 to 3 feet of snow. The Farmington SNOTEL station recorded the highest in the zone, with 3.55 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 41 inches of snow. In addition, many automated weather stations recorded strong wind gusts, including 82 mph at Ogden Peak, 81 mph at LOGAN PEAK, and 80 mph at Peter Sinks Rim.

Several SNOTEL stations including Silver Lake Brighton, Thaynes Canyon, and Mill-D North recorded between around 2.4 to 3.1 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 2 to 3 feet of snow. Similar amounts were reported by many cooperative observers. The Snowbird SNOTEL station recorded the highest in the zone, with 4.7 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 57 inches of snow.

Several SNOTEL stations including Redden Mine LWR, Spirit Lk, and Trial Lake recorded between around 1.1 to 1.3 inches of snow water equivalent, or approximately 13 to 16 inches of snow. In addition, many automated weather stations recorded strong wind gusts, including 96 mph at CHEPETA, 86 mph at Windy Peak, and 75 mph at Duchesne Ridge.

Several SNOTEL stations including Daniels-Strawberry, Clear Creek #1, and Huntington Horse recorded between around 1.1 to 2.4 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 12 to 29 inches of snow.
Several SNOTEL stations including Kolob, Brian Head, and Clayton Springs recorded between around 1.2 to 3.7 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 14 to 44 inches of snow.

The Agua Canyon SNOTEL station recorded 1.9 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 23 inches of snow. Additionally, Bryce Canyon NP HQRS recorded around 0.7 inches of snow water equivalent, which resulted in approximately 7 inches of snow. In addition to the snow, the Bryce Canyon Airport ASOS recorded many gusts around 60 mph through the event, with a peak gust of 63 mph.

A peak wind gust of 73 mph was recorded by the Cedar City Regional Airport ASOS, as well as the I-15 at MP 62.5 North Cedar City mesonet site. Other selected strong wind gusts measured included 68 mph by the I-15 at MP 54 Hamiltons Fort station, 67 mph by the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field ASOS, and 62 mph by the I-15 @ Black Ridge station.

Several SNOTEL stations including Klondike Narrows, Parley's Summit, and Ben Lomond Peak recorded between 1.0 to 1.3 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 19 to 31 inches of snow. An additional report from Powder Mountain recorded around 1.0 inch of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 22 inches of snow.

The SNOTEL station at Snowbird recorded around 1.3 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 18 inches of snow. Additionally, reports were received of 0.9 inches of snow water equivalent and 19 inches of snow by the BRIGHTON CREST station at Brighton, and 1.0 inches of snow water equivalent and 18 inches of snow by the ALTA - COLLINS station at Alta Ski Area.

Several SNOTEL stations including Hobble Creek, Daniels-Strawberry, and Strawberry Divide recorded between around 0.7 to 1.0 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 12 to 14 inches of snow.
Several SNOTEL stations including Buck Flat, Red Pine Ridge, and Seely Creek recorded between around 0.7 to 1.4 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 12 to 18 inches of snow.

Snow Squall. A snow squall moved eastward through portions of the Toole and Rush Valleys during the morning hours. A wind gust of 59 mph was recorded by the I-80 @ mp 78 automated station at 5:10 am MST, along with moderate precipitation and lowered visibility. Similarly, wind gusts of 63 mph and 66 mph occurred at 5:15 am MST and 5:30 am MST respectively at the VERNON HILL mesonet site.
The Evanston airport ASOS reported a maximum wind gust of 77 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Several wind sensors in the northwest desert received wind gusts greater than 58 mph, with the strongest recorded gust being 64 mph at the Playa Station sensor.
The sensor in Lehi recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
Sandy received a maximum wind gust of 63 mph, while Herriman received a gust of 67 mph. Damage was reported in Cottonwood Heights, where a medium-sized tree was knocked over and fell onto a car.
South Ogden received a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
An NWS employee reported 7.0 inches of snow in Clearfield. Other accumulations include 6.5 inches in West Haven, 6.5 inches in West Weber, and 6.0 inches in Layton.
Snowfall accumulations include 7.8 inches at Magna, 7.0 inches at Kearns, 6.0 inches at Taylorsville, and 6.0 inches at West Jordan.
Snowfall accumulations include 13.0 inches at Providence, 12.0 inches at Hyrum, 12.0 inches at Logan, 10.0 inches at Nibley, and 8.0 inches at Hyde Park.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: A wind gust of 82 mph was recorded at the I-80 at MP 40 Knolls mesonet site. Other wind gusts include 67 mph at the Salt Flats mesonet site, 64 mph at the Causeway mesonet site, 62 mph at the Wig Mountain mesonet site, 61 mph at the I-80 @ mp 29 mesonet site, 58 mph at the Callao Gate mesonet site, and 58 mph at the Wendover Port of Entry mesonet site.
The Vernon Hill mesonet site recorded a wind gust of 67 mph. Other wind gusts included a 64 mph gust at the SR-201 at I-80 mesonet site and a 63 mph gust at the I-80 at MP 79 Timpie mesonet site.
A peak wind gust of 63 mph was recorded at the Pioneer Crossing mesonet site.

A 95 mph wind gust was recorded at the Central Wasatch Peak mesonet site. Other wind gusts include 78 mph at the Deer Valley - Mount Baldy mesonet site, 78 mph at the Deer Valley - Empire Peak mesonet site, and 77 mph at the Sundance - Arrowhead Summit mesonet site.
A wind gust of 89 mph was recorded at the Lofty Lake Peak mesonet site. A wind gust of 80 mph was recorded at the Windy Peak mesonet site.

A wind gust of 70 mph was recorded at the I-15 at MP 57 Cedar City mesonet site. Other wind gusts include a 69 mph wind gust at the I-15 at MP 62.5 North Cedar City mesonet site, 62 mph at the I-15 at MP 54 Hamiltons Fort mesonet site, 60 mph by the Cedar City Regional Airport ASOS, and 59 mph at the Brimestone Reservoir mesonet site.

A large naturally occurring avalanche took place in the morning hours near Bridal Veil Falls in Provo Canyon. Snow with the avalanche flow covered the entire base of the falls in Provo Canyon and deposited snow onto State Route 189. According to the Utah Highway Patrol, trees were included within the flow, resulting in blocking and damming of the Provo River for a period of time. Several hours after the avalanche, an employee with the water conservancy district was inspecting a flooded building, at which time a portion of the snow dam holding back the river current broke free. The employee was caught in the floodwater to an extent, managed to cling to a tree until water began to recede, and then was able to find safe ground on a cement stack in the middle of the river until rescue crews could get to him. The employee was taken to a nearby hospital to be treated for hypothermia. Per the Utah Avalanche Center, avalanche danger was rated in the high category along all slopes and elevations in the Provo area for the day.

A group including two guides, eleven clients, and two snowcat operators were in the Western Uinta Mountains for backcountry skiing. For their final run, the group ascended to the top of a point in the Upper Weber Canyon approximately 10400 feet in elevation with a southeast aspect and slope angle of around 37 degrees. After one guide and two skiers descended, a third skier began descending and fell part way down. A fourth skier began their descent, with the avalanche subsequently releasing at approximately 3:21 pm. The avalanche caught the third and fourth skier, carrying them downhill and fully burying them. A guide called for medical and search and rescue aid, and began searching for the buried skiers. One skier was found buried around 5 feet deep, but was breathing and alert when uncovered. The skier was fully excavated and then transferred via air ambulance to a local hospital. Some time later, the transceiver signal for the second buried skier was located. The skier was found buried upside down around 6 feet deep, not breathing, and with no pulse. The skier was pronounced dead approximately 1 hour and 20 minutes after the avalanche.

events.event_narrative: At some time between approximately 5:30 pm to 6:15 pm Monday 3/27, a large avalanche in the Pole Canyon area of the southern Oquirrh Mountains resulted in the full burial of a snowmobiler. A second snowmobiler who was not buried was able to call for emergency services, and search and rescue began soon thereafter for the buried snowmobiler. The buried snowmobiler was equipped with a beacon, and by 8:48 pm the body of the deceased 38-year-old man was recovered under approximately 13.2 feet of snow. The buried avalanche victim had deployed an avalanche airbag, but the airbag was deflated when the victim was found. This large avalanche was reported to have a fracture line 4250 feet wide, traveling a horizontal distance of 1.26 miles (2360 vertical feet downhill).
The Cedar City Regional Airport ASOS and the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field ASOS both recorded multiple wind gusts from 58 to 62 mph throughout the event time period.

A group of hikers went on a three day trip to Buckskin Gulch and were set to return Sunday night. Family members reported them missing Monday morning when they did not return as scheduled. A search began shortly thereafter and one of the hikers was found alive Monday evening and was taken to a hospital via helicopter. The search broke off early Tuesday morning but resumed during the day Tuesday. On Tuesday evening the body of one of the other hikers was found and the third was found Wednesday afternoon. While the search was being conducted for this group of hikers, two other groups of hikers also signaled for help, bringing the total of people rescued from Buckskin Gulch to 11. The conditions were found to be treacherous in the canyon due to high water from snowmelt that has accumulated in the canyon. Given the narrow nature of the canyon in places, it takes a relatively small amount of accumulation of water to make the canyon impassable. Additionally, the location of the canyon allows water to flow into it from the south (from Arizona) as well as from the north (with origins in the vicinity of Bryce Canyon). Recent heavy rains from the ongoing atmospheric river event also hampered rescue efforts.

Broad areas of sheet flooding were observed in the greater Tremonton area due to rain on snow. A two-vehicle crash occurred just before 7PM MDT on U.S. Highway 89, and resulted in 3 fatalities. The Utah Department of Transportation reported that it was snowing at the time of the accident and the road was snow-covered. The Utah Highway Patrol indicated that weather was a likely factor in the crash. Though surface observations in this area are sparse, a nearby RAWS site reported 33 degrees near the time of the crash, with ongoing precipitation.

Snow showers caused reduced visibilities in addition to wetting area roads. By 9:45 pm, continued falling temperatures caused the on-ramp to northbound Interstate 15 from northbound Legacy Parkway to become covered in ice. This resulted in multiple vehicles to lose control, blocking the entire on-ramp. In total, 17 passenger vehicles and 2 semitrailer were involved in the accident. In total, 5 vehicle occupants were transported to area hospitals with non-life-threatening injuries.

At around 11:30 am, a large avalanche occurred near the Gold Ridge / Hardscrabble backcountry area, approximately 7 miles ESE of Farmington. At the time of the avalanche, one snowcat carrying two occupants was caught in the slide and buried. A second snowcat and its five occupants were able to quickly uncover one of the buried snowcat occupants, who had sustained minor head injuries. This occupant was subsequently taken to an area hospital by ambulance. The second occupant was buried with their leg trapped beneath the snowcat, but was uncovered enough that they could breath. When rescue crews arrived, they were able to uncover the buried occupant, who was then transported by helicopter to a nearby hospital with a serious leg injury.

At approximately 0830 MST on Thursday, May 11, 2023, high flows on the Lower Ogden River eroded the embankment supporting state Route 39 through Ogden Canyon which caused one lane of the two lane road to collapse. An upstream river gauge reported flows above action stage (greater than 1264 cfs) from April 14 through May 2, and again from May 4 through the time of the incident. Flows approached minor flood stage (1610 cfs) within 100 cfs throughout this time, but exceeded minor flood stage by 5 cfs at one observation time on May 9, 2023. The road was closed for approximately 11 hours, with the one stable lane allowed to reopen thereafter.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southern Utah on Saturday, moving across the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument towards the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Locally heavy rainfall was associated with these thunderstorms, with radar estimated rainfall from around 0.75 inches to 1.5 inches noted across the Buckskin Gulch area. Two flood waves resulted, as noted on the Paria River at Lees Ferry gauge, downstream of the canyon. This gauge showed an initial gradual increase to around 50 cfs over the course of 2 hours, followed by a rapid increase to approximately 150 cfs over 15 minutes. The second bump would correlate to roughly a 1 foot rise at Lees Ferry, which would be much higher in the narrow slot canyon area of Buckskin Gulch. During the time of flood waves propagation through the slot canyon, at least 2 permitted hikers were hiking through the canyon. They were reported to be planning on hiking approximately 5 miles into Wire Pass and the Buckskin Gulch slot canyon areas. Kane County Sherriff's department received word of a deceased person within the trail, and subsequently recovered the bodies of two deceased individuals. It is believed that the men drowned in the initial flood wave, and were then washed 7 to 10 miles downstream.

Scattered thunderstorms moved across the area from late morning through the afternoon hours. Radar estimates indicated 1.25 inches to 2.5 inches of total rainfall near the affected area. A Park Ranger with the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument subsequently reported and sent pictures of Hole-in-the-Rock road near the 25 Mile Wash area, where floodwaters associated with the rain overtopped road culverts and resulted in a minor road washout.

All creek road crossings were closed for 2 to 3 hours, and the Hilldale Street Creek crossing was heavily damaged and subsequently closed indefinitely until repairs could be made. This flooding is the result of strong thunderstorms which per Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor, produced approximately 3.00 to 4.00 of rainfall, largely within the span of 2 hours, though some of this can likely be attributed to hail contamination. Dirt roads on the outskirts of town were impassable. Additionally, Kane County Sheriff's office officials reported that several homes had some minor basement flooding. This flooding is the result of strong thunderstorms in the area, with Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor estimates of approximately 0.75 to 1.50 of rainfall in around 3 hours.

As warmer weather set in during the spring, the prior winter's record setting snowpack began to melt, with runoff leading to cold, elevated, and fast flowing rivers accordingly. For context, the river gage at the outlet of Pineview Reservoir (which has controlled releases that subsequently flow into the Weber River downstream) rose to 7.37 feet by 5:00 pm MST on May 1, just below the historical record peak of 7.38 feet. On Monday May 1 around 4:45 pm MST, the first of many 911 emergency calls were received, stating that a person in distress was seen within the waters of the Weber River, and that they could hear screaming. First responders and emergency personnel began search and rescue operations on the Weber River from approximately Uintah to Marriott-Slaterville soon thereafter. By around 8:00 pm MST, search and rescue crews shifted to a recovery mission. Recovery crews continued for a time in the following days, but ultimately a body was never found and the missing person was presumed to have drowned. The missing person was later identified as an adult woman, age 28, and a family friend had disclosed that the woman had been walking her dogs along the Weber River at her family farm on the afternoon of the incident.

A group of 3 hikers went on a three day trip through Buckskin Gulch, and were set to return Sunday night. Family members reported them missing Monday morning when they did not return as scheduled. A search began shortly thereafter with one of the hikers found alive on Monday, and taken to a hospital via helicopter. The body of a deceased hiker was found late in the day on Monday.  A second deceased individual was discovered on Wednesday, 3 miles south of the Utah/Arizona border on a patch of land in the middle of the Paria River. It is presumed this hiker suffered fatal injuries while within Buckskin Gulch in Utah, and was subsequently washed downstream into the Paria River. During the search and rescue operations, two other groups of hikers signaling for help were rescued, bringing the total number of people rescued from Buckskin Gulch to 11. ||The conditions were found to be treacherous in the canyon due to high water from rain and snowmelt. Given the narrow nature of the canyon in places, it takes a relatively small amount of water to make the canyon impassable. Additionally, the location of the canyon allows water to flow into it from the south (from Arizona) as well as from the north (with origins in the vicinity of Bryce Canyon).

At approximately 1:20 am MST on 1/6, an incident was reported to law enforcement of an accident involving an F-150 pickup truck travelling on southbound I-15 near milepost 81, just north of Paragonah. Utah State Highway Patrol concluded that the driver lost control of the vehicle on black ice, causing the vehicle to spin left into the median, roll over, and eject all three occupants of the vehicle before coming to rest on its side blocking the northbound lanes of the interstate. Of the three occupants, an adult female (age 26) died at the scene, an injured adult male (age not specified) was transported to the hospital via ground transportation, and an injured female infant (age 1) was transported to the hospital via helicopter transportation. The occupants were reported to not be wearing seatbelts, which in turn was deemed a likely contribution to the severity of the crash. Despite both the adult male and infant female being described as in critical condition for a period following the accident, both are reported to have recovered. The northbound lanes of I-15 near the crash site were closed for approximately 2.5 hours following the incident in order to allow Utah Highway Patrol to conduct the investigation.

Snow Squall. At 4:45 pm MST, the Clarkston mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 54 mph as a well defined band of snow moved through. Between 5:00 pm MST and 5:30 pm MST, the Logan-Cache Airport ASOS recorded a period of wind gusts in excess of 30 mph with a peak gust of 52 mph as this feature moved through. During this time, the ASOS also recorded periods of heavy snow and visibility to as low as 1/4 of a mile. This snow squall continued southward through the area thereafter. Many mesonet sites also reported temperatures rapidly falling below freezing as this snow squall passed.

Snow Squall. Multiple mesonet stations recorded periods strong wind gusts (multiple periods in excess of 30 mph) and significant reductions to visibility (at times 1/4 of a mile or less) as a well defined band of snow moved through the area. The most significant observations were noted from the I-15 at MP369 North Brigham City UDOT RWIS mesonet sensor, which recorded a peak wind gust of 70 mph with visibility as low as 1/8 of a mile. Some additional mesonet sensors which also recorded supporting observations included the Honeyville South mesonet site (peak wind gust of 52 mph) and the I-15 @ Willard POE mesonet site (peak wind gust of 56 mph, visibility less than 1/4 of a mile). Many of these mesonet sites also reported temperatures rapidly falling below freezing as this snow squall passed.

At Ogden-Hinckley Airport for example, a period of wind gusts to 60 mph was observed between 5:53 pm MST to 6:02 pm MST, with visibility to 1 1/2 of a mile. Some additional mesonet sensors which also recorded supporting observations include the POWER PLANT mesonet site (peak wind gust of 56 mph, visibility less than 1 mile), the US-89 at East Layton Bench mesonet site (peak gust of 53 mph, visibility less than 1 mile), and the Shepard Creek mesonet site (peak gust of 52 mph). Many of these mesonet sites also reported temperatures rapidly falling below freezing as this snow squall passed.

Some examples include the I-80 @ mp 78 mesonet site (peak wind gust of 59 mph, visibility below 1/2 of a mile), the I-80 at MP 79 Timpie mesonet site (peak wind gust of 65 mph), the I-80 at MP 81 Dolomite mesonet site (peak wind gust of 56 mph), and the Grantsville South mesonet site (peak wind gust of 54 mph). Many of these mesonet sites also reported temperatures rapidly falling below freezing as this snow squall passed.

events.event_narrative: COOP observers reported snowfall amounts of 21.0 inches in Laketown, and 8.0 inches in Randolph. Additionally, strong winds were noted with the storm. At around 6:20 am MST, a natural avalanche occurred near the Dugway section of Logan Canyon. Per the Utah Avalanche Center report, this slab avalanche of wind-drifted snow started around 6000 feet on a west facing slope, had a vertical run of 150 feet, a width of 80 feet, and a depth of 2 feet. The avalanche hit a car on US-89 and pushed it against a guard rail, but no injuries were reported. This avalanche resulted in closure of US-89 in Logan Canyon between milepost 460 (near Logan) and milepost 490 (near Garden City/Bear Lake) for over 24 hours.

Strong winds were also noted, with several observations at the Snowbasin - Straw Top mesonet site in excess of 70 mph (with a peak gust of 104 mph at 2:30 am MST 1/14), and wind gusts in excess of 70 mph also noted at Logan Peak, Logan Summit, Peter Sinks Rim, and several other mesonet sites.

Baldy and Arrowhead Summit.

Other mesonet stations in the area showed frequent gusts at or above 50, and periods of sustained winds in excess of 40 mph.

A group of several skiers were backcountry skiing in the of Porter Fork area within Millcreek Canyon on Friday, January 12. The group completed multiple runs in the West Porter Fork portion, and on their third ascent, opted to exit Main Porter Fork from West Porter Fork. As they were exiting, an avalanche was triggered, and one of the skiers in the group was unable to get to a safe location before the slide caught and fully buried him. After several minutes of beacon searching, they were able to successfully locate and probe the buried skier approximately 4 feet deep. The group worked quickly to uncover the buried skier, and once uncovered, it was discovered the buried skier was unconscious and was breathing very shallowly. While calling emergency services and deliberating who should preform CPR on the injured skier, the skier gradually began to show improved breathing, and slowly regained consciousness. While further injuries were initially feared, after some time the skier was able to ski out of the area. The Utah Avalanche Center danger rating for the day was listed as High at elevations above 8000 feet, and Considerable at elevations below 8000 feet. Specific timing of the avalanche was not stated, thus event time is estimated.

A group of snowmobilers (estimated at 5 total) were riding in American Fork Canyon Saturday January 13 at an elevation of approximately 10000 feet on a northeast aspect. An avalanche was unintentionally triggered, catching 3 of the members, resulting in partial burial of 2 members, and full burial of 1 member. Of the 2 partial burials, one member deployed an airbag and was able to dig themselves out. The other was buried with a hand sticking out, and was able to be immediately dug out by other group members (with no injuries reported). The group member who was fully buried was buried for around 5 minutes before the group could locate and uncover them. They were unconscious and reportedly turning blue, but regained consciousness thereafter with no further injury reported. An avalanche accident and rescue summary was  reported by a third party, and specific timing of the avalanche was not stated, thus the event time is estimated.

events.event_narrative: A period of very strong winds were noted, with some mesonet sites observing both sustained winds in excess of 40 mph for an hour or more, and gusts in excess of 58 mph. The earliest observed high wind gust was noted at the CALLAO GATE mesonet site at 5:35 am MST (60 mph), and the final observed high wind gust was noted at the CAUSEWAY mesonet site at 1:45 pm MST (58 mph). A peak wind gust of 77 mph was observed at the CAMEL BACK MTN mesonet site at 12:05 pm MST. Some additional selected gusts at mesonet sites in the zone included 74 mph at Gunnison Island, 73 mph at I-80 @ mp 29, 71 mph at INTERSTATE 80, and 64 mph at I-80 at MP 1. At least some of the strongest of the gusts may have been partially influenced by convective segments along the advancing cold front. Due to the winds, I-80 was closed from the morning hours of 3/2 onward until winds began to subside behind the frontal passage later in the afternoon. Aside from the winds, accumulating snow was observed at both mountain and lower elevations, but widespread warning amounts were not noted.

The Hans Flat COOP Observer reported wind gusts with a peak gust of 66 mph, as well as downed trees in the area (and graupel from storms associated with the cold front). Two other automated mesonet stations within the forecast zone recorded strong gusts in excess of 50 mph.

A period of very strong prefrontal winds were noted throughout the forecast zone. The BKROCK mesonet site marked the start and end times of wind gusts exceeding high wind criteria, with an initial gust of 59 mph observed 3/1 at 4:09 pm MST, and a final gust of 59 mph observed 3/1 at 4:20 pm MST. The BKROCK mesonet site recorded the peak wind gust of 78 mph 3/2 at 2:57 pm MST. Some additional selected observed gusts at mesonet sites in the zone through the event time included 70 mph at King Canyon, 69 mph at Eureka Ridge, 65 mph at Oak City, and 62 mph at Portable RWIS 5. Many sites recorded multiple wind gusts in excess of 58 mph throughout the event.

A group of three backcountry skiers set out early in the morning to ski in the Big Willow Aprons area near Lone Peak. After skiing for several hours without issue, an unintentionally triggered soft slab avalanche occurred on the north aspect of the slope (approximately 40 degree angle) around 10,600 feet elevation. The avalanche was approximately 18 inches deep, 150 feet wide, and had a vertical run of 800 feet. All three skiers were caught by the avalanche. One skier was partially buried and was able to self-extricate. After self-extricating, the skier attempted to find the transceiver signal of the buried skiers. Approximately 13 minutes after the avalanche, the skier successfully probed one of the buried skiers and uncovered them, but they were ultimately unresponsive when rescue breaths were attempted. In the subsequent minutes, the second buried skier was probed and uncovered, but also found to be unresponsive to any resuscitation attempts. Around 1-1.5 hours after the avalanche, a helicopter ambulance was able to hoist the injured skier out, and this skier was subsequently taken to the hospital and released later in the day. Due to unfavorable weather, search and rescue recovered the deceased skiers bodies the following day.

The US-89 at Park Lane mesonet site also measured the zone's peak wind gust during the event, with a gust of 66 mph observed 5/10 at 1:15 am MST. Between 5:15 am MST and 6:15 am MST 5/10, the US-89 at Park Lane mesonet site also measured a period of sustained winds at or above 40 mph. Finally, some additional selected observed gusts at mesonet sites in the zone through the event time included 64 mph at CENEWS, 64 mph at KJ7NO-2 Farmington, 60 mph at Centerville, and 59 mph at US-89 at MP 406 Weber River. Many sites recorded multiple wind gusts in excess of 58 mph throughout the event. Given this was a downslope-style wind event, the highest concentration of sustained winds and gusts were closer to the terrain rather than spread further across the zone.

This heat burst was characterized by a period of severe wind gusts, with the Ogden-Hinckley Airport ASOS recording a period of gusts to 78 mph, followed by a final gust to 64 mph before winds subsided. Temperatures initially around 75F or so prior to winds increasing peaked at 83F during the strongest winds. Broadcast media disseminated a picture of a large tree toppled and on a car near the Cotton Bottom Restaurant near the mouth of Big Cottonwood Canyon. Highest winds and gusts throughout the Salt Lake Valley occurred approximately between 1:00 pm MST and 4:00 pm MST, with many observations of gusts in the 30 mph to 45 mph range. At approximately 2:30 pm MST, park rangers and search and rescue units from local law enforcement found and began treating two hikers in Snow Canyon State Park who were suffering from heat exhaustion. While treating the injured hikers, the units were notified by a passerby of an unconscious woman nearby. First responders subsequently located the unconscious woman, ultimately determining her to be deceased. Temperatures around the park at the time ranged from 107F at a CWOP site in Ivins to 99F at a higher elevation site near Yellow Knoll. The St George Regional Airport AWOS  was reporting temperatures of around 104F at the time. Excessive Heat Warnings were in effect for several days leading up to and during the event, and Snow Canyon State Park had been running a Drink Up campaign with signs at trailheads urging recreators to stay hydrated and limit outdoor activity during the hottest times of day.

A 38-year-old man drowned Saturday in the waters of the northwest portion of Willard Bay during stormy conditions. This individual attempted to rescue another who went into the water to rescue another who had a life jacket. Nearby wind gusts with an associated outflow boundary ranged from 28 mph (Willard POE RWIS, located just east of Willard Bay) to 32 mph (Great Salt Lake Minerals Site, located just SW of Willard Bay). Small showers with microbursts were also observed in the area, which may have also impacted Willard Bay, in addition to the more consolidated outflow boundary that was moving through the Northern Wasatch Front from south to north during the afternoon.

Around 430 p.m., three paddleboarders were near the dock at Quail Creek Reservoir when gusty winds pushed them away from the dock. They were not wearing life vests. Two of the people were able to swim back and reach the shore, but a third person was later found unconscious and unresponsive by Quail Creek State Park rangers. The individual, a 50-year-old male, was pronounced dead on the scene. The closest observation, from the White Reef RAWS, indicated southwest winds sustained at 26 mph, gusting to 41 mph at 5 p.m. Note that RAWS report the highest gusts for the previous hour.

A pickup truck collided head-on with a semitrailer after the driver of the pickup truck lost control on state Route 96. Archived liquid precipitation measurements suggest around 0.2-0.5 had fallen in the area by that point, with National Operational Hydrologic Remote Sensing Center data indicating a snow depth of 2-4 inches at the time of the crash.

Snow Squall. Wyoming DOT and the public reported Interstate 80 Westbound closure near milepost 13 due to multiple crashes and a pileup as a result of a snow squall. In the hour preceding the incidents WYDOT RWIS sensors at West Divide and Painter recorded heavy snow and visibility down to between one quarter and one eighth of a mile with an accompanying flash freeze. Gusty winds did not accompany these squalls. Time is approximate.

At approximately 10:02 pm, a Toyota Prius travelling southbound on I-15 lost control and hit a concrete barrier near milepost 354, eventually coming to rest facing sideways on the interstates shoulder. A male passenger exited the car, while the female passenger remained and opened her door. A second vehicle, a Ford Expedition, hit the male outside of the car and then crashed into the passenger side of the Prius head-on, killing the female passenger. The male passenger outside of the car was transported to the hospital in critical condition. The 2 left lanes of southbound I-15 were closed for an undisclosed amount of time for accident investigation, with Utah Highway Patrol ultimately believing weather to be the primary factor. During the time around the accident, lake enhanced snow showers were moving through the area, with a nearby DOT sensor reporting moderate to heavy snowfall, slushy road conditions, pavement temperatures dropping below freezing, and snowfall rates of a half inch per hour.

events.cz_name: BEAR LAKE AND BEAR RIVER VALLEY
events.event_narrative: A storm total snowfall of 8.2 inches at Laketown COOP, 6.5 inches at Woodruff COOP, and 5.9 inches at Randolph.
A storm total snowfall of 9.0 inches at Weber Basin Pump Plant COOP, 7.4 inches at Bountiful Bench COOP, and 6.6 inches at Bountiful CoCoRAHS.

Per Utah Highway Patrol, a crash involving 14 vehicles occurred, closing down all northbound lanes of I-15 in Spanish Fork for at least 30 minutes, after which point some flow of traffic resumed. One driver was reportedly transported to a hospital in stable condition. Light snow showers associated with the final portion of a winter system were ongoing around this time, likely with some periods of lake induced enhancement. Nearby, the Spanish Fork Municipal Airport AWOS (KSPK) reported deteriorated conditions ahead of the incident, with observations nearest the time of the incident indicating snow and freezing fog with visibility of 0.25 miles.

Two boys fell through ice into Glasmann Pond in South Ogden while fishing, approximately around 4:30 pm LST. While one was able to get out, the other was rescued by divers and later passed from the injuries sustained. Temperatures nearby reported from the Ogden-Hinckley Airport ASOS (KOGD) around the time of the incident were 39F, with clear skies reported. The maximum temperature that day (1/27) was 40F, the prior day (1/26) was 40F, and one more day prior (1/25) was 35F.

A snowfall accumulation of 29.0 inches with 3.51 inches of snow water equivalent was measured at Snowbasin. Other snowfall accumulations include 23.0 inches with 3.20 inches of snow water equivalent at Powder Mountain.

Sometime during the day, a party of backcountry skiers started a day in Big Cottonwood Canyon, eventually working their way up to the Park City ridgeline. The skiers then planned a descent into the Katie's area. One of the skiers started a descent, causing a hard slab to break approximately 30 ft above them on the second turn of their run. This avalanche caused the skier to be pulled into a chute in the woods, and carried the skier an estimated 500 ft. The skier was able to extract themselves from the snow, and while a life flight had been called, the skier reportedly only suffered minor injuries and significant bruising, and emergency services deemed to be not needed.
Several SNOTEL stations including USU Doc Daniel, Powder Mountain, and Ben Lomond Peak recorded from 1.4 to 4.6 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 19 to 55 inches of snow.

A report of a skier who failed to return home by 500 pm MST was received by Summit County Dispatch on the evening of the event 3/7. A search and rescue operation was started that evening, and crews found evidence of a recent slide, but due to reportedly extremely hazardous conditions the crews had to wait to until the following morning. Search and continue the search rescue crew ultimately found the body of a deceased 51 year old man at 1049 am MST, with a determination that he had been caught in the avalanche on a steep northeast aspect of Hoyt Peaks NE bowl. A forecaster with the Utah Avalanche Center stated that warm and strong spring sunshine may have been a contributing factor to reactivate multiple weak layers buried beneath the current snowpack. A nearby SNOTEL, Beaver Divide, recorded 1.1 inches of water from the start of the event through 500 pm MST 3/7, which at a reasonable 13 to 1 snow to liquid ratio would equate to 14.3 inches of snow. The closest SNOTEL, Redden Mine LWR, through the same time period recorded 2.5 inches of water, or at the same ratio approximately 32.5 inches of snow.

Utah Highway Patrol troopers reported a crash occurred shortly after 6:30 a.m. on the southbound side of U.S. Highway 89 in Fruit Heights. All 20 vehicles involved were headed south when the pileup occurred. Authorities said drivers were traveling too fast for the slick, snow-covered roads. Around the same time, a separate crash involving nine vehicles occurred on the northbound side of the highway. Troopers stated weather was a contributing factor in this crash as well, and some drivers may have lost control while looking toward the earlier southbound pileup. At the time of the event, light snow had created accumulations in spots on area roads.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: A period of high winds accompanied a frontal passage into western Utah. The first high wind gust was observed at 7:10 PM MST at the I-80 @ mp 1 mesonet station with a gust of 64 mph. The highest wind gusts recorded occurred at the Wendover Port of Entry mesonet station at 7:15 PM MST and at the I-80 @ mp 29 mesonet station at 7:40 PM MST, with gust magnitudes at both peaking at 67 mph. The final high wind gust was recorded at the Wendover Peak mesonet station at 9:30 PM MST with a gust of 61 mph. Several other mesonet stations observed high wind gusts within this period as well.

A period of strong post-frontal winds were observed in terrain adjacent locations in Castle Country. The Emery County EM reported that in the town of Emery 2 houses lost roofing materials, 1 house lost its roof, and in one location approximately 50 ft of vinyl fence was blown over. The EM also reported that there were overturned semi trucks on I-70 in this time period, likely due to the strong winds. The MUDDY CREEK NEAR EMERY 4N mesonet station recorded a peak gust of 57 mph at 1:15 PM MST. The FREMONT JUNCTION mesonet station recorded a peak gust of 73 mph at 11:30 PM MST, and also observed several hours of winds roughly gusting in the 60-70 mph range.

Numerous public and spotter reports of snowfall accumulations between 2 to 9 inches were received throughout the day. Given the onset time of snow, adverse to dangerous driving conditions were observed during the morning commute hours particularly, with numerous accidents and slide-offs reported.

Several SNOTEL stations including Cascade Mountain, Mill-D North, and Atwater recorded from 1.6 to 2.6 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 19 to 34 inches of snow. Additionally, many snow safety community partners, including those within the Utah Department of Transportation, observed snow water equivalent ranging from approximately 1.2 to 2.1 inches, resulting in 18 to 32 inches of snow. Finally, high winds were also observed at some of the Higher Peaks of the Wasatch such as Hidden Peak and Mount Baldy, with a peak gust of 102 mph recorded.

Law enforcement in addition to the Utah Avalanche Center reported a natural avalanche in Little Cottonwood Canyon between Snowbird and Alta, which resulted in the partial burial of 3 vehicles containing a total of 5 or 6 passengers. No injuries were reported, and the main canyon road was reopened at approximately 7:30 PM MST.

Two individuals went out on the water at Willard Bay State Park on an inflatable raft during the afternoon of Saturday, August 2. Outflow winds from thunderstorms near the Utah-Idaho border pushed through Willard Bay area around 4:20 p.m. with wind gusts at nearby weather stations reported to be as high as 25-30 mph with the initial pass of the boundary. Winds remained elevated out of the northwest, with gusts upwards of 25-35 mph around 1.5 hours following the outflow boundary. The two individuals on the raft were reported to have been thrown off the raft when the boundary came through. One person resurfaced while the other did not.

Perry Police Department was called to Perry Park just before 5 PM Wednesday, June 11 for reports of traumatic injuries due to a large tree branch falling on two individuals. One individual, an 80-year old woman, died on the scene. The other individual, a 28-year old woman, was transported to the hospital in serious condition. There were no thunderstorms in the vicinity of Perry during this time, but strong thunderstorms capable of producing strong outflow winds were ongoing over southeast Idaho. Outflow winds from those distant thunderstorms produced wind gusts in the 30-40 mph range, but it is unknown if the strong winds were the direct cause of the tree branch falling.

The Forsyth Fire started on Thursday, June 19th, 2025. Initial reports from fire officials state the fire is suspected to have originated as a holdover from lightning in the Pine Valley Mountains. A long stretch of hot, dry, and windy conditions prevailed ahead of the fire's discovery on the 19th. A nearby RAWS station in Pine Valley (TT900) observed Red Flag conditions (wind gusts >25 mph and RH <15%) for about 16 hours from the afternoon of the 19th to the early morning hours on the 20th. A mandatory evacuation order for the Pine Valley community was issued at 9:21 PM on the 19th. Red Flag conditions redeveloped late morning on the 20th, with strong southwest winds eventually pushing the fire into the community of Pine Valley. Washington County Sheriff reports 14 homes and 4 outbuildings destroyed in Pine Valley despite mitigation efforts. Red Flag conditions continued June 21st with the TT900 RAWS station reporting wind gusts upwards of 44 mph with RH in the single digits to teens. This resulted in the fire spreading to the north side of the valley and making a run at the communities of Grass Valley and Pinto, which were placed in an evacuation order at 5:37 PM on June 21st. Evacuation orders were lifted at 10 AM Friday, June 27. A total of 15,563 acres were affected by the wildfire.

The Redwest Music Festival, being held at the Utah State Fairpark, was paused and crowds were evacuated preemptively around 5 p.m. Saturday due to a cold front approaching the area. It is estimated that 60,000 people attended each day of the three day event. The cold front brought wind gusts from 35-50 mph at the nearest sensors starting around 5:15 p.m. Wind gusts in that range continued through around 7 p.m. Following the cold front, thunderstorms tracked into the area, bringing lightning and moderate to heavy rain. Thunderstorms diminished around 8 p.m. with rain through around 9:30 p.m. The event was called off around 9:30 p.m. due to unsafe conditions. The event remain paused with the fairpark evacuated through then. News reports say that a woman was taking shelter in a vehicle parked near the fairpark at 1055 W. North Temple St. Some reports say she was in the vehicle and had exited, while others say she had evacuated the festival and was standing outside the vehicle. A large plank from scaffolding of a nearby construction site was blown off, striking the woman and the vehicle. The woman died from the injuries.

For example, a Utah Department of Transportation RWIS reported periods of deteriorated conditions from around sunrise to early afternoon, with peak snowfall rates near 2 per hour, visibility at times to near 1/4 mile (and frequently below 2 miles), and periodic slush-ups on I-215.

Several SNOTEL stations including Ben Lomond Peak, Lightning Ridge, and Garden City Summit recorded from 1.5 to 3.2 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 19 to 40 inches of snow.

Utah Highway Patrol reported numerous traffic accidents on I-15 between approximately the Nephi exit and roughly two miles northward. The volume of accidents resulted in the southbound lanes of I-15 being closed and traffic being detoured through the city itself. The winter weather is assumed to be the likely cause of the incident.

Law enforcement (including dispatch, fire department, and other associated first responders) responded to a report of a collision between a semi truck and passenger vehicle on I-15 southbound near mile marker 384 shortly before 1:30 pm. Thereafter numerous other rollover and collision accidents were reported between mile marker 383 to 387. A total of two individuals were transported for medical attention with minor injuries. Winter weather is assumed to be the cause.
