In addition to strong winds throughout the zone, a trained spotter reported a wind gust to 60 mph recorded on a personal weather station early in the morning.

A powerful winter storm brought heavy snow and strong winds to the area. Reported snow observations include 27 inches of snow in the Logan Mountains (3.1 inches water), 23 inches of snow at Powder Mountain (2.5 inches water), and 18 inches of snow at Snowbasin - Base (1.9 inches of water). Additionally, several SNOTEL stations including Lightning Ridge, Ben Lomond Peak, and Monte Cristo recorded from 1.6 to 2.7 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 21 to 37 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 97 mph at Snowbasin - Straw Top, 78 mph at Snowbasin - Strawberry Tower 15, and 76 mph at Ogden Peak. Inclement conditions also resulted in widespread winter driving conditions along higher elevation routes. Examples include a multi-vehicle pileup on I-80 near the Wyoming border, closure of Sardine Canyon for road snow mitigation, and numerous accidents and slide-offs on I-80 through Parleys Canyon. Incidences of additional accidents and slide-offs are noted elsewhere through the zone.

A powerful winter storm brought heavy snow and strong winds to the area. Reported snow observations include 47 inches of snow at Alta - Collins (4.7 inches water), 36 inches of snow at Brighton Crest (3.7 inches water), 32 inches of snow at Solitude (3.3 inches water), and 28 inches of snow at Park City Mountain (2.7 inches of water). Additionally, SNOTEL stations including Thaynes Canyon and Mill-D North recorded from 2.2 to 2.4 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 31 to 34 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 103 mph at Arrowhead Summit, 96 mph at Hidden Peak, and 84 mph at Alta - Mt Baldy. A prolonged period of intense snow rates at or in excess of 3 inches per hour along with the strong winds 2/18 resulted in premature closure of area ski resorts, and full closure of both Big Cottonwood Canyon and Little Cottonwood Canyon. Little Cottonwood Canyon remained closed into the following morning for avalanche mitigation. Numerous slide-offs and accidents were also reported in the Cottonwood canyons in addition to Provo Canyon.

Several SNOTEL stations including Lily Lake, Lakefork #1, and Chalk Creek #1 recorded from 1.1 to 2.6 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 16 to 37 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 93 mph at Windy Peak, 86 mph at Lofty Lake Peak, and 78 mph at Chepeta.

Several SNOTEL stations including Timberline, Clear Creek #2, and Daniels-Strawberry recorded from 0.9 to 2.2 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 13 to 30 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 78 mph at Monument Peak and 76 mph at Soldier Summit Ridge. Additionally, numerous accidents and slide-offs were reported along US-40.

Several SNOTEL stations including Seely Creek, Upper Joes Valley, and Red Pine Ridge recorded from 0.9 to 1.5 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 12 to 21 inches of snow. Some peak wind gust observations through the event include 84 mph at Signal Peak, 80 mph at Scipio Summit, and 76 mph at Bull Claim Hill. Multiple vehicle accidents and slide-offs were also reported along I-70.
Several SNOTEL stations including Lonesome Beaver, Gardner Peak, and Webster Flat recorded from 0.9 to 3.2 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 13 to 44 inches of snow.

Combination of spotter and public sources indicated widespread snowfall amounts in excess of 6 inches across much of the Cache Valley, with some specific reports including 7 inches in Hyrum, 9 inches at Logan 0.9 NNE, and 10.5 inches at Logan Radio KVNU. Impacts were significant enough the Utah State University in Logan canceled classed for the day.

A combination of report sources indicated widespread snow amounts of 3 to 7 inches across many portions of the zone. Strong winds widespread in excess of 40 mph (peak gust of 75 mph at 9:00 AM at Cedar City Municipal Airport) combined with periods of very heavy snow resulted in snow squall conditions with visibility in some areas reduced to less than one quarter of a mile. Numerous accidents and slide-offs were reported, especially along higher sections of I-15.

Just following noon two children and their father entered a backcountry area by leaving the Brighton Ski area boundary west of the Crest lift. One of the children, an 11 year old female ahead of her other family members, traversed into the backcountry along an apron above Rock Garden towards the Mary Main bowl at which time bystanders on the ridge reported that an avalanche released above her. She was reported to have been caught and carried over 200 feet, becoming buried just downhill of a tree. Bystanders quickly called Brighton Ski Patrol and 911. The family did not have avalanche rescue equipment, and attempted to use phone location to narrow the burial location. With the aid of a ski dog, Brighton Ski Patrol located the girl roughly 17 minutes after initial burial. Rescuers performed CPR, but poor weather conditions prevented helicopter transport from landing. She was transported by ambulance for emergency care, but succumbed to her injuries.

Wyoming Highway Patrol in addition to other law enforcement and first responders reported that a multi-vehicle accident occurred on I-80 near Evanston at mile marker 18 at approximately 3:00 PM 2/18/26. The crashes are said to have happened more or less simultaneously, involving 32 vehicles (20 semi trucks, 12 passenger vehicles), which blocked and closed both the westbound and eastbound lanes. The interstate was closed from mile marker 6 to mile marker 34, lasting from roughly 3:28 PM  until 4:00 AM the following morning. As a result of the collisions, 2 fatalities were confirmed, as were 22 injuries, 3 of which required helicopter transportation to Utah emergency facilities. Additionally, a tractor trailer carrying livestock suffered severe enough impact to kill 6 of the cattle inside. Around the time of the pileup a nearby mesonet sensor was observing conditions including gusts in excess of 30 mph and visibility around one quarter of a mile, likely due to blowing snow. Wyoming Highway Patrol suspects excessive speed for the ongoing poor winter weather conditions to be a likely cause.

In the late afternoon hours a man and his juvenile son were riding snowmobiles in the Snake Creek/Ant Knolls area of the Wasatch Mountains roughly between Alta and Midway. The father reportedly became stuck at the bottom of a steep bowl like slope around 4:00 PM, with the son also becoming stuck upon attempting to help. An avalanche released from higher up on the slope, narrowly avoiding the son, but catching and carrying the father and his snowmobile roughly 300 feet down the hill, burying him near a tree under around two feet of snow. The son called 911 and began searching for his father, but by the time he was able to partially unbury his father, the father had passed.

Snow Squall. Numerous mesonet sensors across southwest Utah reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts between 30 to 60 mph, visibility between 0.10 to 0.25 miles, and very low road grips indicative of a flash freeze. Multiple crashes were reported near mile post 54 and resulted in 2 minor injuries. 4 semi trucks were involved in the accident, and one jackknifed.

events.cz_name: BEAR LAKE AND BEAR RIVER VALLEY
events.event_narrative: Snow Squall. Mesonet sensors reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts between 40 to 50 mph, visibility around 0.10 miles, and very low road grip indicative of a flash freeze.

Snow Squall. Numerous mesonet sensors across the southern mountains reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts between 30 to 60 mph, visibility as low as 0.07 miles, and very low road grips indicative of a flash freeze.

Snow Squall. Mesonet sensors across the Bryce Canyon area reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts between 30 to 40 mph, visibility of 0.25 miles, and very low road grips indicative of a flash freeze.
Snow Squall. Mesonet sensor in the Bryce Canyon area reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts to 33 mph, and visibility of 0.25 miles.
Snow Squall. Mesonet sensor across the southern mountains reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts of 38 mph, visibility of 0.07 miles.

Snow Squall. Mesonet sensor in the western Canyonlands area reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts of 32 mph, visibility of 0.24 miles, and low road grips indicative of slick roads.
Snow Squall. Numerous mesonet sensors across eastern Millard County reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, and wind gusts between 30 to 40 mph.

Snow Squall. Numerous mesonet sensors across the central mountains reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts between around 30 to 40 mph, visibility between 0.18 to 0.25 miles, and low road grips indicative of snow covered roads.
Snow Squall. Mesonet sensor in the Sevier Valley near Richfield reported snow squall conditions, including heavy snow, wind gusts of 45 mph, and visibility of 0.25 miles.

A cold frontal passage followed by several hours of snow showers, including a corridor of lake enhanced snow with snowfall rates at times in excess of 1 inch per hour, brought significant winter weather impacts to portions of the Salt Lake valley. Accumulation amounts varied throughout the valley, with generally around 1 to 4 inches (closer to 6 inches on benches), with the higher totals noted at areas that sat beneath the lake enhanced snow showers. The combination of the snow on 2/18 and subsequent refreeze overnight into the morning of 2/19 resulted in hundreds of motor vehicle accidents, some of which included Utah Highway Patrol vehicles. No fatalities or major injuries were reported. Rocky Mountain Power reported power outages across the valley peaked at over 28,000 customers. The Center Weather Service Unit reported major impacts (quoted as likely a top 5 event) to operations at the Salt Lake City International Airport, including a ground delay from FAA command center, temporary runway closure due to snow, and around 38 to 42 flight diversions due to the combination of the snow and strong crosswinds.

Several SNOTEL stations including Sun Ranch, Little Grassy, and Kolob recorded from 1.0 to 2.1 inches of snow water equivalent, resulting in approximately 13 to 29 inches of snow. 16 inches of snow was also reported in Duck Creek Village.
Combination of COOP reports and other observations showed snowfall measurements including 10 inches in Orderville, 10 inches in Kanab, 8.7 inches in Kodachrome Basin Park, and 7 inches in Tropic.

A group of seven snowbikers met in Big Cottonwood Canyon and the Guardsmans Pass trailhead with the intention to ride in the area during the afternoon. Most of the group had extensive backcountry, including formal avalanche training, and members of the group were equipped with transceiver (though no transceiver check was performed), probe, shovel, and avalanche airbag. While they were aware of the conditions, including considerable avalanche danger rating (per Utah Avalanche Center), they set out planning to stick to low-angle slopes in Caribou Basin which they knew well. While riding, they observed numerous avalanches, and noted the loose underlying snow characteristics when getting one member unstuck from deep snow. After taking a break, the group decided to do one more session around the basin before returning to the trailhead. The group set out and subsequently regrouped, but noticed one member was missing. They backtracked and found a spot where a fresh avalanche had overrun an area which they had ridden. The members called 911 and began a transceiver search, but could not find a signal given the large debris pile. Eventually after several minutes, one member spotted the missing member's snowbike. The group began spot probing, but were unsuccessful. Wasatch Search and Rescue and AirMed responded to the site, but due to conditions getting dark and the likelihood further avalanche mitigation would be required for rescuer safety, rescue efforts were halted for the night. Multiple agencies resumed rescue efforts, and avalanche mitigation was performed. In time an avalanche dog located the missing member, and the victim was found deceased beneath roughly 2 feet of snow. The victim was wearing an avalanche transceiver, but it was not turned on. Additionally, the avalanche airbag the victim had been wearing had not been deployed.

Two skiers left the Butler Fork trailhead in Big Cottonwood Canyon Saturday morning 2/21 with the plan to do a run known as The Triangle. This is in Butler Basin, a Big Cottonwood Canyon drainage east of Gobblers Knob. The skiers ascended a steep north-facing slope next to the desired run, when near the top an avalanche broke. Both skiers were caught and carried around 100 feet down the slope, becoming fully buried at the bottom. Other groups of skiers in the basin witnessed the avalanche occur, and notified 911, Alta Central, and began rescue efforts. Around 10 minutes after the avalanche, one of the bystanders made their way to the debris, conducted a beacon search, and eventually found a splitboard binding still attached. Additional bystanders arrived and helped uncover the first victim, cleared their airway, allowing them to breathe and gain consciousness. The victim had suffered a leg injury, but was moved to a safer location. Around this time others began transceiver searching for the other victim, eventually exposing the boot. The skier was buried around 150 cm and face down. The second victim was unburied and CPR efforts were initiated. An EMT was longlined to assist the first victim who had regained consciousness, and the second victim was airlifted from the scene but later succumbed to their injuries.
The Gunnison Ridge mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 58 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
Heavy rain caused a large flash flood on North Creek flowing out of Zion National Park. Flows increased on the Virgin River, north of the town of Virgin, from 54 cfs to 2562 cfs.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused flash flooding in Snow Creek Canyon. This drainage eventually flows into the Santa Clara River.
Park rangers in Zion National Park reported flooding in Hop Canyon.

Rainfall in Croton Canyon above Lake Powell produced a large flash flood that ran over a dirt road in area. Glen Canyon dispatch received reports from boaters of large amounts of debris from the drainage flowing into Lake Powell.
A flash flood occurred in Quail Creek, above I-15 near Hurricane. Rainfall amounts estimated by radar were as high as 2.9 inches in many areas.
Law enforcement reported flooding across SR-24 near Caineville due to heavy rain on Caineville Wash.

A rapid and very large river rise on the Dirty Devil River occurred on the morning of August 8th, topping out at 8400 cfs.  This flood was due to heavy rainfall the day before in the Little Wild Horse Canyon area in the San Rafael Swell.
Flash flooding was reported in the town of New Harmony. Radar estimates of rainfall over the area averaged around 4 inches for the day, with estimates as high as 7 inches.
Park Rangers reported water flowing over Notom Road near Capitol Reef National Park.
Heavy rain in the Henry Mountains caused flash flooding on multiple forest service roads south of Hanksville.
A spotter in Grantsville reported 0.75 inch diameter hail.
A member of the public reported 1.00 inch hail in Herriman. In addition, an airline pilot near Riverton reported nickel size hail (0.88 inches in diameter) fifteen minutes later.

Nickel size hail (0.88 inches in diameter) fell near East Millcreek, but the NWS employee at the location reported that the hail fell apart as it hit the ground. In addition, hailstones with a diameter of 1.00 inch were reported by a member of the public in a similar location.
One inch diameter hail was reported near Riverton.
Heavy rain caused large scale flash flooding along the Paria River drainage, including the Wawheap and Big Water areas.
The Syracuse mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 59mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of convective snow showers moving through the area.
The Ogden Airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 61mph.
A trained spotter reported broken tree branches knocked down by severe wind gusts from a thunderstorm near the Ogden Country Club.
A trained spotter discovered a power pole that was snapped by associated severe wind gusts from a thunderstorm that had fallen onto a vehicle.
A trained spotter reported medium sized tree branches that were snapped from severe wind gusts from an associated thunderstorm.
A trained spotter discovered multiple snapped trees from severe wind gusts associated from a thunderstorm within Leavitts Mortuary and  Aultorest Memorial Park in Ogden.
A trained spotter reported that a street light was knocked over by severe wind gusts associated with a thunderstorm.
A severe thunderstorm wind gust to 60mph was measured at the I-15 at MP 333 Antelope Drive UDOT RWIS sensor.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 hail.
A severe thunderstorm wind gust of 61mph was recorded at Hat Island by Mesonet station HATUT.
Public reported 1.25 hail via MPING near Logan, UT.

The tornado is estimated to have touched down at 2:25PM MT approximately 1 mile south of the Sink Rd./HWY 89 intersection in far northwestern Rich county. The tornado promptly produced EF-1 damage snapping a few softwood trees. The tornado continued tracking north along the terrain into Cache county, increasing in width and producing a notably wider swath of softwood tree damage consistent with an EF-1 rating. The tornado then took a slight turn to the northeast and slightly weakened, producing a few more instances of EF-1 damage to softwood trees before dissipating in far southern Cache county at around 2:27PM. The maximum width of this tornado was 100 yards with a path length of 0.44 miles. Special thanks to the Cache and Rich county emergency managers for the assistance getting to the damage location, and another special thanks to our local spotters for reporting the damage.
A severe wind gust to 60mph was recorded by an ASOS station at Hill Air Force Base.
Public reported a large tree snapped at the base following a severe wind gust from an associated thunderstorm.
Public reported a large branch to around 6 inches in diameter was snapped from a severe wind gust associated with a thunderstorm. A photo was shared on social media.
A 59mph severe wind gust associated with a thunderstorm was measured by the CENWWS UPR weather station.
A 58mph severe wind gust associated with a thunderstorm was measured by the Milford Municipal Airport ASOS station.
A wind gust to 64mph was measured by the I-15 at Pine Creek Hill UDOT Mesonet station.
Goblin Valley State Park rangers reported all area dry washes and slot canyons were running. Chute Canyon wash was flooding across Wild Horse road. Time estimated.

Emery county emergency management reported an ongoing flood and search and rescue  operation in Little Wildhorse Slot Canyon. Water was at least 1 to 2 feet deep with locally deeper water. Rescue was successful with no significant injuries reported.
Back country rangers reported a flash flood on a road along Last Chance Creek, which flows into Lake Powell.
Additional flooding in the lower Paria River drainage closed the Cottonwood Canyon Road.

Landspout. Location:  41.940N, -112.660W. A brief landspout occurred near Snowville, UT along I-84. It was recorded by the public and discovered on social media. No damage was reported from this short lived landspout as it occurred over an open field.

A strong thunderstorm brought multiple severe gusts measured by the Evanston-Uinta County Airport - Burns Field ASOS. The first severe gust, which occurred at 1455, was measured at 59mph. This was then followed by a gust to 64mph at 1457, followed by the third and final severe gust to 64mph at 1502 as multiple storms tracked over Evanston, WY.
A strong thunderstorm produced a severe wind gust to 69mph at the N7SHZ Medicine Butt Mountain WY US CWOP site.
A strong thunderstorm produced a severe gust to 66mph at the WYDOT First Divide sensor.
A strong thunderstorm produced multiple severe wind gusts to 58mph at the WYDOT I80 - Coal Road sensor.
A strong thunderstorm produced multiple severe wind gusts at the VERNE1 UPR station. The first two severe wind gusts were to 70mph, followed by the third and final gust to 60mph.
A strong thunderstorm produced a severe wind gust to 62mph at the Grantsville South Pacificorp sensor.

Waterspout. Location: 40.820N, -112.27W. Two waterspouts were photographed over the Great Salt Lake and promptly posted to social media by the public. Exact location and time are estimated based off observations, radar, and all photos shared on social media.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding along the Escalante tributaries of Pine Creek and Wide Hollow drainages, north of Escalante. The Escalante River gauge rose to 1088 cfs.

A strong wind gust associated with a passing cold front resulted in a semi truck blow over on I-15, which resulted in another car being pinned. Wind speeds were estimated using nearby stations, generally ranging from 35-55mph at the time of occurrence. The truck driver was reported to have sustained minor injuries.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: A strong cold front traversed across northern UT in the early morning hours bringing numerous wind gusts in excess of 58mph at sites such as Hat Island, UDOT I-80, UDOT I-80 at MP 1, and I-80 at MP 40 Knolls. The highest observed wind gust within this forecast zone was measured to be 67mph at the Wendover Peak site.

A strong cold front traversed across northern UT in the early morning hours bringing numerous wind gusts in excess of 58mph at sites such as South Mountain, UDOT SR-201 at I-80, and Pacificorp Kennecott Rd. Lake Point. The highest observed wind gust within this forecast zone was measured to be 70mph at the South Mountain site.

A strong cold front traversed across northern UT in the early morning hours bringing numerous wind gusts in excess of 58mph to Davis county, particularly the Syracuse, UT area where a peak gust to 58mph was measured at the University of Utah Syracuse site.

Widespread flash flooding occurred across much of Kane County. Flooding impacted the Cottonwood Canyon Road, as well as multiple other roads throughout the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

A strong cold front traversed across northern UT in the early morning hours bringing numerous wind gusts in excess of 58mph at sites such as UDOT I-15 at I-80, Monroe Canyon, and UDOT I-80 at MP 107. The highest observed wind gust within this forecast zone was measured to be 69mph at the UDOT I-80 at MP 107 site.

A strong cold front traversed across northern UT in the early morning to southwest WY by the afternoon bringing numerous gusts in excess of 58mph. The highest observed wind gust within this forecast zone was measured to be 59mph at the I-80/US-189 - First Divide and Pacificorp Evanston North sites.
The Callao mesonet site measured a 67 mph wind gust.
The Fish Springs sensor in the Dugway mesonet recorded a 61 mph wind gust.
The Wendover Port of Entry mesonet site recorded a maximum wind gust of 65 mph.
The Gunnison Island mesonet site measured a maximum wind gust of 65 mph.
The University of Utah mesonet site recorded a wind gust of 61 mph.

A line of thunderstorms moved across the Great Salt Lake with several severe wind gusts. The strongest recorded gust was 79 mph at the Lakeside mesonet site. In addition, several sites along the northern Wasatch Front reported damage from these winds, including large tree branches down in Tremonton and large trees down in Brigham City. The strongest wind gust on the east side of the lake was a 77 mph gust recorded at West Warren.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down a large tree and several large tree branches near Layton. Twenty-five minutes later, the Ogden Peak mesonet site recorded a wind gust of 61 mph.

Flash flooding occurred in a small, but popular, slot canyon called Egypt 3, located near the Escalante River in the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. This flooding resulted in two fatalities and two more injuries. ||The drainage of Egypt 3 is very small, measuring approximately 1.2 square miles. The area is void of vegetation and soil, and the underlying parent matter is Navajo Sandstone, which is virtually impermeable. Radar rainfall estimates indicated that approximately 0.2 to 0.4 inches of rain fell on the drainage. Based on calculations after the event, the peak discharge was estimated to be approximately 450 cfs, and the time from the beginning of the rainfall to peak discharge was estimated to be 24 minutes. With the dimensions of the channel, it is probable that the depth of the flood exceeded 20 feet.
The St. George AWOS recorded a wind gust of 59 mph, caused by a thunderstorm in the area.

Ben Lomond SNOTEL received 3.90 inches of precipitation over the two day period, with 3.00 inches of that falling in about 9 hours. This particular site received mostly liquid precipitation, but higher elevation sites received mostly snow, with similar snow water equivalent amounts.
The Snowbird SNOTEL received 1.50 inches of liquid precipitation, including 1.00 inch in 12 hours. Sites above 9,000 feet received all snow.
The Indian Canyon SNOTEL, located at 9,100 feet elevation, received 1.00 inch of precipitation in about 9 hours.
Pickle Keg SNOTEL, located at 9,600 feet, received 1.50 inches of precipitation, including 1.00 inch in 12 hours.
Kolob SNOTEL, at 9,250 feet elevation, received 1.40 inches of precipitation, including 1.00 inch in about 12 hours.
The Flattop Mountain sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph ahead of a cold front.
North Salt Lake received 7 inches of new snow, and Olympus Cove received 6.5 inches of new snow.

Roy and West Haven received 11 inches of new snow for the event, while South Ogden received 8 new inches. Heavy snow and winds knocked down many tree branches and a few small trees in Roy, Bountiful, and surrounding areas, including branches that blocked 5600 South in Roy.
Evanston received 3.5 inches of new snow, and several large trees were knocked down outside Evanston, blocking some county roads.
The Vernon Hill sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 75 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Several sensors in the west deserts recorded strong wind gusts, including 62 mph at Wendover Peak and 58 mph at the English Village sensor in the Dugway mesonet.
Snowbasin received 18 inches of new snow over a 24 hour period.
Alta received a storm total of 46 inches of new snow, while Snowbird and Brighton received 41 and 27 inches respectively.
Chalk Creek #1 SNOTEL received approximately 12 inches of new snow in 12 hours.
A lake effect snow band dropped 6 inches of new snow on North Salt Lake.
A lake effect snow band formed over Salt Lake County, dropping 11.5 inches of snow on Sandy, 9.5 inches at Olympus Cove, 8 inches at Upper Millcreek, and 6 inches of snow in Draper.
Many strong gusts were recorded along the Central Wasatch Peaks, with the highest gust being 111 mph.
Strong winds were recorded over 25 hours at the Chepeta RAWS, with the highest gust being 93 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Lakeside Mountain sensor recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.
The sensor at the Mouth of Parley's Canyon recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.

Damage due to gusty winds was reported one mile east of Logan, where a 15 foot boat and a trailer were both flipped over into a yard. Also, a screen door was ripped off a house, and ten inch diameter tree branches were downed.
A lake effect snow band formed over Salt Lake County, dropping 11.5 inches of snow on Sandy, 9.5 inches at Olympus Cove, 8 inches at Upper Millcreek, and 6 inches of snow in Draper.
The I-15 sensor at Alpine recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Several automated sites in the west deserts of Utah recorded strong wind gusts, including a 63 mph gust at the Playa Station sensor in the Dugway mesonet.
A spotter 2 miles southwest of Logan reported 6 inches of new snow over a 10 hour period.

Significant snow fell across the northern Wasatch Front with the initial cold front, and the snowfall was extended into the morning of December 14th due to lake effect snow. Storm totals for the event included 11 inches of new snow at Layton Bench, 10.5 inches at Bountiful Bench, 9.5 inches at North Salt Lake, and 9 inches of snow at Kaysville.

The majority of the snowfall in the Salt Lake Valley came with the initial cold front on the 13th, with some light snowfall on the 14th due to lake enhancement from the Great Salt Lake. Storm totals for the event included 9.5 inches of new snow in Upper Millcreek, 9 inches in Olympus Cove, and 6.5 inches of snow in Sandy.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Multiple sensors in the Great Salt Lake Desert indicated about 0.40 inches of liquid, or about 4 inches of new snow. These snowy conditions combined with strong winds to create hazardous conditions on I-80. The strongest wind gusts were generally in the 60-66 mph range, including 62 mph at the Playa Station sensor.
Liberty received 17 inches of new snow for the event.
Snowbasin Mid-Bowl received 23 inches of new snow for the storm.
Brighton received 17 inches of new snow from this event, with 12 of those inches falling in 12 hours. Other totals included 16 inches of snow at Alta and 15 inches at Snowbird.
Fillmore and Kanosh both received 6 inches of new snow in about 8 hours. In addition, the sensor at Fish Springs recorded a maximum wind gust of 65 mph during the event.
Cedar City received 7 inches of new snow for the event, most of which fell in only 5 hours with the cold frontal passage.

Following the snow storm the previous day, the Mt. Baldy side of Snowbird resort was open to the public for the first time in the season. Prior to the avalanche, over a period of about 3 hours, an estimated 300 people crossed the starting zone of the avalanche or skied over the slope that eventually slid. At 12:24, a male snowboarder was on the high traverse of Northwest Mt. Baldy and initiated the avalanche. A 27-year-old female, who was hiking up the slope to retrieve a ski, got caught in the avalanche and was buried; she eventually died in the hospital due to injuries sustained from the avalanche.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: New Harmony received a storm total of 22 inches of snow for the event, while Pintura received 13 inches of snow.
Mount Carmel Junction received a storm total of 12 inches of snow.

Kolob SNOTEL received 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent, or approximately 20 inches of new snow for the event. Long Valley Junction also received 1.40 liquid equivalent, much of which fell in a 12-hour period.
New Harmony received a storm total of 17 new inches of snow.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: Pintura received 8 inches of new snow for the event, with 6 of those inches falling in less than 12 hours.
Brian Head received 24 inches of new snow for the event.
Orderville received 8 inches of new snow for the event.
Snowbasin Mid-Bowl received 13 inches of new snow, with gusty winds blowing through much of the event. The strongest winds occurred at the Sherwood Hills sensor, with a maximum wind gust of 75 mph.
Snowbird received a storm total of 9 inches of new snow in windy conditions, with the maximum wind gust along the Central Wasatch Peaks reaching 81 mph.
Logan received 7 inches of new snow over a period of 10 hours.
North Salt Lake Bench received 6 inches of new snow in about 11 hours.
Tooele received 8 inches of new snow for the event. Most of this snow fell on the afternoon of the 19th, with lake effect snow lingering into the 20th.
Eden received a storm total of 10 new inches of snow.

On Christmas Eve morning, the first clear day after several consecutive days under stormy weather conditions, four experienced snowmobilers ventured out into a common snowmobiling area at Logan Peak. They were riding near the summit of the east face of Logan Peak at the head of Providence Canyon, in an area known by local snowmobilers as the Rodeo Grounds, when an avalanche was triggered, catching and killing two of the snowmobilers.

A father and his three sons left the Bear River Service trailhead in the Western Uinta Mountains for a day of snowmobiling on the morning of December 30th. They eventually made their way to Yamaha Hill (which Utah riders call Avalanche Hill), where one of the sons triggered a large avalanche. He got carried by the avalanche and was killed.
Providence received 9 inches of new snow for the storm.
Layton Bench received a storm total of 8 inches of new snow.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Vernon Creek received 1.20 inches liquid for the event, or about 12 inches of snow. Snowville also received 6 inches of snow, and I-84 was closed from Snowville to the Idaho border.
Snowbasin Mid-Bowl received 37 inches of new snow for the event. Also, wind sensors at Snowbasin recorded gusty winds through the event, including a maximum gust of 84 mph.
Much of Utah Valley received a blanket of 8 inches of new snow from the storm, including Springville, Provo BYU, Orem, Payson, and Saratoga Springs.
Liberty received a storm total of 28 inches of new snow.
Brighton Crest received 27 inches of new snow for the event, while Alta received 25 inches and Sundance received 21 inches of snow.
Jupiter Peak received 20 inches of new snow for the event. Winds were also gusty during the snowfall, with the sensor on Ogden Peak recording a maximum wind gust of 90 mph.

Alta UDOT received 37 inches of new snow for the event, with Snowbird receiving 33 inches and Brighton Crest receiving 31 inches of snow. Winds were also gusty during the event, with the maximum wind gust along the Central Wasatch Peaks reaching 80 mph.
Mammoth-Cottonwood SNOTEL received a total of 1.80 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 18 inches new snow.
Midway Valley and Kolob SNOTEL each received 2.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation for the event, or about 30 inches of new snow.
Smithfield received 18 inches of new snow for the event, while Providence received 11 inches of new snow.
Layton Bench received 8 inches of new snow and South Ogden received 7 inches of new snow, with 6 of those inches falling within a 12 hour period.

West Jordan received a storm total of 17 inches new snow, with Upper Millcreek receiving 11 inches and the Salt Lake Airport receiving 9 inches of snow. In addition, winds were gusty during the snowfall, with a 71 mph wind gust recorded at Olympus Cove and a 68 mph wind gust in Sandy.
Spanish Fork received 11 inches of new snow for the storm.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Gusty winds combined with snowfall created hazardous travel conditions across northwest Utah. Multiple wind gusts above 65 mph were recorded, including 70 mph at the Upper Cedar Mountain sensor. In addition, near-blizzard whiteout conditions were reported on the roadways, and I-84 was closed near the Idaho border.
Liberty received a storm total of 22 inches of snow, while Eden received 16 new inches of snow.
New Harmony received a storm total of 8 inches new snow.
Kanab received a storm total of 6 inches new snow.
Alta received a storm total of 37 inches new snow. Snowbird received 24 inches, and Brighton Crest received 22 inches of snow.
Liberty received a storm total of 21 inches new snow.
Snowbasin Mid-Bowl received a storm total of 28 inches of new snow.
Alta and Brighton Crest both received 40 inches of new snow for the storm.
Chalk Creek #1 SNOTEL received a storm total of 4.00 inches liquid equivalent, or approximately 30 inches new snow based on snow ratios at similar elevations.
The Mammoth Cottonwood SNOTEL received 3.10 of liquid equivalent for the storm, or about 24 inches of new snow based on snow ratios at similar elevations.
Kolob SNOTEL received 3.50 inches of new liquid, some of which fell as rain, making the approximate snowfall 25 inches for the storm.
Layton Bench received a storm total of 18 inches new snow. Other totals included 10 inches of snow in South Ogden and 9 inches on the Northeast Ogden Bench.
Snowbasin Mid-Bowl received a storm total of 24 new inches of snow.
Alta received 29 new inches of snow for the storm, while The Canyons received 27 inches and Solitude received 25 inches of new snow.
Chalk Creek #1 SNOTEL received 1.40 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches new snow based on ratios at similar elevations.
Indian Canyon SNOTEL received a storm total of 1.80 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow.

Kolob SNOTEL received 3.60 inches liquid equivalent precipitation and Midway Valley SNOTEL received 2.60 inches liquid equivalent, or about 30-40 inches of new snow over a 2 day period for the southern mountains.

Following several days of fresh snowfall, a skier triggered an avalanche just out-of-bounds of the Snowbasin resort, in the area known as Hell's Canyon. He was caught, carried, and partially buried by the avalanche. By the time other skiers and rescuers got to him, he had already passed away.

A skier triggered an avalanche in an area known as Meadows, a backcountry area in Big Cottonwood Canyon, out-of-bounds of nearby Solitude Ski Resort. The avalanche buried the victim; he was found and dug out less than an hour after the avalanche occurred, but had already passed away.

A man was snowmobiling with some friends on Grandview Peak, east of the city of Bountiful, when he and another man triggered an avalanche. The other man was able to outrun the avalanche on his snowmobile, but the victim was not, and he was buried under about 6 feet of snow. He was buried for approximately 15-18 minutes, before being completely dug out, and was flown to University Hospital in Salt Lake in extremely critical condition. He passed away two days later.

One snowmobiler was killed in an avalanche that he triggered on Sunday, April 4th. He was traveling north along a ridge, when a cornice he was on, cracked and broke off. This caused an avalanche to release below the cornice. He was carried over a cliff band. He was buried approximately 1,000 feet below the ridge under 2 to 3 feet of debris. He was located by his partner with a beacon, and was taken away from the scene via helicopter. However, the helicopter medical crew could not find a pulse, and the man was pronounced dead an hour later.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The strongest winds in the northwest corner of Utah were recorded just as the cold front moved through the area, with the Camel Back Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recording a maximum gust of 63 mph, and the I-80 sensor at Grassey recording a gust of 58 mph.
When the cold front passed through Lake Powell, the Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded gusts above 60 mph for half an hour, with the maximum recorded gust being 63 mph.
The Hat Island sensor recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.
Part of a midsized pear tree was blown down from thunderstorm winds.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches and 1.00 inch were both reported with this storm near Lehi.
Both 1.00 inch hail and 0.75 inch hail were reported across the Salt Lake Valley with this storm.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was reported near North Ogden, with the hail accumulating 2 to 3 inches deep.
The Parleys Canyon sensor recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.
The roof of a carport was blown off near 2000 East and 2700 South.
The sensor in Wellsville recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.
Strong wind gusts recorded in the northern Wasatch Front included 62 mph at the sensor at I-15 at Willard POE, and 59 mph in South Ogden.
The I-80 at Silver Creek Junction sensor recorded a wind gust of 62 mph.
The Signal Peak RAWS recorded a wind gust of 77 mph.

Maximum recorded wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys included 83 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 82 mph at Vernon Hill, 74 mph at South Mountain, 65 mph at Stockton Bar, 65 mph in Baccus, 63 mph at the Lake Point at I-80 sensor, and 61 mph at Olympus Hills. Trees were uprooted in Sandy, tree limbs were broken and shingles were blown off some roofs in Tooele, and a semitrailer truck was knocked over along I-80 just east of Saltair.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The strongest recorded wind gusts in the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains included 83 mph at Hat Island, 72 mph at Rosebud, 70 mph at I-80 at White's Valley, 69 mph at the North Salt Flats sensor, 64 mph at Promontory Point, and 62 mph at the Wendover POE sensor. The major damage in the area occurred near the National Weather Service radar at Promontory Point, where 21 power poles that supply power to the radar were snapped.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 105 mph at Cardiff Peak and 95 mph at Empire Peak in the Deer Valley Resort mesonet.
The U.S. 6 at Eureka sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 88 mph, while the Fish Springs sensor recorded a gust of 60 mph.
Enterprise RAWS recorded multiple wind gusts above 58 mph, including a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
Over a five day period, both Alta Ski Area and Snowbasin Resort received a storm total of 66 inches of snow.
Over a five day period, both Alta Ski Area and Snowbasin Resort received a storm total of 66 inches of snow.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Measured wind gusts across the west desert included 64 mph at Rosebud RAWS, 59 mph at the SR-30 at Curlew Junction sensor, and 58 mph at the Camel Back Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet.
As the northwest pressure gradient tightened behind the cold front on the 5th, winds become gusty again in the southern Wasatch Front, with the sensor in Lehi recording a gust to 58 mph.
The Signal Peak RAWS recorded multiple wind gusts of 78 mph.
The Flattop Mountain RAWS recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Camel Back Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded multiple wind gusts to 58 and 59 mph.

The Richfield Airport AWOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph, with winds greater than 50 mph for 3 hours. Damage near Richfield included an awning that was ripped off of a greenhouse. In another part of town, the arches fell off of a sign for a McDonald's restaurant, landing on a car in the parking lot. That car was totaled, while two other nearby cars had minor damage. In addition, a 14 year old who was in one of the cars at the time, was injured.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was reported in Herriman, Utah.
The Evanston, Wyoming ASOS recorded a wind gust to 58 mph.
The sensor at the Utah Test and Training Range Thermal Treatment Unit recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.

Thunderstorms in Hurricane, Utah damaged two twenty year old trees, with an ash tree being snapped and a plum tree being uprooted. In addition, a building along the street of 600 North received roof damage.
A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded in South Ogden. In addition, some trees and power poles were snapped in Farmington.
The First Divide sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
The Arrowhead sensor at Sundance Resort recorded a maximum wind gust of 78 mph.

Measured wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys included 79 mph at Vernon Hill, 74 mph at Baccus Highway, 67 mph at the University of Utah, 62 mph at the sensor at I-15 at I-215, 62 mph at Point of the Mountain, and 58 mph at the Salt Lake City ASOS.
The sensor in Highland recorded a maximum wind gust of 68 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: High wind reports across the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains included 65 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 64 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 63 mph at Promontory Point, 62 mph at the Causeway sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, and 58 mph at Hat Island.
Recorded wind gusts in west central Utah included 62 mph at the sensor at U.S. 6 at Eureka, as well as 58 mph in Fillmore.
The western Uinta Basin received its strongest winds post-frontally, with the maximum recorded wind gust being 62 mph at U.S. 40 at Starvation.
Maximum wind gusts included 63 mph at the Milford ASOS, 59 mph at the Enterprise RAWS, and 58 mph at the Cedar City ASOS.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: The St. George Airport AWOS recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.

Flooding occurred on both the Black's Fork and the Smith's Fork Rivers, with flooding reported near both Robertson and Mountain View, Wyoming, though not much damage was reported. The Black's Fork river gauge rose the most during this event, peaking at 3642 cfs.

Little Cottonwood Creek flooded for multiple days, with the gauge located on Little Cottonwood Creek at Crestwood Park peaking at 891 cfs on June 7th. Damage was reported in homes, apartments and businesses in Sandy, Cottonwood Heights, Murray and Midvale. Many of these buildings experienced flooding in backyards, basements, patios, and parking areas. Some damage in these areas was avoided due to an extensive sandbagging effort.||Some of the most extensive flood damage occurred in areas of Murray Park, State Street near the park, and surrounding structures to the park, with water as deep as 4 to 5 feet reported in parts of Murray Park. It was in this area that the street flooding was most widespread; multiple lanes of traffic on State Street were closed due to flooding, with water as much as a foot deep in some spots. Flooding also occurred on Vine Street, one block west of State Street.  ||Damage also occurred in Little Cottonwood Canyon, where the creek had cut 20 to 30 feet into the mountain below the road near the mouth of the canyon.

Flooding was reported along the Weber River from Oakley to Hoytsville. The gauge on the Weber River near Oakley exceeded the flood stage of 4.5 feet on June 6th, with flooding continuing into June 10th. The gauge reached a peak of 3179 cfs on the evening of June 8th. ||Damage was reported in the communities of Oakley and Peoa, with water going over the top of some bridges and ending up in homes. Many homes and summer cabins were damaged, especially in basements and yards. Much of the damage occurred to structures at the mouth of the upper Weber River, and in homes along State Route 21 in Oakley. Residents used sandbags in several areas to try to control some of the flooding. Flood waters also ran over a portion of State Route 32, causing the road to close.
The  US-40 at Starvation sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.

A tornado touched down near Wellington, with multiple members of the public seeing the tornado and taking pictures. The tornado damaged a trailer, rolling it over onto its side, and uprooted a few large trees.
After heavy rains passed over the area, park rangers reported water flowing along State Route 24, as well as flash flooding on the Scenic Drive, the Grand Wash, and a few other washes in the area.
Flash flooding was reported along Calf Creek and in surrounding drainages at the headwaters of the Escalante River.

After an estimated rainfall of about 4 inches in 2.5 hours, the Paria River flooded basements in the city of Tropic, and flowed over small bridges leading to nearby residential areas. The flood wave continued down the Paria all the way down to the Utah/Arizona border.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding on Highway 6 near Woodside. Water was running across one lane of the highway, forcing local law enforcement to reduce traffic flow down to one lane until the waters receded.
Flash flooding occurred along Bullfrog Creek. This flooding damaged a dirt road that crosses the creek near its confluence with Lake Powell.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Sheets Gulch, on the eastern edge of Capitol Reef National Park. Water also flowed over the Notom Road, forcing rangers to close the road. People in the area, who observed the flash flooding, described it as a class 4 rapid coming out of the slot canyon.
Thunderstorm winds caused damage in Neola, knocking over several trees and a small barn.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding in multiple slot canyons and high travel areas in Zion National Park. These areas included Lodge Canyon, Pine Creek Canyon, Spry Canyon, Clear Creek, and Highway 9. Three hikers were caught in the Spry Canyon flood and went over two cliffs, the first of which was 40 feet high, and the second 60 feet high. All three men survived the ordeal.
Highway patrol reported one foot of water, as well as mud and debris, across State Route 12 between mileposts 1 and 4.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding on US-89 in Marysville Canyon, near Big Rock Candy Mountain. Mud flowed across the road, blocking traffic and causing several vehicles to get stuck.
Flash flooding occurred in Buckskin Gulch and several surrounding washes.
Rosebud RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
The Vernon Hill RAWS recorded a wind gust of 63 mph.
Local law enforcement reported one inch diameter hail in Santa Clara.
Multiple power lines were reported down in Santa Clara.
The West of Wildcat Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.

Heavy rain fell on the Mill Flat burn scar near New Harmony, causing a debris flow and flash flooding in New Harmony. The flooding emanated primarily from Pinto Creek, and to a lesser extent, from Main, Dam, and Straight Canyons.
Flash flooding caused roads to be damaged and washed out in Croton and Last Chance Canyons. Park rangers could not access these canyons due to the road damage.
Flash flooding was reported in Wahweep Wash and Warm Creek, causing road damage across the area.
Flash flooding occurred along the Skutumpah Road slot canyons, including Johnson Wash.
Extensive flash flooding occurred across the area, including flooding in Croton Canyon, Warm Springs, and other tributaries. Minor flooding also occurred on Wawheap Creek.
Houses and basements were flooded in both Santa Clara and Ivins. In addition, the water flowing over Santa Clara Drive was 1 foot deep and 40 feet wide.
Flash flooding occurred in Red Canyon, with 2 feet of mud and water flowing over Highway 12, making the road impassable.
Flash flooding occurred in Bottom, Gate, and Cottonwood Canyons.  Bulldozers had to clean off nearby roads to open them for business, and some tourists had to be rescued.
Flash flooding in Zion National Park occurred in Keyhole Canyon and Pine Creek Canyon, a technical slot canyon.

Heavy rain over the Lake Fork burn scar caused a flash flood and debris flow, with Highway 89 being covered in water, mud, and rocks near Birdseye. The flood closed the highway in both directions between mile markers 305 and 307, and some cars were stuck in the debris.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding along the Scenic Drive of Capitol Reef National Park, including the Fremont River, Sulphur Creek, the Grand Wash, and Capitol Gorge. People stranded in the Grand Wash had to be rescued.
Heavy rain north of Koosharem caused a mudslide that blocked SR-62 near milepost 40. All lanes along the highway were closed until the slide could be cleaned up.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced very heavy rain, and caused flash flooding along SR-24 between Loa and Koosharem. There were several accidents on the highway as the storm was overhead. Note that this storm also produced severe hail.

Hail, that was estimated to be one inch in diameter, pitted cars traveling along SR-24 near Loa. This storm was slow moving, and 5 inches of hail accumulated in the same area. Several accidents were reported on the highway as the storm was overhead. Note that this storm also caused flash flooding in the area.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding near the Skutumpah Road, damaging the road. As a result, rangers were cut off from traveling throughout the Grand Staircase Escalante National Monument.
Flash flooding occurred at the headwaters of several creeks at the north end of Capitol Reef National Park, with the Fremont River gauge at Caineville rising from 58 cfs to 700 cfs in one hour.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Alvey Wash, North Creek, and many other washes in the area.
Flash flooding was reported along House Rock Valley Road, as well as in Buckskin Gulch, in which water rose to 5 feet high.

Heavy rain caused the Paria River to increase from 20 cfs to 4000 cfs. Travel time on the flood was a little more than 6 hours, with the majority of the rain falling just southeast of Bryce Canyon National Park.

Flash flooding occurred in the Cathedral District on the north end of Capitol Reef National Park. The heavy rain made roads impassable and virtually destroyed them, leaving much of the area impassable until county road crews were able to rebuild the roads.
The Price River gauge rose from 50 cfs to 480 cfs. Widespread rainfall amounts of more than 2 inches in 3 hours were observed in the area.
State park rangers reported that heavy rains washed out roads in multiple locations north of Goblin Valley State Park.
Hail measured to be one inch in diameter was reported in Beaver.
Penny-sized hail, or hail of approximately 0.75 inches in diameter, was reported near Sandy.
Hail stones ranging in size from 0.75 inches to 1 inch in diameter were reported near Highland.
Hail estimated to be 0.75 inches in diameter was reported near Riverton.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was reported in Pleasant Grove.
The WYDOT sensor at First Divide along I-80 reported a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Muddy Creek RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The Lakeside Mountain Snownet sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The White Sage sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 68 mph.
Hail covered the ground near Myton, with the hail stones generally measuring one inch in diameter.
The Locomotive Springs sensor recorded a wind gust of 62 mph.
A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the Gunnison Island sensor.
The Hat Island sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 71 mph.
The Curlew Junction mesonet sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 75 mph.

Heavy rain at the headwaters of the Fort Pearce Wash, with an estimated total of over 3.5 inches of precipitation, caused flash flooding along the wash. The travel time to St. George was  over 6 hours. The Fort Pearce gauge rose from zero to 680 cfs. The golf course attendant at St. George indicated the flood was the greatest he had seen in 6 years.
The Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The English Village sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.
The Fish Springs sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
Strong thunderstorm winds caused damage in Richmond, snapping trees and telephone poles.

A very large flash flood occurred in the Buckskin Gulch and the Paria River. The river gauge further downstream, at Lee's Ferry in Arizona, recorded a rise on the Paria from 25 cfs to 5620 cfs in less than two hours.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding on Wahweap Creek.

Flash flooding occurred in numerous slot canyons in the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, including Moody Wash, East Moody Canyon, and Middle Moody Canyon. In addition, multiple roads were made impassable due to the flooding.

Flash flooding occurred in Twenty-five Mile Wash. In addition, roads were impassable in the surrounding area, including damage to Hole-in-the-Rock road, further north than the road was damaged earlier in the day.

Multiple slot canyons were flooded on the western edge of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, including Coyote Gulch. Roads were impassable near Coyote Gulch and Sunset Flats, and Hole-in-the-Rock road sustained damage.
Heavy rain caused a flash flood at the Ivie Creek rest area, located at mile post 87 along I-70, with water and debris flowing into the rest area.
Flash flooding occurred in Grand Wash in Capitol Reef National Park, with water 6 to 8 feet deep in Grand Wash, as well as water from Grand Wash flowing across the Scenic Drive.
After 1.5 to 2.0 inches of rain fell near Parowan, flash flooding occurred on SR-143, with two feet of water and debris crossing the road.
Heavy rain over Johnson Pass caused mud and debris to flow across Highway 199, temporarily closing the road.
Flash flooding was reported southwest of Green River, with rainfall of up to 5 inches recorded in the area.
Flash flooding occurred in the early morning hours along the North Fork of the Virgin River, with the gauge there rising from 92 cfs to 1378 cfs in one hour.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Buckskin Gulch, with water flowing over nearby US-89.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding across the northern portions of Capitol Reef National Park, including Cathedral Valley, further damaging roads that were already in disrepair from previous flash flooding. In addition, several washes east of the park were flooded, and water was flowing over SR-24.
Flash flooding occurred along the Scenic Drive of Capitol Reef National Park, as well as the Grand Wash and several roads further south in the park.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Little Wild Horse Canyon, with water there estimated to be 10 feet deep. Several roads in the area were also washed out.
Multiple roads at the southern end of Capitol Reef National Park were flooded and damaged, most notably the Notom-Bullfrog road.

Flash flooding in Coyote Valley and Buckskin Gulch was reported by BLM backcountry rangers. Logs were removed that were 10 feet overhead in the slots, and new pools of water had formed. In this event, the Buckskin Gulch flooding was primarily due to rain that fell over Coyote Valley.

Flash flooding occurred in portions of Zion National Park and the surrounding area, including in North Creek, Deep Creek, and the North Fork of the Virgin River. An increase in flow of over 500 cfs was measured at the Virgin River gauge.
Flash flooding occurred in Oak Creek Canyon in Zion National Park, with multiple waterfalls forming over the rim of a plateau near the canyon.
Yet another flash flood occurred on the North Fork of the Virgin River, which brought rocks and debris into the Upper Narrows and created dangerous conditions in that area.
A 59 mph wind gust was measured at the Wasatch Hills sensor.
The South Mountain sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The West Jordan air quality sensor near Salt Lake City Airport #2 recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The Great Salt Lake Marina sensor recorded a wind gust of 62 mph.

A strong line of thunderstorms moved through the Salt Lake Valley. Recorded wind gusts included 76 mph at the Salt Lake City International Airport FAA sensor, 65 mph at the Salt Lake City International Airport ASOS, and 64 mph at the Baccus/SR-111 sensor. Damage from this thunderstorm included large trees knocked down in the Avenues neighborhood of Salt Lake City, power poles knocked down along I-80 west of the Salt Lake City International Airport, and damage to the Airport fences, hangers, and signs.

A strong line of thunderstorms moved through the northern Wasatch Front, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 64 mph at the Bountiful KSL sensor and 59 mph at the Centerville UDOT sensor. Power poles were knocked down along the Legacy Highway, causing a closure while crews repaired the damage.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong post-frontal winds occurred across the desert of northwest Utah, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 69 mph at the White Sage sensor, 64 mph at the Camel Back Mountain sensor, 62 mph at the Wendover Peak sensor and English Village sensor, 61 mph at the Lakeside Mountain sensor, and 58 mph at the Causeway sensor.
Strong post-frontal wind gusts were reported along the southern Wasatch Front, including 62 mph at the Pleasant Grove RAWS, 61 mph in Lehi, and 60 mph at the Eureka UDOT sensor.
The Milford ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.

Heavy rain caused a debris flow from the south end of the Corner Canyon burn scar, damaging about 20 homes with mud and debris. Highland Drive was closed, and the police station, courts, and city hall were all flooded.
The Playa Station sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
The I-80 sensor at Grassey recorded a maximum wind gust of 67 mph.
The Lake Point at I-80 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 69 mph.
The Lakeside Mountain sensor recorded multiple wind gusts of 59 mph over a half hour period.
The Gunnison Island sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
Hail with a diameter of 1 inch was reported by an NWS employee at Ridgeline Elementary School in Highland.
Flash flooding occurred along the Wahweep Creek near Big Water. The flood was 4 to 6 feet deep and 100 feet wide at the peak, with logs and other debris reported with the flooding.
Flash flooding occurred in the Twenty-five Mile Wash, with water crossing the Hole-in-the-Rock Road.
Flash flooding occurred along Last Chance Creek and multiple other drainages in the surrounding area.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Warm Creek and multiple surrounding drainages.
Flash flooding occurred in the southern end of Capitol Reef National Park, with the Burr Trail road impassable due to the flooding.

The Utah National Guard took target practice on their machine gun firing range at Camp Williams on the afternoon of September 19th. Shrapnel from this exercise ignited brush around the area and, with the help of wind gusts generally in the 30-40 mph range and relative humidity values between 5 and 10 percent, the fire quickly spread. This wildfire eventually threatened the nearby town of Herriman, specifically the subdivisions of The Cove at Herriman Springs and the High Country Estates II, resulting in the mandatory evacuation of an estimated 5,000 people in over 1,600 homes. By the time the fire was stopped and contained, it had burned over 4,300 acres, completely destroying 3 houses and damaging at least 400 other houses. Several people were injured due to the fire, primarily police officers and firefighters responding to the blaze, with the most common injury being smoke inhalation. The listed end time is when the fire was 100% contained.

Two 17 year old males were struck by lightning just outside Snow Canyon High School in St. George. The two boys were waiting for a ride home shortly after school let out; they took shelter from the rain under a nearby tree, where lightning struck and injured them both. CPR was performed at the site, and they were both in critical condition when they reached a hospital in Las Vegas, but both survived and are expected to make a full recovery.

Alta Ski Lifts received 20 inches of new snow for the event, while higher elevations, above the snow level for a longer period of time, received much more. Liquid equivalent precipitation totals across the area were generally between 2.00 and 4.00 inches.

In the first storm of the season, more than a foot of snow fell on the highest elevations of the northern Wasatch Mountains. Liquid equivalent precipitation totals of 2.00 to 4.00 inches were common across the area.

In the first storm of the season, heavy snow fell over the Uinta Mountains. The area generally received 1.00 to 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, almost all of which fell as snow at the highest elevations.
In the first storm of the season, 1.00 to 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation fell across the central mountains of Utah, with much of that falling as snow over the higher peaks.

The Wasatch Plateau and Book Cliffs received between 1.00 and 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation in the first storm of the season, with much of that falling as snow in the highest elevations of the area.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Several sensors across the west desert of Utah recorded strong wind gusts, including 72 mph at Lower Cedar Mountain, 71 mph at the Interstate 80 sensor, 70 mph at Promontory Point, 65 mph at Rosebud, and 60 mph at SR-30 at Curlew, among others.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 60 mph at The University of Utah, 59 mph at the Pony Express Marker sensor, and 58 mph at the Lake Point I-80 sensor.
The Stockton Bar sensor recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.
Nickel size (0.88 inch diameter) hail was reported near Price.
Hail with a diameter of 2 inches was reported near Green River.
Hail with a diameter of 1 inch to 1.5 inches was reported at Padre Point.
The Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 65 mph.
Hail with a diameter of 1.5 inches was reported near Halls Crossing.
Rainfall of 0.60 inches in an hour, combined with antecedent moisture from three days of rainfall, led to flash flooding in Kodachorme Basin State Park and drainages east of the park.
Flash flooding occurred in Capitol Reef National Park, including along SR-24 and in the Cathedral areas of the park.

An EF0 tornado touched down west of Canyonlands National Park, at the south end of Robbers Roost Flat. Approximately 30 juniper trees were either snapped or uprooted by the tornado. No monetary damage occurred as the tornado occurred in a rural area and no trees fell on the nearby dirt road, so no cleanup was necessary.

Flooding occurred across many drainages in Garfield County, including Calf Creek and the Escalante River. The Escalante River, which typically flows below 10 cfs, reached a peak of 1300 cfs on October 5th. In addition, the Dirty Devil River, which normally flows at 10 to 20 cfs, reached a peak of 6300 cfs on October 6th.
Multiple drainages flooded in Emery County, particularly near Goblin Valley State Park, where water flowed over the Little Wildhorse Road.

Water and flood debris flowed across the Scenic Drive in Capitol Reef National Park, closing the road to all tourists. In addition, the Dirty Devil River, which normally flows at 10 to 20 cfs, reached a peak of 6300 cfs on October 6th.
Flooding was reported across Zion National Park, including in the Oak Creek and Emerald Pools areas.

Flooding occurred in many drainages in Kane County, including Wahweep Wash and Bullfrog Creek, with the Burr Trail at Bullfrog Creek becoming impassable due to water flowing over the trail. In addition, basement flooding was reported in Johnson Canyon.
The sensor at First Divide, I-80 east of Evanston, recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.

Two experienced snowmobilers from Evanston, Wyoming were riding in the Humpy Creek drainage in the western Uinta Mountains. Since they did not plan to ride on steep terrain, they left their avalanche beacons and shovels in their vehicles. One rider, a 54 year old man, apparently decided to at least partially ascend a popular snowmobile slope called Cherry Hill, where he triggered an avalanche and was buried. By the time his friend was able to get help, he had been buried under two feet of snow for more than half an hour, and he died at the scene.

Strong winds and heavy snow occurred in the northern Wasatch Mountains. The Monte Cristo SNOTEL recorded 1.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 15 inches of new snow. The strongest recorded wind gust in the area was 78 mph at Logan Summit.

Strong winds and heavy snow occurred in the Wasatch Mountains south of I-80. Alta Ski Lifts received 12 inches of new snow, with more snow on the higher peaks, as over 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation was recorded over the area. The strongest recorded gusts in the area were 96 mph at the Alta - Mt. Baldy sensor and 75 mph at the DV - Mount Baldy sensor.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Maximum wind gusts across the Great Salt Lake desert and mountains included 68 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 66 mph at Promontory Point, 63 mph at the SR-30 at Curlew sensor, 61 mph at the Thermal Treatment Unit sensor at the Utah Test and Training Range, and 58 mph at the Rosebud RAWS.
The Kimball Junction at I-80 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
Storm total snowfall in the Wasatch Mountain valleys included 20 inches in Morgan, 17 inches in Liberty, and 11 inches in Jeremy Ranch.

The Tony Grove SNOTEL received 3.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 35 inches of new snow based on snow ratios from similar elevations. Winds were also strong on the mountain peaks, including wind gusts of 88 mph at Ogden Peak and 81 mph at the Snowbasin Resort Wildcat sensor.
Brighton Crest received a storm total of 39 inches of new snow. Other snowfall reports included 30 inches at Solitude Mountain Resort and Deer Valley Resort, and 28 inches at Alta Ski Lifts.
The Chalk Creek #1 SNOTEL received 3.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 30 inches of new snow based on snow ratios at similar elevations.
The Daniels-Strawberry SNOTEL received 2.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow based on snow ratios at similar elevations.
Maximum wind gusts in the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys included 70 mph at Vernon Hill and 61 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 59 mph at the Fish Springs sensor and 58 mph at the Delta AWOS.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Maximum recorded wind gusts included 66 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain and 64 mph at Camel Back Mountain.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: The St. George AWOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
Storm total snowfall across the Salt Lake valley included 15 inches in West Jordan, 14 inches in Upper Millcreek, 13 inches in Sandy, and 10 inches in Cottonwood Heights.
Snowfall totals in the northern Wasatch Front included 12 inches on the Bountiful Bench, 10 inches on the North Salt Lake Bench, and 6 inches in South Ogden.

Though blizzard-like conditions did not last more than about an hour in the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys, significant snowfall accumulation still occurred in a short period of time. Storm totals included 8 inches of new snow in West Jordan, 7 inches in Stansbury Park, and 5 inches in the Upper Avenues. UDOT studies showed that commuters paid heed to the warnings, as peak PM hour traffic was approximately 58% less than historic volume, while pre-peak shoulder traffic was higher. UDOT also  calculated that 50,000 hours of travel time was saved by people leaving for the|commute early, equating to a savings of $1,000,000.

Blizzard conditions occurred over the western Uinta Mountains, with a maximum wind gust of 70 mph recorded at the Chepeta RAWS. For the storm, the Chepeta RAWS received 0.80 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 12 inches of new snow.

Blizzard conditions occurred across portions of the Wasatch Mountain valleys, with low visibilities, snow, and winds up to 45 mph in Heber City. Jeremy Ranch received a storm total of 10 inches new snow.

Blizzard conditions occurred across parts of the northern Wasatch Mountains, with wind gusts up to 86 mph on Ogden Peak and up to 75 mph at the Snowbasin Resort Wildcat sensor. Both Tony Grove Lake and Monte Cristo SNOTEL sites received 1.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 15 inches of new snow based on snow ratios from similar elevations.

Blizzard conditions occurred across parts of the Wasatch Mountains south of I-80, with low visibilities and wind gusts up to 73 mph at the Sundance - Arrowhead sensor. Storm totals included 17 inches of snow at Brighton Crest and 11 inches at Alta Ski Lifts.
Maximum recorded wind gusts ahead of the cold front included 63 mph at Vernon Hill, 59 mph at South Mountain, and 59 mph at the Salt Lake #2 airport.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The maximum recorded wind gust ahead of the cold front was 63 mph at the I-80 at Grassey sensor.
The U.S. 6 at Eureka sensor recorded strong winds for a few hours straight, with a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.

Blizzard conditions occurred across the Cache Valley, with the Logan Airport ASOS reporting 4 hours of visibilities below 0.50 miles, along with snow and wind gusts up to 47 mph. Logan and Richmond both reported 6 inches of snow for the storm.

Heavy rain caused widespread significant flooding across Washington County. Rainfall and significantly increased river flows began on December 19th, with many rivers and streams around Zion National Park and St. George near bankfull. Reports of road flooding began on December 20th. SR-9 was closed in Zion National Park due to flooding between the tunnel and Mt. Carmel Junction, and flooding and rockslides occurred on SR-18 between Enterprise and Central.||The worst of the flooding occurred on December 21st, when the flow of the Santa Clara River increased to an estimated 5000 cfs, and the Virgin River near Bloomington was measured at 12400 cfs. Zion National Park was closed due to flooding, and the Zion Park Lodge was evacuated due to the danger of landslides. One historic landslide, in particular, was moving through the day as the riprap structure was eroded away. Old Highway 91 was also closed, as flooding and debris washed out and damaged much of the road. Many other roadways across the county were flooded, including many roads in the city of St. George, many rural roads along the Santa Clara, SR-18 south of Central, in Enterprise along Center Street and Main Street, and the road into Snow Canyon State Park, which closed the park to tourists. Many bridges were damaged or destroyed, including the foot bridge over the Fort Pearce Wash, the Tobin Wash Bridge near Gunlock, a foot bridge at the Sunbrook Golf Course, the bridge at 2500 South in New Harmony, and the bridge at Brookside. Residential flood damage was reported in Enterprise, Springdale, Rockville, and St. George. Contaminated water became a problem along the Virgin River, and culinary water became unavailable in the town of Gunlock. The Southgate Golf Course in St. George suffered extensive damage due to erosion.||Flooding continued on December 22nd. Flood waters damaged a bridge in New Harmony Heights, closed many roadways including a bridge near the Enterprise Reservoir, and up to 15 homes were damaged to varying degrees in Brookside. River flows stayed high on December 23rd before receding.||Damage estimates were obtained from the Utah Emergency Management Association, and included damages of $4.7 million to infrastructure and $15 million to other properties. In addition, $300,000 worth of heavy construction equipment was saved when the NWS forecast office in Salt Lake City called the Washington City Public Works, notifying of them of the upcoming high flows expected on the Virgin River. The Public Works pulled all of their equipment out of the Virgin River, which they said would have been swept away and lost if not for the phone call.

While flooding in Kane County was less than in nearby Washington County, significant damage still occurred. Many roads were closed or impassable due to flood waters, including Highway 14, the 3rd South Connector in Kanab, and US-89 east of Kanab, the last of which had 12 inches of water flowing over the road. A landslide also occurred on US-89 near milepost 93, where debris was approximately 4 feet deep and 50-60 feet wide. Residential flooding occurred in Orderville and Glendale, and many private roads in those two towns were washed out.

A group of very experienced backcountry skiers went to explore Big Horseshoe Bowl, an area near Ephraim, Utah, on the morning of March 26th. They had read the avalanche forecast, which had an overall hazard of Moderate with pockets of Considerable, so they were being careful, testing different slopes for avalanche activity before deciding if they should ski the slope. As they were testing one of these slopes, and about to decide that that particular slope was too dangerous, a large avalanche was triggered. ||The avalanche caught and carried 3 of the individuals. Two of these three were freed relatively quickly, but the third was completely buried. Using their beacons, they located him and eventually dug him out of the snow. They were able to revive him after extensive use of CPR, and the entire group was recovered by a SAR team later that day, but the individual died the next day.

Some homeowners received as much as a foot of water in their basement, and others had to clean up dirty conditions due to overflowing raw sewage. In addition, some heavy construction equipment was damaged near the mouth of Weber Canyon, where it had been parked along the river bank.

Many local creeks went over their banks in Morgan County, with the worst of the flooding occurring along Morgan Valley Drive near the town of Peterson, where authorities had to spend a day cleaning up the debris that had spilled over the roadway. In addition, a couple of homes sustained flood damage in the towns of Peterson and Mountain Green.
