events.event_narrative: Strong wind gusts were recorded across much of the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains, including peak wind gusts of 71 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 67 mph at Wendover Peak, 66 mph at Simpson Springs, 64 mph at Badger Island, 63 mph at I-80 at Milepost 1, 62 mph at Hat Island, and 61 mph at White Sage.

Maximum wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 64 mph at the Salt Lake City International Airport midfield sensor, 62 mph at the Bolinder           Field-Tooele Valley Airport sensor, and 61 mph at the Center Tailings Center sensor. In addition, a light pole at the airport was knocked over by the strong winds.
A CWOP sensor in Lehi recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph with the passage of the cold front.
The Fish Springs sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Evanston, Wyoming ASOS reported a maximum wind gust of 71 mph, and the Evanston WYDOT sensor reported a 61 mph wind gust 11 minutes later.

Multiple sites near Wendover recorded strong wind gusts with this thunderstorm, with peak wind gusts of 71 mph at the Wendover Point of Entry, 65 mph at the I-80 at Milepost 1 sensor, and 59 mph at Wendover Peak.

Multiple sensors recorded severe wind gusts as a thunderstorm moved through the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, with the strongest gusts being 78 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 68 mph at English Village, and 62 mph at White Sage, Simpson Springs, and Fish Springs.
The Playa Station sensor recorded a wind gust to 59 mph, while the Upper Cedar Mountain sensor recorded a max gust of 58 mph. Both of these sensors are in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet.

A line of thunderstorms produced strong winds on the western edge of the Great Salt Lake, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 73 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 70 mph at Gunnison Island, 63 mph at the Utah Test and Training Range, and 59 mph at the I-80 at Grassey sensor.
A sensor at Snowbasin Resort recorded a wind gust of 63 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong synoptic scale winds were observed in the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains behind the cold front. The maximum recorded wind gust across the area was 71 mph at Wendover Point of Entry. In addition, strong gusts were observed in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, with max gusts of 70 mph at Callao, 66 mph at Causeway, 65 mph at Faust, and 64 mph at V-Grid.
The Ditto sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The Vernon Hill sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 83 mph.
The sensor in Lehi recorded a wind gust of 61 mph.
Multiple trees were knocked down in Tremonton, and there were also reports of a few windows being blown out in vehicles.
The Lake Point sensor recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.

The Ogden Peak sensor recorded a wind gust of 77 mph. Many trees were knocked down near Ogden and Huntsville, with at least two dozen large trees knocked down in the Huntsville area. Several of these trees landed on buildings, with at least one causing moderate damage to a house. Many power lines were also knocked down across the county.

The Salt Lake City International Airport ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 67 mph. Wind gusts of 62 mph were also reported at the Baccus sensor and the Parley's Canyon at Quarry sensor. A light pole that was knocked over at the Salt Lake City International Airport, landed on two cars. Large trees were knocked over in Rose Park, and a 18-24 inch diameter tree snapped and landed on a house in the Avenues, causing minor roof damage. In addition, a semitruck was blown over near the I-80/I-215 interchange near Salt Lake City International Airport.
The Lakeside Mountain sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The Ogden Peak sensor recorded a wind gust of 73 mph.

Flooding occurred in several drainages in Morgan County, including East Canyon Creek, Deep Creek, and Hardscrabble Creek. East Canyon Creek rose from 200 cfs to 800 cfs overnight. The flooding was primarily in agricultural areas, but flood waters also impacted roads in the town of Peterson, as well as low lying bridges along the creeks.

Chalk Creek near Coalville rose as high as 1496 cfs, up from a mere 60 cfs from three days prior, and above the flood stage of 1341 cfs. These flood waters approached homes upstream from Coalville, and threatened bridges along the creek, including water flowing over the bridge at Border Station Road.
Emigration Creek, which had been flowing as low as 18 cfs the previous day, rose as high as 136 cfs, above the flood stage of 130 cfs.

The worst affected area in Cache County was the Riverside RV Park on 1700 South in Logan, just across from the Country Manor neighborhood; the park was filled with water before crews could divert the water downstream. The area near State Route 89 at the south end of the town of Logan also experienced flooding. Flood waters also flowed over the Logan River Golf Course and along Park Avenue.

Flooding occurred along the Weber River all the way to Plain City. The Weber River at Plain City gauge peaked at 4761 cfs, above its flood stage of 4713 cfs. While flooding threatened some homes in Riverdale, most of the damage was restricted to buildings  in agricultural areas.
The Weber River at Gateway gauge reached a peak of 4640 cfs, above its flood stage of 4140 cfs. No damage was reported in this section of Morgan County with these increased flows.

Lightning struck the KMTX WSR-88D, operated by the National Weather Service Salt Lake City Weather Forecast Office, and located at Promontory Point. The lightning strike immediately disabled the radar, and it was out of service for almost 24 hours. Some wiring and two circuit boards had to be replaced. In addition, 16 panels of the radome were damaged and had to be replaced.
The Interstate 80 sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
Penny-sized hail was reported in Lehi.
The Playa Station sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 61 mph.
The Camel Back Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 66 mph.
The Cardiff Peak sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 78 mph.

The northern Wasatch Front experienced both easterly canyon winds and southerly prefrontal winds. The maximum recorded wind gust was 52 mph at Hill Air Force Base, but damage due to winds was reported in multiple locations. In Brigham City, shingles were blown off a roof and several branches were broken off of trees. At the mouth of Weber Canyon, two separate trucks with camper trailers were knocked over due to strong winds coming out of the canyon.

Maximum wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 66 mph at South Mountain, 65 mph at Vernon Hill, 63 mph at Stockton Bar, and 59 mph at Baccus Highway. With these strong southerly winds, a truck with a camper trailer was blown over on Interstate 80 at mile marker 107.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Maximum recorded wind gusts across the Salt Lake Desert and Mountains, including the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, were 80 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 79 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 67 mph at Simpson Springs,  66 mph at Grassey, Salt Flats, Callao, and I-80 at Milepost 29, and 65 mph at Durand Road.
The Fish Springs sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 63 mph at the Brimstone Reservoir RAWS, 61 mph at the Milford ASOS, and 58 mph at the Enterprise RAWS.

The Blacksmith Fork River reached flood stage on May 8th, with a peak flow of 978 cfs, above the flood flow of 934 cfs. Several roads around Logan were flooded and closed, including areas near 600 West and Park Avenue, and areas near 1700 South and US Routes 89 and 91. In addition, areas around the town of Millville received minor flooding.

The Blacksmith Fork River experienced flooding again in mid-May, peaking at 1434 cfs on May 16th, well above the flood flow of 934 cfs. Flooding was reported in Logan, Millville, and Hyrum. The bridge in Millville at 2900 South was washed out on both ends, and other low-lying bridges and roadways were impacted. The worst of the damage was at the Country Manor subdivision, where nine homes were flooded and evacuated.

Flooding occurred along the South Fork of the Ogden River from the Causey Reservoir to the Pineview Reservoir, with the gauge near Huntsville peaking at 1554 cfs on May 16th, well above the flood flow of 1019 cfs. This flooding impacted campgrounds and summer homes in and around Huntsville.

Flooding occurred along the Weber River from the mouth of Weber Canyon downstream to Plain City. Only minor flooding occurred through the month of May, as the flood stage was mitigated, but this flooding began to damage the levee system at Plain City, which would eventually fail in June. Note that this event continued into June.

Flooding occurred along the South Fork of the Ogden River through the end of May, with the gauge near Huntsville reaching a peak of 1417 cfs on May 24th. This flooding impacted campgrounds and summer homes near Huntsville. In addition, flooding did major damage to Old Snow Basin Road, which officials estimated would take $500,000 to repair.
Lost Creek reached flood stage for the last week of May. Multiple bridges along Lost Creek were impacted by rising flood waters, and low lying roads were damaged as well.

Flooding occurred along the Sevier River, with the gauge at Sigurd topping flood stage on May 23rd, and slowly rising through the rest of the month with the accelerated snowmelt. This flooding effected low lying roads and bridges, including Sevier River Road and Nebeker Lane. Both of these roads were closed for several weeks, and Nebeker Lane suffered severe damage due to the flood waters. Note that this event continued into June.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Camel Back Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The Evanston, Wyoming ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
The A-Paid observer in Delta reported a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.

Hail with a diameter of one inch was reported in the Cache Valley near Trenton, Utah. The report was received via the NOAA Hazardous Weather Testbed - Experimental Warning Program Severe Hazards Analysis and Verification Experiment project.
The sensor on Antelope Island recorded a maximum wind gust of 65 mph.
Maximum wind gusts in the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 63 mph at Vernon Hill and 59 mph at Baccus Highway.
Synoptic-scale wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 75 mph at Stockton Bar and 66 mph at South Mountain.
The West Ogden CWOP sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.

A strong thunderstorm moved through the Salt Lake Valley, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 75 mph at the Center Tailings Center sensor, 69 mph at the Baccus Highway sensor, 66 mph at the FAA sensor at the Salt Lake City International Airport, and 60 mph at the Salt Lake City International Airport ASOS. In addition, a Russian olive tree was knocked over at the north side of the Salt Lake City International airport, and fell onto a building.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Maximum recorded wind gusts across the west desert included 73 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 64 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 60 mph at Wendover Peak and English Village, 59 mph at Salt Flats and V-Grid, and 58 mph at Playa Station.
The Price ASOS recorded several minutes of severe wind gusts, with a maximum recorded gust of 62 mph.
The U.S. 6 at Eureka sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
The U.S. 6 at Eureka sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Brimstone Reservoir RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The Otter Creek RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 64 mph. In addition, the Rich County sheriff reported that a large tree was knocked over in Woodruff.
The Lake Point at I-80 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 66 mph.
The Logan ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
Maximum wind gusts across the northern Wasatch front included 60 mph in West Ogden and 59 mph at the Ogden ASOS.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong winds blew across much of the West Desert through the late morning and afternoon. Maximum recorded wind gusts included 73 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 67 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain and V-Grid, 66 mph at Salt Flats and West Salt Flats, 65 mph at Causeway, 64 mph at Gunnison Island, 63 mph at Lakeside Mountain, and 62 mph at Playa Station.
The Snowbasin Straw Top sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 79 mph.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 66 mph at the I-15 at Sevier River sensor and 65 mph at the Sevier Reservoir sensor.

Recorded wind gusts across west central Utah included 66 mph from the Delta A-Paid observer, 64 mph at the Mud Spring RAWS, 61 mph at the Delta Municipal Airport, and 58 mph at the Fish Springs sensor.
Maximum wind gusts in southwest Utah included 66 mph at the Milford ASOS and 59 mph at the Brimstone Reservoir RAWS.
The Dog Valley sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 81 mph, while the Signal Peak RAWS recorded a gust of 78 mph.

The South Fork of the Ogden River remained above flood stage for much of the first half of June, peaking at 1318 cfs on June 8th, before finally dropping below flood stage for the rest of the season in mid-June. Most of the damage was already done in earlier parts of the season, but this flooding continued to impact summer homes and campgrounds along the river.

The Sevier River flooded in Sanpete County, with many roads damaged in the Gunnison and Centerfield area. Water was a foot deep along parts of the Clarion Road, damaging both the road and a nearby hunting club. There was extensive flooding along the Gunnison Farmers Freeway, with some road and bridge damage in that area. Damage was also reported along River Bridge Road in the Fayette area.

The Sevier River at Sigurd peaked at 1728 cfs on June 1st, then remained above flood stage for more than a week after that as it slowly receded. Many roads across Sevier county continued to be impacted and damaged, including State Road 118 between Joseph and Monroe, the Sevier River Road between Central Valley and Annabella, and Seegmiller Lane near Richfield. In addition, flood waters seeped into about a dozen homes, while threatening more than a dozen others.

The Weber River continued to flood through early June, and became significantly worse when a levee near Plain City broke on June 9th. These flood waters impacted barns and houses along the river, though the houses were spared from interior damage. Many fields and yards across the area were inundated by significant amounts of water.

Flooding along the Weber River continued through mid-June, then subsided once the levee near Plain City was fixed. Standing water continued to be a problem after the levee repairs, leaving residents with water-logged properties.
The Sevier River flooded again in mid-June, with the focus further south along the river this time. Low lying roads and bridges in the town of Hatch were impacted, including the Old Hatch Bridge.

The Logan River flooded again beginning in mid-June. The Logan River Golf Course and walking trail was partially closed when a breach in the river bank sent a large stream of water down the middle of the golf course. Damage occurred to a few low lying bridges, including the Millville Bridge and a railroad bridge in Logan.

Flooding occurred on the Upper Weber River in late June due to the accelerated snowmelt, with the Weber at Oakley gauge peaking at 3133 cfs on June 30th. Much of this flooding was mitigated, but the high water did impact some buildings close to the river. Note that this event continued into July.

The Logan River continued to flood through the end of June. This flooding damaged  summer homes in the Birch Glen area, and continued to significantly impact the Logan River Golf Course. Note that this event continued into July.

Spring Creek near the town of Providence, Utah experienced flooding at the end of June. Most of the damage occurred when gravel clogged culverts along the creek, making the creek divert around the culverts, and causing damage to driveways and roads. At one point, flooding threatened houses, and a couple families were voluntarily evacuated. Throughout the event, a few houses along the creek experienced basement flooding. Note that this event continued into July.

Several rivers in the Uinta Basin reached flood stage in late June, including Rock Creek, and the Duchesne River at a few different points. These floods were largely mitigated, but some minor damage was observed to low lying bridges and a few buildings near the banks of the rivers, including a few homes in Tabiona. Note that this event continued into July.

Little Cottonwood Creek reached flood stage for a couple days in late June, peaking at 916 cfs at Crestwood Park on the night of June 24th. Much of the flooding was mitigated, but some damage was observed along the creek. The culvert at 2000 East and 3500 South was severely damaged, resulting in an extended closure of the road. There was a road closure and some damage at 1200 West between 3300 South and 3400 South, after Little Cottonwood enters the Jordan River. Erosion and damage occurred to riverbanks and park areas along the creek, including Murray Park and Crestwood Park.
The SR-30 sensor recorded strong wind gusts for half an hour, with a maximum gust of 76 mph.
A large barn was knocked down in Richmond and several trees were reported down across the area.

A few different sensors just east of Wendover recorded strong wind gusts, including 64 mph at the UDOT I-80 at Milepost 29 sensor, 60 mph at the West Salt Flats sensor, and 59 mph at the North Salt Flats sensor.
The Provo Municipal Airport reported a maximum wind gust of 69 mph.
Hail with a diameter of 1 inch was reported in Tabiona.
The Baccus/SR111 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The West Salt Flats sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 61 mph.
The Wig Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.
The Diddle Knoll sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Locomotive Springs sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
Flash flooding was reported on Gordon Creek, west of Price, after a radar-estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain fell over the area.

Flash flooding occurred in several places across Capitol Reef National Park. The Scenic Drive was closed, with 6 to 8 inches of water flowing over the road. The Grand Wash experienced flash flooding, which also impacted a part of the Scenic Drive. Flash flooding was also observed along Sulphur Creek.
Flash flooding occurred in Croton Canyon, washing out a road in the area.
The Beaver Municipal Airport sensor reported a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
Flash flooding occurred in the Cathedral Valley area of Capitol Reef National Park. This flooding washed out roads and made the area inaccessible.
Flash flooding occurred along the Alvey Wash and Harris Wash, washing out Hole-in-the-Rock Road and Alvey Wash Road.
A visitor in Zion National Park reported a flash flood between Mountain of the Sun and the Twin Brothers. The flash flood was very short-lived.

A fast-moving thunderstorm moved through the Scofield Scout Camp on the morning of July 13th. Lightning struck two of the scouts as they were trying to return to their campsite; one of them, a 12-year-old male, was killed. The other scout suffered burns, but survived.

Flash flooding was reported along State Route 95, with large trees and rocks covering part of the road. In addition, damage was reported to State Route 276 going toward Bullfrog. Flash flooding also occurred along Poison Spring on the north aspect of the Henry Mountains.
Flooding was reported along River Road in Duchesne, and the Duchesne River quickly rose 800 cfs.
Flash flooding was reported near State Route 95 in southern Emery County, with one of the roads near there being washed out.

A heavy rainstorm produced flash flooding across parts of the Salt Lake Valley, and the hardest hit areas were Kearns, Taylorsville, and Murray. In Kearns, water was 9 to 12 inches deep across several roads, making them impassable. In Taylorsville, at least a half dozen homes had flooded basements near the intersection of 5400 South and 3200 West. Water caused a sinkhole to form in the roadway around 6200 South and 2700 West, buckling and collapsing the street. In Murray, approximately 25 homes were flooded, with some basements filling with 4 to 6 feet of water.

About an hour after a heavy rainstorm caused flash flooding in Salt Lake County, another storm moved through Utah County, causing flash flooding in Orem. Storm drains were overflowing and water covered the roads up to 3 inches deep. At least seven homes had flooding in their basements or garages.
A fast moving thunderstorm just north of Big Water created a large flash flood in the Wahweep drainage. This flood stranded two people for some time.
Park rangers in Capitol Reef National Park reported flash flooding along Sulphur Creek.
Flash flooding in Zion National Park stranded visitors along the North Fork of the Virgin River, specifically in the Orderville Canyon area.

Widespread flash flooding occurred in Capitol Reef National Park. Water crossed the Scenic Drive in multiple locations from the visitors center to the Slickrock Divide, forcing rangers to close the road. In addition, flash flooding was reported in Sulphur Creek.

In an area already experiencing river flooding, heavy rainfall caused flash flooding near Tabiona. The primary road damage was along State Route 35, where a gulch running under the road was heavily backed up for hundreds of yards, and the pressure from the backup eventually washed out the road. The resultant damage was an area 30 feet deep and 40 feet across where the road was entirely missing.||Around 11:45 pm MDT, two vehicles drove directly into the washed out area. The occupants of the first vehicle suffered one fatality and one injury.  The occupant of the other vehicle was injured.

Several rivers in the Uinta Basin remained at or near flood stage in early July, including Rock Creek, and the Duchesne River at a few different points. These floods were largely mitigated, but some minor damage was observed, including temporarily reducing access to potable water in Myton. A couple of vehicles were also severely damaged in the fast-flowing flood waters. Note that this event began in June.

Spring Creek near the town of Providence, Utah continued to experienced flooding through the beginning of July. Another clogged culvert along the creek washed out a road in early July, but otherwise additional damage was minimal as waters began to recede and impacts were further mitigated. Note that this event began in June.

The Logan River continued to flood into the beginning of July. This flooding continued to damage and cause the partial closure of the Logan River Golf Course, but otherwise the impacts were largely mitigated, and the waters receded quickly as the snow began to run out. Note that this event began in June.

Flooding continued on the Upper Weber River in early July, with the Weber at Oakley gauge peaking at 3390 cfs on July 1st. Much of this flooding up to Rockport Reservoir was mitigated, but once the Rockport Reservoir was filled, it increased the challenge for people trying to manage the flood threat downstream. At the Camper World downstream in Coalville, many of the 158 RV pads in the park were covered with water, as water flowed from canals in adjoining fields and through broken areas of a berm around the park. The park was evacuated except for employees. Other areas downstream of Rockport Reservoir also experienced minor flooding. Note that this event began in June.

The Sevier River once again experienced flooding in the month of July, but this time it was areas of Millard County that received the worst of the damage. The access road between Highways 50 and 257 was closed due to water running over the roadway. Water from Sevier River also flowed over portions of Highways 6 and 50, but did not result in any damage or closures. Flooding occurred at various points on the Sevier River channel from Leamington through Lynndyl, in the Delta and Deseret areas, and all the way to Sevier Lake. A few different county roads and bridges were closed or damaged, including the Leamington Bridge in Leamington and the access road to the Gunnison Massacre Historical Site west of Hinckley.

A 56-year-old man was with his family near the Wedge Overlook in the San Rafael Desert when he was struck by lightning. CPR was performed by family members and emergency personnel who responded to the scene, but he was unable to be revived and died at the scene.
Flash flooding was reported along Pleasant Creek, Sandy Creek, and Burro Wash in and near Capitol Reef National Park.
Park rangers at Capitol Reef National Park reported a large flash flood along Sulpher Creek.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Wahweep Canyon near Big Water.

Flash flooding occurred along Clear Creek Canyon Road near Fremont Indian State Park. This flooding was exacerbated by the rain falling on an old burn scar, which allowed debris to flow over the road.
Flash flooding occurred near the town of Angle due to heavy rainfall.
Flash flooding occurred in Capitol Reef National Park, just south of the visitors center. Doppler radar indicated rainfall estimates of about an inch of water in 3 hours time.

Flash flooding occurred on the northern tributaries of the Escalante River, especially on North Creek and the North Fork of Birch Creek. This flooding eventually made its way down the Escalante, with a gauge along the Escalante quickly increasing to 1700 cfs. Note that flash flooding also occurred further downstream in Kane County.

Flash flooding that began further north on the Escalante River eventually made its way downstream, with the strong flow of water finally dissipating when it reached Lake Powell. Note that this flooding began in Garfield County, with most of the rainfall also occurring in the basins further upstream.
Light but steady rain over Capitol Reef National Park produced flash flooding in the Grand Wash.
Personnel from the Grand Staircase Escalante-National Monument reported flash flooding along Alvey Wash.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Sulpher Creek in Capitol Reef National Park; the flood was categorized as impressive by one of the park rangers.

A 51-year-old German tourist in Bryce Canyon National Park was hiking with his family along the Rim Trail near Sunset Point, when an isolated thunderstorm moved into the area. Most of the family ran toward their car, but the man sought refuge under a large Ponderosa Pine. A bolt of lightning stuck the tree, with some of the energy being transferred to the man, and he died at the scene.

A construction worker, who was walking toward his truck at the Granite Construction Company supply site in West Haven, was thrown back from the truck when a bolt of lightning struck the vehicle. He was thrown several feet in the air and landed on his face, suffering facial injuries and hand abrasions. He would survive his injuries.

Heavy rain occurred over the northern portions of Capitol Reef National Park, particularly over Deep Creek. This caused flash flooding along the Fremont River, which was measured at 3922 cfs at the gauge near Caineville.

Flash flooding occurred along the Paria River drainage, with some washes still running the morning after the event, and debris and other evidence of flash flooding observed in several other small washes.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Alvey Wash.

Heavy rain over Pleasant Creek in Capitol Reef National Park caused flash flooding. This flooding ran downstream to the Fremont River, which was measured at an increased flow of 1296 cfs near Caineville.
Large hail was observed on the west side of the Salt Lake Valley, with 1.5 inch diameter hail reported near Kearns and 1 inch hail reported in West Valley City.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was reported near Payson.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was observed near Circleville. This thunderstorm also produced very heavy rain over the area.
A participant of the Cooperative Observer Program, near Alpine, reported hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches.

Two sensors in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded strong wind gusts with a thunderstorm moving through the area. The Juliet Road sensor recorded a maximum gust of 59 mph, while the North Salt Flats sensor recorded a 58 mph wind gust.
The Causeway sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The Interstate 80 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The University of Utah WBB sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was reported along the Scenic Drive in Capitol Reef National Park.
The Emery County Dispatch reported hail with a diameter of 1 inch in Huntington.
The I-15 Northbound at the Sevier River UDOT sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 66 mph.
The Interstate 80 sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
The wind sensor at Antelope Island State Park recorded a maximum wind gust of 70 mph.
The Playa Station sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 68 mph.
The North Salt Flats sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.
The Syracuse sensor in the air quality mesonet recorded a wind gust of 65 mph.
Hail with a diameter of approximately 0.75 inches was observed near Murray.
Hail with a diameter of 0.75 inches was reported in Escalante.
A strong thunderstorm moved over the Wendover area, with the Wendover Point of Entry sensor recording a maximum wind gust of 62 mph, and the Wendover Peak sensor recording a wind gust of 59 mph.

Three separate sensors in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded strong wind gusts with a passing thunderstorm, with a 66 mph gust observed at both the Camel Back Mountain site and Tower Grid site, as well as a 59 mph gust reported at the Ditto sensor.
The Causeway sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The West Granite sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.

A trained spotter observed a tornado west of Apple Valley, Utah. The weak tornado was short-lived and caused no damage; tall grasses in the area were disturbed, but nearby bushes and trees remained undamaged.
The Lake Point I-80 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
Hikers who were caught in Crack Canyon during a thunderstorm reported hail that was approximately 1 inch in diameter.
A Kanab Visitor Center ranger reported a large flash flood in upper Johnson Canyon.
The Utah Department of Transportation reported a flash flood near Rockville, with water flowing across State Route 9.
Large flash floods were reported in Pine Creek and Clear Creek in Zion National Park, with flowing water as much as 7 to 8 feet deep.
Flash flooding was reported in Zion National Park along the East Fork of the Virgin River, with the gauge along this river rising to 1665 cfs.
The Big Water Visitors Center reported a very large flash flood in the Wahweap drainage.
Flash flooding was reported along Fortymile Creek.
Heavy rain over the Fort Pearce Wash caused flash flooding along that drainage, with the measured flow at the gauge going from 0 cfs to 763 cfs in a single hour.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding along the Paria River drainage. The gauge on the Paria near Kanab went from 185 cfs to 1212 cfs in one hour.

Flash flooding occurred in many locations of Zion National Park, with floods reported over a large portion of the southern half of the park. Pine Creek and Spry Canyon both experienced large floods, with water in Pine Creek reportedly 6 to 7 feet high. Large rocks and other debris impacted some of the roads around the park. In addition, many of the smaller drainages that flow south to Rockville experienced flooding.

Flash flooding occurred in Crack Canyon, Little Wildhorse Canyon, and other washes near the Little Wildhorse Canyon trailhead. The floods were generally large and hikers caught in Crack Canyon had to run from the water, eventually making it back to the road before the water caught up with them.

Moderate to heavy rainfall fell over a broad area near Capitol Reef National Park. This initially caused flash flooding along Sulphur Creek and other parts of Capitol Reef. Eventually this water made its way downstream, causing flash flooding along the Dirty Devil River, which went from 538 to 1419 cfs in a few hours.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Causeway sensor in the Dugway mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.

A landslide occurred 8 miles east of Cedar City, along Utah State Route 14. The landslide occurred sometime before 5 a.m. on the morning of October 8th, when the slide was discovered and the road was closed by the Utah Department of Transportation. The landslide was 1,700 feet in length, and destroyed an 800 foot section of State Route 14. The dirt on the road was as much as 100 feet deep in some places, and it was estimated that the slide consisted of 1.5 million cubic yards of dirt, rock, and debris. This led to the closing of a 12-mile stretch of State Route 14, which is a widely used road in southern Utah, particularly for tourists trying to get to Cedar Breaks National Monument and Bryce Canyon National Park. Early estimates from the Utah Department of Transportation indicated that the cost to repair the damaged section of State Route 14 would be around $12 million.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong southerly winds were observed across the Great Salt Lake Desert ahead of the cold front, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 73 mph at Badger Island and 59 mph at Lower Cedar Mountain.
The Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph when the cold front passed through the area.

In the first storm of the season, the sensor at the mid-bowl of Snowbasin Resort Company received 1.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, most of which fell as snow, or approximately 12 inches of snow.
In the first storm of the season, Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort received 11 inches of new snow. Higher elevations likely received more, with estimates of around 2 feet of snow from some spotters.
In the first storm of the season, the Brown Duck SNOTEL received 2.80 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow.
In the first storm of the season, the Horse Ridge SNOTEL received 1.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 11 inches of new snow.
In the first storm of the season, the Pine Creek SNOTEL received 1.60 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 16 inches of new snow.

In the first storm of the season, Brian Head Resort received 17 inches of snow. In addition, the Midway Valley SNOTEL received 2.80 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 28 inches of snow.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: The White Reef RAWS recorded strong gap winds, with a maximum recorded wind gust of 63 mph, as well as gusts above 50 mph for several hours.

In addition to gusty winds in the lower elevation gaps, strong winds also occurred in the higher elevations of southwest Utah. The White Reef RAWS measured the strongest winds across the area, with a maximum recorded wind gust of 63 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The West Granite sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet was the first sensor in the Great Salt Lake Desert to record strong wind gusts with this storm. A wind gust of 64 mph was recorded just before midnight. Note that this event continued into December.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: Both the Badger Spring RAWS and White Reef RAWS recorded strong northerly wind gusts beginning on November 30th, with a maximum wind gust on the 30th of 72 mph at the Badger Spring RAWS. Note that this event continued into December.
The Signal Peak RAWS recorded strong winds for several hours, with a maximum wind gust of 91 mph.
With strong prefrontal winds on the morning of November 4th, the Cedar City ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.

A cold front moved through the Salt Lake Valley, followed by lake effect snow through the morning of November 5th. Snowfall accumulations across the area included 9 inches of new snow in Cottonwood Heights, 8 inches of snow in Upper Millcreek, and 7 inches in both Sandy and the Upper Avenues.
The Chepeta RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 83 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Maximum recorded wind gusts across the Great Salt Lake Desert included 64 mph at both the Promontory Point sensor and the SR-30 at Curlew Junction sensor.
Storm total snowfall across the Cache Valley included 11 inches of snow in Clarkston, 10 inches in Smithfield, 9 inches in Logan, and 8 inches in both Richmond and North Logan.
The Milford ASOS recorded wind gusts of 59 mph several times throughout the afternoon of November 18th.
The US-6 @ Eureka sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 64 mph, as well as several other gusts greater than 58 mph.
The Tony Grove Lake SNOTEL received 2.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 21 inches of new snow for the storm.

Two expert skiers were traveling along the well-known terrain of Alta Ski Lifts and Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort on November 13th; however, the resorts were not open yet, and the snowpack was very unstable, with considerable to high avalanche danger. When the two skiers reached Gad Valley, one of them triggered an avalanche, which carried him approximately 800 feet through steep rocky terrain and over a small cliff. The victim, a 38-year-old male, was only partially buried, but had already passed away when emergency crews reached the scene.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong gusty winds continued across the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains through the morning of December 1st. Peak recorded wind gusts included 67 mph at Lower Cedar Mountain, 65 mph at the Utah Test and Training Range Thermal Treatment Unit sensor, 62 mph at Camel Back Mountain and Gunnison Island, and 58 mph at the Rosebud RAWS. Note that this event began in November.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: Both the Badger Spring and White Reef RAWS recorded very strong wind gusts, with gusts greater than 60 mph for the entire day of December 1st. Badger Spring recorded a maximum wind gust of 89 mph, while White Reef's strongest recorded gust was 69 mph. Note that this event began in November.

The Price ASOS recorded strong downslope wind gusts for several hours on the morning of December 1st, with a maximum recorded gust of 62 mph. The US 6 at Helper sensor also recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.

The strongest winds in the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys occurred as the cold front moved through the area. Peak recorded wind gusts included 66 mph at the Baccus Highway sensor, 65 mph at Vernon Hill, 61 mph at the Salt Lake Airport #2 and Grantsville sensors, 60 mph at the Salt Lake International Airport ASOS, and 59 mph at Olympus Hills.
The Chepeta RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 80 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong winds occurred across the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains as the cold front moved through the area, then tapered off fairly quickly after the front exited the area. The strongest recorded wind gusts included 73 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 71 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 70 mph at Promontory Point, 61 mph at Wendover Peak, 60 mph at the SR-30 at Curlew and Hat Island sensors, and 58 mph at Gunnison Island.
A breaking wave event occurred in Castle Country, with peak wind gusts in the area of 66 mph at Fremont Junction and 64 mph at the Joe's Valley RAWS.

The Pleasant Grove RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 66 mph overnight. In addition, damage was reported across Utah Valley, with the most damage reported in the Provo area. The winds knocked over several trees, including a few large pine trees, and a couple of these trees landed on cars. Wind gusts also knocked smaller branches off of trees, blew around loose debris, including trampolines, and knocked some shingles off of roofs.

A strong and destructive downslope windstorm impacted the northern Wasatch Front, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 102 mph in Centerville, 92 mph in West Bountiful, 86 mph in Farmington, and numerous other reports in the 60 to 80 mph range.||Damage from this windstorm was substantial and widespread, with the most extensive damage occurring between North Salt Lake and South Ogden. UDOT reported that 11 semitrailers were knocked over along I-15, which eventually led them to close the road to semis for several hours. In Fruit Heights, a steeple was blown off the roof of a church. Hundreds of trees, power lines, and light poles were knocked over, and some of these caused additional damage when they landed on houses, cars, and other property. The winds were strong enough to shatter windows in some locations, as well as bend or uproot many metal road signs. In the area of the strongest winds, almost all homes experienced damage to roofs, fences, and siding. Flying debris caused a few injuries, but there were no fatalities associated with the wind. ||Monetary damage to infrastructure was calculated to be about $6.5 million, almost all of which occurred in Davis County. Private insured losses were a little over $75 million.

While not as strong or long-lived as in the northern Wasatch Front, the Salt Lake Valley also experienced damaging downslope winds. Maximum recorded wind gusts included 69 mph at the University of Utah and 63 mph at the Mouth of Parley's. In addition, a middle school student in Salt Lake City was seriously injured when a large tree branch fell on him as he was walking to school.

Three men, a skier and two split-boarders, went up Big Cottonwood Canyon on the morning of January 28th. They eventually reached Kessler Peak, and began to descend the west face, with one of the split-boarders in the lead. The man in the lead triggered a hard slab avalanche, which averaged 3 feet deep and nearly 1,000 feet wide.  The avalanche ran 2,500 feet vertically. The man was buried in the avalanche, and the other two friends, who were above the avalanche path, began attempts to locate him. They eventually found him and dug him out, but he died on the scene.

Heavy rainfall in the Cache Valley, combined with frozen ground and snowmelt, produced flooding in portions of Mendon and Wellsville. Culverts in those areas quickly became clogged with debris, and several homes reported basement flooding. State Route 23 was also closed for a period of time due to water flowing across the road.
Heavy rainfall on frozen ground, combined with some snowmelt, led to the flooding of some residential basements in Liberty, Utah. This flooding was eventually mitigated with pumps and sandbags.

Heavy rain caused flooding in and around the town of Morgan, Utah, with the most damage occurring along Morgan Valley Drive. Four residential basements were flooded in this area, and water flowed over some roadways.
More heavy rainfall occurred across the Ogden Valley, causing isolated flooding incidents. Water flowed across several roadways, and six homes near the Wolf Mountain ski resort experienced flooding.

Four snowmobilers were finishing up a day of riding west of Lost Creek Reservoir. They were well aware of the avalanche danger, and as such, had avoided climbing any hills through the day. However, wanting to get back home quicker, they cut across one of the hills, and an avalanche was triggered. One rider was quickly caught in the slide, but was able to stay on his sled, and grabbed the throttle, which propelled him out of the slide area. A second rider was caught and fully buried in the snow. After more than an hour of searching by his fellow riders, he was eventually found and dug out, but he had already passed away.

The Dump Fire began on June 21st on the west side of Utah Lake, and was caused by target shooters using explosive targets. This fire threatened the communities of Saratoga Springs and Eagle Mountain, leading to the evacuation of nearly 600 homes and 2,500 people beginning on June 22nd. Fire suppression was able to keep the fire from reaching the communities, and the evacuations were lifted by the end of June 23rd. The fire was 100% contained on June 25th, after it had burned a total of 5,507 acres. Two firefighters were injured; one received a first degree burn, and the other became dehydrated and required transport to a local hospital. The only reported property damage was power line infrastructure damaged in the fire. In addition to this damage, fire suppression costs totaled $2.1 million.

The Wood Hollow Fire began on June 23rd near Fountain Green, Utah in Sanpete County. The fire was ignited when gusty winds caused a power line to come too close to the top of another power pole, sparking a grass fire at its base. The electrical ground wires had been removed by copper thieves, which eliminated the system's ability to properly dissipate the electrical current. This fire caused one fatality, a 60-year-old male whose body was found inside a burned car. Two firefighters also sustained minor injuries.||In total, the Wood Hollow Fire burned 47,387 acres, and caused extensive property damage. The communities of Indian Ridge, Elk Ridge, Big Hollow, and Oaker Hills all experienced mandatory evacuations.  52 residential buildings were destroyed, 108 other non-residential buildings were destroyed, and there was damage to local power infrastructure and the Indian Ridge water system. Some livestock was lost, with approximately 300 sheep killed and approximately 15 horses killed. In addition to these losses, fire suppression costs totaled $5.8 million. Note that this fire continued into July, and the monetary property damages will be listed in July's report.

A tree fell onto a power line in West Jordan, Utah, igniting a field. This fire quickly spread into nearby homes, burning two houses. In addition, a third home suffered significant smoke damage, and the fire damaged a fence and a gazebo. One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion while battling the blaze, which was put out later that day.

A fire started in a field in Draper, Utah, damaging one home and threatening two others. The fire burned through 150 feet of wooden fencing, and caused light damage to a garage and a vehicle at one of the homes, before being contained 25 minutes later.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: The Quail Fire began near Leeds, Utah on June 23rd, and was ignited by people burning debris. The fire threatened some residences in the area, with approximately 60 homes being evacuated, and also threatened a desert tortoise habitat. Two sheds were destroyed in the fire, local power infrastructure was damaged, and one firefighter suffered a heat-related injury. The fire burned 1,708 acres before being 100% contained on June 25th, and fire suppression cost a total of $250,000. This fire is not to be confused with another Quail Fire that began in July near Alpine, Utah.

The Seeley Fire began on June 23rd in the Manti-La Sal National Forest, and was caused by lightning. This fire burned for nearly a month, consuming 48,050 acres before it was 100% contained on July 18th. The fire closed several campgrounds and youth camps, shut down a major oil and gas field, shut down several working coal mines, and caused the evacuation of approximately 250 residences. Two non-residential buildings were damaged in the fire. In addition to the property damages, fire suppression efforts on the fire cost a total of $8.7 million. Note that this event continued into July, and monetary property damages will be listed on the July report.

The Church Camp Fire began on June 24th, approximately 22 miles south of Duchesne, Utah. The cause of the fire is unknown, but it was believed to be human-caused. The fire caused the evacuation of Argyle Canyon, a popular summer cabin and recreation area. A total of 7,211 acres were burned before the fire was 100% contained on July 7th. Three injuries to firefighters were reported, with one back injury and two heat-related injuries. The fire destroyed 15 cabins and 78 other non-residential buildings. In addition to the property damage, fire suppression costs totaled $12.2 million. Note that this event continued into July, and monetary property damage totals will be listed on the July report.

The New Harmony Fire started on June 27th near New Harmony, Utah, due to a water pump malfunction on private land. The fire burned 1,957 acres before it was 100% contained on June 30th. 7 residences were destroyed, 22 non-residential buildings were destroyed, and numerous vehicles were heavily damaged. At least 60 power poles were damaged in the fire, and there was one injury, a firefighter who received first and second degree burns. In addition to physical damages, fire suppression costs totaled $421,000.

The Clay Springs Fire began on July 27th east of Delta, Utah, and was human-caused. Clay Springs was the largest fire of the year in the state of Utah, burning a total of 107,846 acres before it was 100% contained on July 21st. The fire forced the evacuation of nearly 1,000 people, including the entire communities of Oak City and Fool Creek. Damages from the fire included one cabin that was destroyed, minor damage to a few other residences, 3 city storage structures destroyed, and dozens of power poles damaged. Two firefighters were injured by the blaze. In addition to physical damages, fire suppression cost a total of $6.6 million. Note that this event continued into July, and monetary property damages will be listed on the July report.

The Pole Creek Fire started on June 27th, eight miles north of Neola, Utah, and was caused by fireworks. The fire burned 2,058 acres before it was 100% contained on July 3rd. Two firefighters were injured by the blaze. Fire suppression costs totaled $317,000. Note that this event continued into July.

The Rose Crest Fire began on July 29th in Herriman, Utah. The fire was started when a car was parked on a very dry field; the heat from the car ignited the grass, and the fire quickly spread into the residential neighborhood. The fire forced the evacuation of nearly 1,000 residences, and eventually burned 612 acres before it was 100% contained on July 2nd. 4 residences were destroyed, 8 other residences sustained moderate to heavy damage, and 30 non-residential buildings were destroyed. In addition to these property damages, the fire suppression cost a total of $540,000. Note that this event continued into July, and monetary property damages will be listed on the July report.

Note that this event began in June, and monetary property damages listed on this report are for the entire month.

The Seeley Fire began on June 23rd in the Manti-La Sal National Forest, and was caused by lightning. This fire burned for nearly a month, consuming 48,050 acres before it was 100% contained on July 18th. The fire closed several campgrounds and youth camps, shut down a major oil and gas field, shut down several working coal mines, and caused the evacuation of approximately 250 residences. Two non-residential buildings were damaged in the fire. In addition to the property damages, fire suppression efforts on the fire cost a total of $8.7 million. Note that this event began in June, and monetary property damages listed here are for the entire event.

The Church Camp Fire began on June 24th, approximately 22 miles south of Duchesne, Utah. The cause of the fire is unknown, but it was believed to be human-caused. The fire caused the evacuation of Argyle Canyon, a popular summer cabin and recreation area. A total of 7,211 acres were burned before the fire was 100% contained on July 7th. Three injuries to firefighters were reported, with one back injury and two heat-related injuries. The fire destroyed 15 cabins and 78 other non-residential buildings. In addition to the property damage, fire suppression costs totaled $12.2 million. Note that this event began in June, and monetary property damage listed here is for the entire event.

The Shingle Fire began on July 1st, five miles east of Duck Creek, Utah and 4 miles south of State Route 14. The fire was caused by sparks from an ATV. In total, the Shingle Fire burned 8,061 acres before it was 100% contained on July 11th. Four firefighters were injured while fighting the blaze. The fire caused the evacuation of approximately 500 structures, and ultimately destroyed one residence and one non-residential building. In addition to these property damages, fire suppression costs totaled $7.1 million.

The Quail Fire began in the foothills above Alpine, Utah on July 3rd, and was likely caused by a construction crew operating a back hoe. The fire burned 2,222 acres before it was 100% contained on July 10th. Multiple subdivisions in the Alpine area, comprised of more than 500 homes, were evacuated due to the fire. The fire destroyed one large barn and damaged five residences. In addition to these property damages, fire suppression costs totaled $1.5 million. This fire is not to be confused with another Quail Fire that occurred in June near Leeds, Utah.
Flash flooding was reported in the Subway, a popular slot canyon in Zion National Park.
A debris flow occurred on the Seeley burn scar following heavy rains. The flooding originated from near Engineer Canyon, and crossed State Route 31.

The Baboon Fire began on July 12th, five miles southwest of Minersville, Utah, and was caused by lightning. The fire was originally thought to be 100% contained on July 16th, but began to spread again later in the month, when it was truly 100% contained on July 27th. This second flare-up caused no additional structural damage, and burned an additional 1,700 acres, bringing the total acreage consumed by the fire to 20,732 acres. This fire threatened the Circle Four Hog Farm, a very large farm with hundreds of thousands of pigs. Employees were evacuated from the farm for a short period of time, but the pigs were not evacuated. State Route 130 was also closed for about a day due to the fire. Two non-residential buildings were destroyed in the fire, one of them being a commercial building. In addition to these property damages, fire suppression costs totaled $650,000.

A 24-year-old male was fishing at Row Lake, on the west side of Boulder Mountain, on the evening of July 21st. When a thunderstorm moved into the area, both the man and his dog took shelter under a tree. Lightning struck the tree, and both the man and the dog were killed.
A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was measured at the Utah Test and Training Range, and windows were damaged on 7 of the cars in the parking lot.
The Ogden Peak sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 77 mph.
The Target S sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 64 mph.

A strong thunderstorm moved through the Tooele Valley, producing severe winds. Recorded wind gusts included 65 mph at South Mountain and the Great Salt Lake Marina, 62 mph at the Lake Point at I-80 sensor, and 59 mph at the Tooele City and Stockton Bar sensors.
The St. George RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The Salt Flats sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
Flash flooding occurred in the upper portions of the Coal Creek drainage, near Brian Head, temporarily closing State Route 143.

The Wood Hollow Fire began on June 23rd near Fountain Green, Utah in Sanpete County. The fire was ignited when gusty winds caused a power line to come too close to the top of another power pole, sparking a grass fire at its base. The electrical ground wires had been removed by copper thieves, which eliminated the system's ability to properly dissipate the electrical current. This fire caused one fatality, a 60-year-old male whose body was found inside a burned car. Two firefighters also sustained minor injuries. In total, the Wood Hollow Fire burned 47,387 acres, and caused extensive property damage. The communities of Indian Ridge, Elk Ridge, Big Hollow, and Oaker Hills all experienced mandatory evacuations. 52 residential buildings were destroyed, 108 other non-residential buildings were destroyed, and there was damage to local power infrastructure and the Indian Ridge water system. Some livestock was lost, with approximately 300 sheep killed and approximately 15 horses killed. In addition to these losses, fire suppression costs totaled $5.8 million. Note that this fire began in June, and the monetary property damages listed here are from the entire length of the fire.

A sensor near Point of the Mountain, named Portable RWIS #2, recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph. In addition, damage was reported in the Spanish Fork area, with multiple trees and power lines blown over.
A sensor in Nephi, Utah recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
A thunderstorm dropped enough hail on Hurricane, Utah to cover the ground, with an estimated maximum hail size of 1 inch in diameter.
Moderate sized tree branches were downed by thunderstorm winds in La Verkin, Utah.
Multiple slot canyons in Zion National Park experienced flash flooding.
Flash flooding occurred on the Fort Pearce Wash, with the gauge along the wash indicating that the flow quickly increased to 935 cfs.
Flash flooding occurred in multiple small canyons in Zion National Park, including Telephone Canyon.

Flash flooding occurred across parts of Capitol Reef National Park, including along Sulphur Creek. The worst of the flooding was in the Cathedral Valley area of the park, where roads were washed out, with trenches 2.5 feet deep.
A large flash flood occurred on Wahweap Creek and was observed as it passed through Big Water. The high water from Wahweap Creek cut off the Smokey Mountain Road.
An ash flow was reported after heavy rain fell over the Wood Hollow burn scar. Parts of Wood Hollow Road were washed out due to this flash flood.

Major flash flooding occurred in St. George, Utah, as heavy rain fell over the area for nearly an hour. The rain overwhelmed many of the storm drains across the city, with manhole covers popping up in a few locations, including Main Street. Water rose as high as three or four feet on some streets, and several drivers were stranded in their cars with water up to their windows. A few small landslides were reported, and mud and debris flowed onto some streets. Approximately 100 homes and a few businesses experienced at least minor damage.
The Beaver Dam Wash experienced a flash flood, with flow in the wash increasing from zero to 1244 cfs.
Flash flooding occurred along Sulphur Creek in Capitol Reef National Park, impacting a section of State Route 24.
The Fort Pearce Wash experienced a large flash flood, with flows in the wash increasing from zero to 8049 cfs.
Numerous drainages within Zion National Park experienced flash flooding, most notably La Verkin Creek and Spry Canyon.
Flash flooding was reported in Buckskin Gulch and surrounding drainages.
Flash flooding was reported in some drainages near Hurricane, Utah.
Flash flooding was reported along the Paria River, including where the river meets State Route 89.
A large debris flow occurred on the Seeley burn scar, originating from canyons of Nuc Woodward, South Hughes, and Chute, with debris flowing onto State Route 31.
A hiker was struck by lightning near Amethyst Lake, which is located in the Uinta Mountains. He was transported to a hospital in critical condition, but recovered from the injuries and survived.

A large debris flow occurred at the Wood Hollow burn scar. This debris flow damaged multiple homes, with two homes in particular receiving significant damage. The main damage was caused by mud flowing into basements, with one home having muddy water pooled as much as 8 feet deep in the basement. In addition, the debris crossed over State Route 132 and closed the road for several hours.
Flash flooding was reported adjacent to Rockville, Utah, flowing into the Virgin River.
Yet another debris flow occurred at the Seeley burn scar, this one originating from South Hughes Canyon. Debris once again flowed over State Route 31.
Sulphur Creek in Capitol Reef National Park flash flooded once again, this time with a 3 to 4 foot flood wave crossing under the bridge of State Route 24, not far from the visitors center.
A flash flood occurred on Coal Creek, with the gauge there increasing from 44 cfs to 1021 cfs in one hour.

Multiple drainages across Zion National Park experienced significant flash flooding. The North Fork of the Virgin River was included, with the gauge there increasing from 59 cfs to 1433 cfs in two hours.

Gusty west-northwesterly winds were observed across the northern Wasatch Front, with a peak observed wind gust of 51 mph at both Bothwell and Washington Terrace. In addition, an empty semitrailer was blown over on Interstate 15 near Brigham City, briefly causing traffic issues on the northbound thoroughfare.
Flash flooding was reported by the park rangers at Capitol Reef National Park. This flooding primarily occurred along the Scenic Drive, closing the Grand Wash and Capitol Gorge areas.
The Milford ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
The Beaver County Sheriff reported a tornado along the Utah/Nevada border.
The Camel Back Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.

A large line of thunderstorms moved into far western Utah on the evening of August 31st, bringing severe wind gusts. Peak recorded gusts included 72 mph at Wendover Airport, 61 mph at Wendover Peak, and 58 mph at the North Salt Flats sensor.

A line of thunderstorms intensified as it reached the Great Salt Lake, with peak recorded wind gusts of 78 mph at the I-80 at Grassey sensor, 67 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 65 mph at Hat Island, and 62 mph at the Eagle Range sensor.

The Pinyon Fire began on Pinyon Hill on the afternoon of August 5th, and was caused by lightning. Pinyon Hill is located on the property of Army Garrison Camp Williams, a National Guard training site, and the fire largely burned within the confines of Camp Williams. The Pinyon Fire caused evacuations of about 100 homes in Eagle Mountain, and also jumped containment lines at one point to threaten parts of Herriman. Approximately 5,771 acres were burned before the fire was 100% contained on August 12th. The only major structural damage occurred at Camp Williams, where a mock Afghan village used for training purposes was damaged. The village had been built in 2010 at a total cost of $360,000, and 9 of the 15 buildings were damaged by the fire. In addition, fire suppression costs totaled $200,000.
Flash flooding was reported along Buckskin Gulch, blocking the route to The Wave, a popular hiking area.
Flash flooding was reported in Johnson Canyon, with a park ranger in the area calling it an average-sized flash flood.
Flash flooding was reported near Sheets Gulch and surrounding areas, with water flowing across Notom-Bullfrog Road and other roads on the east side of Capitol Reef National Park.
Flash flooding was reported along Sulpher Creek near Capitol Reef National Park, with the leading wave of the flood reaching 4 feet in height.
Flash flooding occurred along the Paria River, with the river gauge reaching a peak observation of 3850 cfs.
Flash flooding was reported by park rangers in the Buckskin Gulch area.

After an estimated 1.25 inches of rain fell over Zion National Park, flash flooding was reported in Spry Canyon, Pine Creek Canyon, and Echo Canyon. The heavy rainfall also caused rocks to fall onto State Route 9, between the switchbacks and the tunnel, which impacted traffic through the park.
Estimated rainfall amounts of 1.5 to 2 inches fell over southern Washington County, causing flash flooding around parts of Hildale.

Major flash flooding occurred in the cities of Enoch and Cedar City on the afternoon of August 17th. Enoch had the most significant damage, with 110 houses damaged by flood waters, while Cedar City mostly experienced street flooding. About 30 of those 110 houses experienced major damage, typically over $30,000 per house, while the rest had more minor damage. Flood waters and some sewage poured into many basements, as well as some ground level floors. The water broke windows and destroyed carpets, walls, and personal belongings in many of the homes.

A large flash flood along the Paria River was observed as it passed under State Route 89. The spotter estimated that the first 200 to 300 yards of the flood was composed of debris, including trees and logs. The gauge along the river increased to 8200 cfs.
Flash flooding occurred once again along the Paria River, with the river gauge readings peaking at 2625 cfs.
Multiple drainages southeast of the Pine Valley Mountains experienced flash flooding.
Flash flooding was reported along the North Fork of the Virgin River and in the Narrows. The river gauge at the North Fork of the Virgin went from 53 to 1054 cfs in one hour.
A large flash flood occurred in the area around 25 Mile Wash, damaging roads in the area.

A large flash flood occurred in the Subway portion of Zion National Park, as well as a few other surrounding drainages. Due to this flood, 22 people in 6 different groups were stranded in the Subway overnight. Two additional people were stranded overnight in Behunin Canyon.
Flash flooding was reported along the Escalante River, where it runs adjacent to State Route 12. Some water crossed over the road west of the city of Escalante.
A large flash flood was reported along the Paria River, with water flowing over the Skudampah Road.
Multiple flash floods were reported in the upper Kanab Creek drainage.

Flash flooding occurred along La Verkin Creek on the evening of August 1st, with significant rises in the water level. At the same time, a 2-year-old girl was noticed missing from her home in the city of La Verkin, which was close to the creek. The girl passed away when she drowned in the Creek, and her body was found a couple hours after she had been reported missing.

After approximately 1.25 inches of rainfall, a very large debris flow occurred on the Seeley Burn Scar. Debris flowed over State Route 31, causing significant damage to a 1/4 mile stretch of the road, as well as a nearby bridge. Debris of up to 3 feet in height was spread over about a mile of the roadway. State Route 31 was closed for over a week, as crews repaired the road damage and cleared boulders and other debris off the roadway. The debris flow also pushed a UDOT front loader off the road and into a ditch, partially covering it with debris.

Multiple flash floods were reported in the Wahweap drainage, the Cottonwood Wash, and the Coyote Wash. Many roads across the area were closed, including Cottonwood Wash Road, Nipple Creek Road, Coyote Wash Road, and Houserock Road.
Penny to quarter sized hail was reported on Interstate 15 between mile markers 230 and 235.
Marble to quarter sized hail was reported along Interstate 80 near Milepost 20.
One inch hail was reported near US-50, close to the Utah/Nevada border.
One inch hail was reported in Farmington.
A maximum wind gust of 62 mph was reported at the Interstate 80 sensor.
A maximum wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the Fremont Junction sensor.
The US-40 at Starvation sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The Beaver Dam Wash experienced a flash flood, with the reading on the gauge along the wash increasing from 96 cfs to 4367 cfs in one hour.

Flash flooding was reported in multiple locations across Capitol Reef National Park. Flooding occurred along Sulphur Creek, and water also flowed across the Scenic Drive, causing park officials to temporarily close the road.

Flash flooding was reported in multiple locations across Zion National Park, including in the Narrows. The North Fork of the Virgin River rose from 52 cfs to 1004 cfs in one hour. Large waterfalls coming off of cliffs closed numerous hikes and temporarily stranded hikers.
Flooding was reported over the bridge where old US Highway 91 crosses the Santa Clara River. This flooding caused the road to be closed for a few hours in the late morning and early afternoon.
Park rangers at Capitol Reef National Park reported flash flooding along both Sulphur Creek and Sheets Gulch.

Heavy rain over the Seeley burn scar caused yet another debris flow in the area. The flooding originated from Pole and Engineer Canyons, and caused damage along State Route 31. Car-sized boulders were deposited on State Route 31 at the base of Pole Canyon.

Flash flooding was reported along Stout Creek. This flooding damaged a fly fishing operation along the creek, including filling a pond with silt, damaging a small bridge, and causing some erosion damage.

An extended period of moderate to heavy rainfall occurred in southwest Utah on the morning of September 11th, during which 3.24 inches of rainfall was measured in Ivins, Utah. In nearby Santa Clara, an earthen dike (called the Laub Dike) burst, releasing all of the water in the associated retention pond. This water and mud flowed into nearby homes and businesses, damaging both public infrastructure and private properties. A total of $3.8 million in damage was done to public infrastructure, including damage to the dike, streets, and sidewalks. The flood also damaged 16 businesses and 63 homes; some of these buildings had internal damage due to water and mud flowing into them, while other buildings experienced serious structural damage.

Heavy rain over the Dump Fire burn scar created a debris flow, flooding a portion of Saratoga Springs, and forcing the closure of Highway 68 for a period of time. Twenty residences experienced flood damage, with 11 of those homes having water in their basements, and 9 of those homes experiencing solely yard damage. Finished basements were completely destroyed in 5 separate homes, with the most impacted home having mud nine feet deep in the basement. Structural damage to homes was estimated at $250,000, and many personal possessions inside the homes were also damaged or destroyed. Public infrastructure was also impacted, with approximately $200,000 worth of damage to a nearby park and $50,000 of fencing destroyed.

Heavy rain over the Clay Springs burn scar caused a debris flow on the afternoon of September 1st. Four homes in the Fools Creek area experienced flooded basements, and one yard was severely damaged. In addition, a single wide trailer in the same area was pushed off its foundation. Six to eight inches of mud and debris crossed Highway 125, causing some damage along the edges of the roadway.

Flash flooding occurred in Capitol Reef National Park, with all washes along Scenic Drive producing 6 to 8 inch flows across the road. This flooding caused many of the dirt roads across the park to be impassable for a few days. In addition, a large tree fell over State Route 24 due to erosion along the Fremont River, closing the highway for about an hour and a half. Water also crossed over State Route 24 at milepost 100 near Caineville.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong wind gusts occurred across the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains with the cold front, with maximum recorded gusts of 64 mph at Promontory Point, 63 mph at the SR-30 at Curlew sensor, 62 mph at the Curlew Junction sensor, 60 mph at Lakeside Mountain, and 58 mph at the Wendover Point of Entry.
The Baccus/SR-111 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
The Flight Park South sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph, and the Pleasant Grove RAWS recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
The Powder Mountain sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 84 mph.

The Wasatch Mountains north of I-80 had the largest snow totals in Utah from this storm. Much of the snow fell early in the event, with Randolph receiving 9 inches of snow in the first 12 hours of the event, and Monte Cristo receiving 26 inches of snow in the first 24 hours of the event. Eventual storm totals included 42 inches of snow at Powder Mountain, 30 inches at Monte Cristo, and 17 inches of snow at both Randolph and Laketown.

Heavy snow occurred across the Ogden Valley, with storm totals of 28 inches of snow in Liberty and 21 inches of snow in Eden. The early snowfall also impacted other parts of the Wasatch mountain valleys, with school being cancelled at Mountain Green Elementary and Morgan Elementary, and downed trees causing power outages in multiple communities, including Kamas.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Gunnison Island sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
Peak recorded wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys included 63 mph at Vernon Hill and 59 mph at Stockton Bar.
The US-6 at Eureka sensor recorded strong winds for several hours, with a peak wind gust of 68 mph.

Heavy snow fell over the northern Wasatch Front, with a storm total of 7 inches of snow reported in South Ogden and 5 inches on the Bountiful Bench. Combined with the fact that many trees still had their leaves intact, fallen tree branches were common, and some smaller trees were completely toppled. In addition to cleanup costs, some of these fallen trees also caused power outages for hundreds of customers across the area, primarily in South Ogden and West Haven.

Generally 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across the southern Wasatch Front with this storm system. Combined with the fact that most trees still had their leaves intact, many fallen tree branches were reported, causing power outages primarily in Lindon and Pleasant Grove.

Storm totals in the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys included 7 inches of snow in Tooele and 6 inches in Upper Millcreek. Combined with the fact that most trees still had their leaves intact, several fallen tree branches were reported across the area.

Snow levels reached the floor of the Cache Valley on the morning of October 23, much earlier in the storm than along the Wasatch Front. Generally 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across the Cache Valley through the storm. Combined with the fact that most trees still had their leaves intact, many fallen tree branches were reported, causing power outages to several hundred homes.

Peak recorded wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 74 mph at Vernon Hill and the Great Salt Lake Marina, 61 mph at Flight Park South, and 58 mph at the I-80 at Milepost 78 sensor.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts in the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains included 59 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, and 58 mph at Simpson Springs, Badger Island, Callao Gate, and Antelope Island.
Storm total snowfall in west central Utah included 13.5 inches of snow in Oak City, 13 inches of snow in Fillmore, and 12 inches of snow in Delta.
The US-6 at Eureka sensor recorded strong winds for several hours, with a peak gust of 67 mph.
The Parrish Creek SNOTEL received a storm total of 3.10 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 27 inches of new snow.

The Wasatch Mountains south of Interstate 80 received heavy snowfall from the initial cold front, and from the subsequent lake effect snowfall, leading to high snow amounts across the area. Storm totals included 54 inches of snow at Alta Ski Lifts, 51 inches at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort, and 29 inches at Brighton Resort.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received a storm total of 2.10 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 27 inches of new snow.
The Clear Creek #1 SNOTEL received a storm total of 1.50 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.
The Farnsworth Lake SNOTEL received 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow.
The Midway Valley SNOTEL received 2.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 35 inches of new snow.

The cold front brought a first round of snowfall to the northern Wasatch Front on November 9, followed by significant lake effect snow accumulations on both November 10 and November 11. Storm total snowfall included 31.5 inches of snow at Bountiful Bench, 22 inches in Centerville, 20 inches at the North Salt Lake Bench, 16 inches in Bountiful, and 12 inches of snow in Fruit Heights. Some minor tree damage occurred due to the wet, heavy snow at the beginning of the event, but damage was less significant than further south along the Wasatch Front. This was partially due to a previous storm in October that had downed many of the weaker tree branches in the northern Wasatch Front.

The Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys received a first round of snowfall on November 9, followed by significant lake effect snow accumulations both November 10 and 11. Storm totals included 27.5 inches of snow at Upper Millcreek, 25 inches at Cottonwood Heights, 23 inches in Sandy, 21 inches in the Upper Avenues, 15 inches at the Salt Lake International Airport, and 11 inches of snow in Tooele. The wet, heavy snowfall on November 9 caused widespread damage to tree branches, many of which still had leaves in place from the warm autumn. Several of these downed branches also caused power outages across the area.

Storm totals for the southern Wasatch Front in this 3-day event included 12 inches of snow in Springville, 12 inches in Suncrest, and 11 inches of snow in Pleasant Grove. In addition, significant tree damage occurred across the area, with the worst of the damage in the Provo area. Several of these downed tree limbs hit power lines, causing temporary power outages across the area.

During a period of lake effect snowfall, a funnel cloud formed over the southern Wasatch Front, near the southern end of Utah Lake. It was spotted by a member of the general public who was near Provo Municipal Airport, and the funnel cloud dissipated fairly quickly without touching the ground.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts across the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains included 68 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 65 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 64 mph at Promontory Point, and 58 mph at the Durand Road sensor.
The strongest winds experienced in the Tooele Valley were southerly winds ahead of the cold front. Peak recorded wind gusts included 63 mph at Stockton Bar and 62 mph at South Mountain.
The Snowbasin Straw Top sensor recorded several hours of strong winds, including a peak wind gust of 82 mph.
Wellington received 9 inches of snow from this event, while Ferron received 6 inches of snow.
The Hans Flat Ranger Station reported 8 inches of new snow for the storm.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow and strong winds both accompanied the storm in the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains.
