Snowville reported 6 inches of new snow, and peak wind gusts included 62 mph at the Utah Test and Training Range Thermal Treatment Unit sensor, 61 mph at  Lakeside Mountain, and 59 mph at Hat Island.

The Wasatch Mountains north of Interstate 80 experienced both heavy snow and strong winds with this event. The Tony Grove Lake SNOTEL received 1.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow. A storm total of 15 inches of new snow was also reported in the mountains west of Laketown. Peak wind gusts across the area included 95 mph at Ogden Peak and 83 mph at the Red Spur RAWS.

Storm total snowfall across the Wasastch Mountains south of Interstate 80 included 56 inches at Brighton Resort, 40 inches of snow at Alta Ski Lifts, and 26 inches of snow at Solitude Mountain Resort.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 1.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 22 inches of new snow.
The Clear Creek #1 SNOTEL received a storm total of 1.60 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 23 inches of new snow.

The cold front on the 17th of December intensified as it moved into central Utah, bringing heavy snowfall to the southern Wasatch Front after it had bypassed the northern Wasatch Front. Storm total snowfall from this area included 13 inches in Woodland Hills, 11 inches in Mapleton, and 10 inches in Springville.
Richfield received 8 inches of new snow, while Ephraim and Gunnison both reported 6 inches of new snow.
Storm total snow reports included 7 inches of snow at Eureka, and 6 inches of new snow at both Delta and Oak City.
Cedar City received 9 inches of snow for the storm.
The Dill's Camp SNOTEL received 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow.
The Kimberly Mine SNOTEL received 1.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.
The Ben Lomond Peak SNOTEL received 1.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow.
Storm totals across the area included 21 inches of snow at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort, 18 inches of snow at Alta Ski Lifts, and 15 inches of snow at Canyons.
Storm totals in the Cache Valley included 9 inches in Richmond and North Logan, as well as 8 inches in Logan and Smithfield.
Liberty received a storm total of 32 inches of snow.
Storm totals from the northern Wasatch Front included 10 inches of snow at Northeast Ogden Bench, 9 inches at North Ogden, and 8 inches of new snow at South Ogden.
For the two-day storm, Alpine received a storm total of 23 inches of snow, while Draper received 18 inches of new snow.
Storm total snowfall included 36 inches at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort and 30 inches of snow at Alta Ski Lifts.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Storm totals across the Great Salt Lake Desert included 14 inches of new snow at Snowville and 13 inches of snow at Ibapah.  In addition, an accident along Interstate 80 in Tooele County resulted in a fatality, when an SUV hit a patch of black ice and rolled. The passenger was ejected and killed, and the driver was seriously injured.
Storm totals from the Wasatch mountain valleys included 9 inches of new snow at Jeremy Ranch and 8 inches of snow at Liberty.
Storm totals in the Cache Valley included 10 inches of snow in Millville and Richmond, 9 inches in Logan and Providence, and 8 inches of snow in Smithfield.
The Ben Lomond Peak SNOTEL received 1.80 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 28 inches of new snow. In addition, Snowbasin Resort received 22 inches of new snow.

Storm totals in the northern Wasatch Front included 12 inches of snow in Centerville and Bountiful, 9 inches in Garland, and 8 inches of snow in Clearfield, West Haven, and South Ogden. In addition, the snow created hazardous driving conditions; Davis County had the most incidents across the entire Wasatch Front, with 40 crashes and 28 slide-offs.

Storm totals across the Salt Lake Valley included 10 inches of new snow at Salt Lake City International Airport, 9 inches in Upper Millcreek, and 8 inches of snow in South Salt Lake and Draper. In addition, the snow created hazardous driving conditions across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys, with at least 20 accidents reported across the area.
The Kimberly Mine SNOTEL received 1.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 17 inches of new snow, with most of this snowfall occurring in the first six hours of the event.

The Pine Creek SNOTEL received 1.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow. In addition, winds were strong with the passage of the initial cold front, with the Signal Peak RAWS recording a maximum wind gust of 80 mph.

The Strawberry Divide SNOTEL received 1.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 23 inches of new snow. Travel was also impacted along State Route 40, including a Greyhound bus that crashed near Strawberry Reservoir; no injuries were  reported with the crash.
Storm total snowfall in west central Utah included 11 inches of new snow in Fillmore, 7 inches in Oak City, and 6 inches of snow in Delta.

The East Fork of the Black's Fork SNOTEL received 0.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 14 inches of new snow. Winds were also strong in the Uinta Mountains during the event, with the Chepeta RAWS recording a peak wind gust of 77 mph.
Storm total snowfall in the area included 21 inches of new snow at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort, 15 inches at Brighton Resort, and 14 inches of snow at Alta Ski Area.

Storm totals in the Wasatch Mountains north of Interstate 80 included 32 inches of new snow in Emigration Canyon, 26 inches of snow at Snowbasin Resort, and 16 inches of snow at Powder Mountain. In addition, winds were strong ahead of and with the initial cold front, with peak recorded wind gusts of 80 mph at the Snowbasin Straw Top sensor.
Liberty received 28 inches of new snow for the event.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains received a combination of heavy snow and strong winds, which led to blowing snow and lowered visibilities across Interstate 80. The Dry Fork SNOTEL received 1.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of snow. In addition, the Wendover Peak sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 65 mph.

A family was out for a day of snowmobiling in the Uinta Mountains, when they decided to take a break for lunch in a wide open basin on the West Fork of the Duchesne River. The kids walked to a edge of a ridge to see over the side when the ledge gave way, catching three of the children in an avalanche, and burying two of them. The two boys were eventually dug out of the snow and carried by helicopter to a local hospital, but they passed away that evening due to their injuries.

Portions of Utah Valley were heavily shadowed during much of this event, with many locations receiving 6 inches of snow or less. However, a few areas had high storm totals, including 22 inches of new snow at Elk Ridge and 20 inches of snow in Payson.

Storm totals across the Salt Lake Valley included 34 inches of snow at Upper Millcreek, 20 inches at Olympus Hills and the Upper Avenues, 19 inches in Holladay, 14 inches in South Salt Lake, and 10 inches of new snow at Salt Lake City International Airport. This snow seriously impaired travel across the area, with Salt Lake County reporting the most accidents in the entire state, with a total of 108 property damage incidents and 128 slide-offs, as well as 7 reported injuries. Strong winds were also observed ahead of and with the initial cold front on January 10, including a 61 mph wind gust at the Great Salt Lake Marina, and 60 mph wind gusts at Olympus Hills and Olympus Cove. These winds knocked over and destroyed the sign for a KFC restaurant in Sandy.

Storm total snowfall in the northern Wasatch Front included 34 inches at Bountiful Bench, 27 inches in Centerville, 21 inches at Woods Cross, 19 inches in South Ogden, and 18 inches of new snow in several locations, including Farmington, Clearfield, Hill Air Force Base, and North Salt Lake. This snowfall greatly impacted transportation in the area, with about 100 reported accidents. Many schools cancelled classes, a rare occurrence in the area, including the entire Davis School District.

The freezing rain was less significant in the Utah Valley than further northward, but still caused travel difficulties. The slick roads were blamed for 90 accidents in the area, two of which caused injuries. In addition, a highway patrol trooper was injured when an out-of-control car struck a cruiser, which was parked while the officer was assisting another vehicle that had slid off the road in Springville. Injuries were also common from people slipping on the ice while walking. Utah Valley Regional Medical Center in Provo reported 70 ice-related injuries, including one death attributed to the icy conditions.

Freezing rain caused hazardous driving conditions along the northern Wasatch Front, with over 50 accidents attributed to the icy roads. Injuries due to slips and falls on the ice were common, with at least 100 injuries reported. Lakeview Hospital in Bountiful reported that the number of patients in the emergency room was the highest single-day total in the history of the hospital.

Of all the areas across Utah, the Salt Lake Valley was perhaps hit the hardest by the freezing rain event. Icy roads caused many automobile accidents, including 128 collisions, 25 accidents resulting in injuries, and 8 slide-offs in Salt Lake County. Two highway patrol officers were struck by out of control cars, with both incidents occurring on Interstate 15. Hundreds of people were injured due to slipping and falling on the ice, with over 100 patients treated for ice-related injuries at Intermountain Medical Center in Murray alone. The freezing rain also had major impacts at the Salt Lake City International Airport, with many flights delayed due to the icy runways. The entire airport was closed for three hours in the late morning and early afternoon, after a Frontier Airlines plane slid down the taxiway.
Logan received 8 inches of new snow from the storm, most of which fell within the first few hours of the cold frontal passage.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Travel was greatly impaired across the Great Salt Lake Desert, particularly along Interstate 80, with very low visibilities and accumulating snow on roadways for a few hours. Winds were strong, creating widespread blowing and drifting snow, with peak recorded wind gusts of 69 mph at the V-Grid sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, 63 mph at the Wendover AWOS, and several other gusts in the 50 mph range along Interstate 80.
Liberty received a storm total of 14 inches new snow. In addition, gusty winds up to 40 mph with the cold frontal passage led to impaired travel, with widespread blowing and drifting snow.
Snowbasin Resort received a storm total of 20 inches new snow, while Powder Mountain received 14 inches of snow.

Storm total snowfall in the Cottonwoods included 18 inches at Brighton Resort, 16 inches at Alta Ski Lifts, and 11 inches of snow at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort. In addition, winds were strong along the peaks, with a maximum recorded wind gust of 80 mph at Cardiff Peak.

Storm totals across the Salt Lake Valley included 10 inches of new snow in Sandy, 9 inches in Cottonwood Heights, and 8 inches of snow in Upper Millcreek. In addition, travel was impaired along the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys; 129 crashes were reported in Salt Lake County alone, with 12 of those resulting in injuries. These adverse conditions included very low visibilities for several hours, as well as strong wind gusts that created widespread blowing and drifting snow. Peak recorded wind gusts included 66 mph at the Lake Point at Interstate 80 sensor, 60 mph at Vernon Hill, and 58 mph at Burmester.

South Ogden received 10 inches of new snow for the storm. In addition, travel was impaired along the northern Wasatch Front, with approximately 60 car accidents reported. Four of these accidents resulted in injuries, including a highway patrol trooper who was hit while providing traffic control for a crash on Interstate 15 in Ogden. Visibilities were very low for several hours, and wind gusts of up to 46 mph created widespread blowing and drifting snow.

Suncrest received a storm total of 10 inches of snow, while Pleasant Grove received 7 inches of new snow. In addition, travel was impaired along the southern Wasatch Front, with approximately 40 automobile accidents reported across the area. Visibilities were low for several hours, and wind gusts up to 40 mph caused blowing and drifting snow.

A group of snowmobilers were recreating on the southern end of the Manti Skyline, just east out of 12 Mile Canyon, in Sevier County. For part of the afternoon, most of the group members were riding independently; however, around 4:00 pm, the group realized one of the members was missing. They had neither heard nor seen the avalanche, but they soon found the path the avalanche had taken, and correctly assumed that the missing group member had been buried under the snow. The group tried to dig out the missing person, a 32-year-old male, and eventually went for help from the local authorities. By the time they were able to find him, nearly five hours later, he had already passed away.

A lake effect snow band formed on the evening of March 22, and persisted through the morning of March 23. Storm totals across the Salt Lake Valley included 8 inches of snow in West Jordan and 6 inches of snow in Draper.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts across the Great Salt Lake Desert included 74 mph at Wendover Peak, 66 mph at Diddle Knoll, and 60 mph at the Interstate 80 at Milepost 29 sensor.
Mountain View, Wyoming received 9 inches of new snow for the storm.
Fillmore received 8 inches of snow for the event.
Kanab received a storm total of 7 inches of snow.
Richfield received 10 inches of snow for the storm.
The Pine Creek SNOTEL received 2.40 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 26 inches of new snow.

The Webster Flat SNOTEL received 2.40 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 30 inches of new snow. In addition, the SR-12 at Boulder Summit sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 80 mph.
The SR-12 at Boulder Summit sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Gusty northwest winds occurred across the west desert, with peak recorded wind gusts of 68 mph at the SR-30 at Curlew Junction sensor, and 58 mph at Diddle Knoll.
Fillmore received 10 inches of new snow for the storm.
Cedar City received a storm total of 9 inches new snow.

Altamont, Utah received the heaviest recorded snowfall from the event, as the cold frontal boundary set up over the Uinta Basin for an extended period of time. For the storm, Altamont received a total of 19 inches new snow.
Heavy snowfall occurred across much of the Uinta Basin, with Altamont recording 6 inches of new snow.
The Lightning Ridge SNOTEL received 2.20 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow for the storm.
Storm total snow amounts included 21 inches at Deer Valley Resort and 18 inches of snow at Park City Mountain Resort.
The Lakefork #1 SNOTEL received 2.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 30 inches of new snow.
The Farnsworth Lake SNOTEL received 2.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 30 inches of new snow.
The Kimberly Mine SNOTEL received 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow.
Summit Park received a storm total of 11 inches new snow.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Gusty north winds developed across the Great Salt Lake Desert and Mountains, with a peak recorded wind gust of 63 mph at both Diddle Knoll and Upper Cedar Mountain. In addition, gusts of 55 to 57 mph were recorded at several sites in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet.

This particular avalanche fatality attracted attention because the victim, a 34-year-old male, was employed by the Utah Department of Transportation to forecast and control avalanche conditions. The victim was on duty, doing fieldwork alone on Kessler Peak (in Big Cottonwood Canyon), when he apparently ventured just a foot or two off of the safer snow. This triggered a small avalanche, but one that traveled through many sparse trees and over a couple cliffs. When he did not report in later that day, the search for him began; he was eventually found on top of the snow near the bottom of the avalanche, but he had already passed away from his injuries.

Easterly downslope winds impacted the Salt Lake Valley, though not as severely as in the northern Wasatch Front. Olympus Cove recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph, while multiple other sensors across the area recorded wind gusts of 55 mph. Several large trees were knocked over across the valley; some of these trees fell onto vehicles, including two vehicles damaged in Olympus Cove and two vehicles damaged in the Sugarhouse area. Power lines were knocked down in multiple locations, most notably in South Salt Lake.

Easterly downslope winds most severely impacted the northern Wasatch Front. Peak recorded wind gusts included 75 mph at Centerville and 65 mph at Farmington. Interstate 15 was closed to high profile vehicles for several hours due to the strong winds. The worst individual incident was a light pole that was blown over at a car dealership in North Salt Lake; the pole landed on several vehicles, causing significant damage to the bed of one pickup truck and some damage to a second truck. Sporadic power outages were reported due to the wind, including multiple transformers that blew out in Weber Canyon. Public infrastructure escaped relatively unscathed, though a few street signs were knocked over or bent. Damage to private property included many downed trees, including a few trees that fell on automobiles, wooden and vinyl fences that were destroyed, shingles that were removed from roofs, and trampolines that went flying out of several backyards. Blowing debris was common, particularly in neighborhoods that had scheduled trash days, but no injuries were reported.
A sensor in Farmington, Utah recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
Lightning struck the top gable of a house in West Jordan; the bolt then traveled about 10 feet and burned part of a satellite dish on the roof of the house.

A plane belonging to the Utah Air National Guard (a KC-135, which is a large plane that provides in-flight refueling for other aircraft) took off from Salt Lake City International Airport on the evening of May 7, and was struck by lightning about 10 minutes after takeoff. The lightning damaged a communications antenna that stretches from the nose to the tail of the aircraft. In addition to knocking out communications, the antenna became loose and hit against the plane repeatedly, damaging the skin of the aircraft. No one was injured in the incident, and the crew was able to use alternate communications to help them return to the airport and land.
The West Salt Flats sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
The Antelope Island State Park sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 68 mph.
The North Salt Flats sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
The Chepeta RAWS recorded several hours of strong wind gusts, with a peak gust of 84 mph.
The Point of the Mountain sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 61 mph.
A strong thunderstorm moved across Interstate 80 in far western Utah, with peak wind gusts of 67 mph at the North Salt Flats sensor and 59 mph at the Interstate 80 at Milepost 29 sensor.
A strong thunderstorm moved across the Great Salt Lake, with the Hat Island sensor recording a 62 mph wind gust, and the Gunnison Island sensor recording a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
Peak recorded wind gusts from a thunderstorm near Wendover included 63 mph at Wendover Peak and 61 mph at the Wendover Point of Entry.
Yet another severe thunderstorm moved through the Wendover area, with peak wind gusts of 67 mph at Wendover Peak and 59 mph at the Interstate 80 at Milepost 1 sensor.

A strong thunderstorm moved through the Salt Lake Valley, with peak recorded wind gusts of 75 mph at the Salt Lake #2 Airport, 66 mph at Baccus Highway, and 58 mph at Mountain View at Dannon Way. In addition, multiple large trees were knocked down in West Jordan, South Jordan, and Taylorsville, including a few that fell on houses and caused damage to roofs.
The Interstate 80 at Grassey sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 68 mph.
A strong thunderstorm moved through the Cache Valley, with the Logan ASOS recording a wind gust of 61 mph.
The Antelope Island sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
Peak recorded wind gusts across the southern Wasatch Front included 72 mph at Flight Park South, 68 mph at Saratoga Springs, 63 mph at the U.S. 6 at Eureka sensor, and 59 mph at Lehi.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet in northwest Utah included 62 mph at Simpson Springs and 58 mph at Diddle Knoll.
The Evanston, Wyoming ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
The Upper Cedar Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
A sensor in Saratoga Springs recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Juilet Road sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Interstate 15 at Black Ridge sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph.
A gustnado formed and was spotted just outside Panguitch, but no damage was reported.
A pair of gustnados formed in close proximity and were spotted just outside Delta, but no damage was reported. Time listed is approximate.
The Locomotive Springs sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph.

Lightning struck the wooden turret of a home near Ogden, setting the roof on fire. The fire spread into one of the upstairs rooms before firefighters were able to put out the blaze. Approximately $20,000 worth of damage occurred, mostly to the roof and electrical wiring.
The Pioneer Crossing sensor near Saratoga Springs, Utah recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Hat Island sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
A sensor in Syracuse, Utah recorded a wind gust of 69 mph.
A sensor in Saratoga Springs recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.

A thunderstorm that rolled through Tooele County caused peak wind gusts of 64 mph at the Interstate 80 at Milepost 29 sensor, 61 mph at the Diddle Knoll sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, and 59 mph at the Wendover Airport AWOS.
The Lower Cedar Mountain sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 64 mph.
The Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded a wind gust of 64 mph.

A long-lived thunderstorm moved through the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, across Interstate 80, and north to the Great Salt Lake. Peak recorded wind gusts along this track included 70 mph at the sensor West of Wildcat Mountain, 69 mph at Interstate 80, 66 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 64 mph at Simpson Springs, 62 mph at Juliet Road, 60 mph at Badger Island, and 58 mph both at Fish Springs and Interstate 80 at Grassey.
The same thunderstorm that produced widespread severe winds in Tooele County eventually moved north into Box Elder County, with a peak recorded wind gust of 70 mph at Gunnison Island.
Peak recorded wind gusts with this thunderstorm included 72 mph at the Great Salt Lake Minerals sensor and 65 mph at Ogden Peak.
The Roosevelt AWOS recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph.
A park ranger at Capitol Reef National Park reported that Sheets Gulch experienced a flash flood, with flooding reaching all the way to the Notom Road, just east of the park boundary.
Another thunderstorm moved through the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, with maximum recorded wind gusts of 64 mph at Juliet Road and 63 mph at Target S.

Multiple sensors recorded severe wind gusts as this thunderstorm crossed Interstate 80. The Interstate 80 at Milepost 29 sensor recorded 66 mph winds; in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, the Diddle Knoll sensor recorded a 65 mph wind gust, and the Interstate 80 sensor topped out at 58 mph.
Peak recorded wind gusts from this thunderstorm included 61 mph at Chaulk Hill and 60 mph at Locomotive Springs.
The Cedar City ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 67 mph.
A gustnado was spotted near Plymouth, Utah, and a picture of the gustnado was captured by a nearby webcam. However, no damage was reported in the area.
The Arrowhead Summit sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The Diddle Knoll sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
The Great Salt Lake Marina sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
The Utah Department of Transportation received a report of hail approximately 0.75 inches in diameter.
Hail approximately the size of a penny was reported near Heber City.
A member of the public in Riverton reported penny-size hail.
The Wendover Peak sensor recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.

Hot temperatures contributed to the deaths of three hikers in southern Utah. On July 3, an elderly couple from California received permits to hike The Wave, a popular destination in far southern Utah. Both victims were found on the morning of July 4, and it is believed that they died during the afternoon of the 3rd, when temperatures were close to 100 degrees.||The third victim, a 35-year-old female from Denver, passed away on the 4th of July. She was hiking with a friend near Spooky Gulch in the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. The two women became lost for a couple hours, before other hikers found them and helped them back toward the trailhead. The victim was struggling in the heat and ran out of water near the trailhead, so her friend ran to find help. When she returned, the victim had no pulse, and all efforts to revive her were unsuccessful.

The Dry Ridge sensor in the Uinta Mountains recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph. In association with this wind event, a large tree fell over at a Boy Scout camp in the Uintas, falling onto a 14-year-old boy. The scout suffered a head contusion, a broken arm, and a broken leg, but the injuries were not life-threatening.
Park rangers at Capitol Reef National Park reported flash flooding on Sulphur Creek, with the flood reaching the Visitor Center at 225 pm MDT.
Park rangers reported flash flooding along Sulphur Creek in Capitol Reef National Park.
A large flash flood occurred along Wahweap Creek, with the water level rising over four feet in a very short period of time.

Heavy rain during the overnight hours caused flash flooding in Little Cottonwood Canyon, resulting in rockslides and mudslides onto the main road along the canyon. The flood deposited debris onto the road, including trees, branches, and rocks. This debris was spread over a large area of the road, from 4 miles down the canyon from Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort, all the way down to the bottom of the canyon. Twelve hours of cleanup was necessary before the road was reopened to automobile traffic. The road was damaged in some locations, particularly along the shoulder, but the integrity of the main roadway was not compromised. The Utah Department of Transportation estimated that the cost of the road repairs would be approximately $80,000.

Another flash flood and rockslide occurred in Little Cottonwood Canyon, less than 24 hours after the first event earlier in the day. In this occurrence, debris blocked a drainage along the road, adding to the water and mud that flowed across the road. Large rocks rolled onto the main roadway, some as large as basketballs. Some additional road damage occurred due to the rocks and flowing water.

Heavy rain over the Salt Lake Valley flooded six residential properties in Midvale and Sandy. A couple of homes had significant basement flooding, while others had flooding on lawns and other outdoor property. The worst of the flooding was near 8000 South and 700 East in Sandy, where two homes had more than $5,000 in damage each.
Flash flooding was reported along Sulphur Creek, including through parts of Capitol Reef National Park.
Flash flooding was reported in Zion National Park, including at the popular canyoneering route called The Subway.
Major flash flooding was reported in the town of Hildale. In addition, water was flowing across State Route 59, moving six to eight inch rocks onto the road between mileposts 4 and 5.
Flash flooding occurred along the Fort Pearce Wash, with the gauge near St. George peaking at 4146 cfs.
Flash flooding was reported in Zion National Park, including in the Subway and all of the headwaters of North Creek.

Hot temperatures returned to southern Utah in late July, and another heat-related death occurred at The Wave, a popular hike near the Utah/Arizona border. A 27-year-old Arizona woman was hiking The Wave with her husband on July 22, when they got lost and spent several hours trying to find their way back to their vehicle. Around 2 p.m., the woman collapsed, and her husband left to get help. When help arrived, she was already in cardiac arrest, and she passed away that afternoon, as emergency responders were unable to revive her.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Taylorsville during the early morning hours of July 4. The flooding occurred at the Atherton Park Apartments, where water flowed into 24 basement-level apartments. Only four of these apartments experienced significant damage, but approximately 75 people were temporarily displaced by the flooding.
Flash flooding occurred in the town of Hildale, closing down the main road through town.

Flash flooding was reported along the Paria River and many of its tributatries, including Buckskin, Lick, Bull, Yellow, and Willis. The flooding impacted Skutumpah Road, with water and mud rising four feet deep along the road.
Flash flooding occurred along the Escalante River and its tributaries, with the Escalante River gauge rising from near zero to 746 cfs in a short period of time.

A debris flow occurred on the Quail Fire burn scar near Alpine after heavy rain fell over the area. Flooding impacted a couple of residential yards and a couple of roads across the area, but major impacts to houses were avoided due to mitigation and rerouting of the flood waters.
Park rangers reported flash flooding across the main portion of Capitol Reef National Park, including in Grand Wash and Capitol Gorge. The Scenic Drive was also closed due to the flooding.
Flash flooding occurred along Huntington Creek, with a three foot rise on the creek observed at the Huntington Power Plant.

A stronger secondary wave of flash flooding occurred along Huntington Creek, with a rise of five feet along the creek observed at the PacifiCorp Huntington Plant. This time, the heavy rain also resulted in a debris flow at the Seeley Fire burn scar, resulting in State Route 31 being covered in sand and silt between mileposts 24 and 34. This also resulted in some debris flowing in the river near Huntington Plant, including a couple of large logs.
A large flash flood occurred along the Wahweap Creek drainage, which included car-sized boulders rolling down the drainage.
Flash flooding occurred along Last Chance Creek, with water flowing over some of the minor roads in the area.
Flash flooding occurred along the Buckskin Gulch, with a three foot rise in water levels through the area.
Flash flooding occurred across the main portion of Capitol Reef National Park, including Grand Wash, Capitol Gorge, and the Scenic Drive.
Flash flooding occurred in Hildale, with widespread standing water across the town.
Flash flooding was reported along the Alvey Wash and other smaller tributaries of the Escalante River.

Flash flooding occurred in Zion National Park, with the largest reported flash floods in Mystery Canyon and the Narrows. A group of people became stranded in Mystery Canyon during the flood, and had to be rescued by park rangers.
Flash flooding occurred in multiple locations in Capitol Reef National Park. Sulphur Creek experienced flooding, and water also flowed through the Grand Wash and over State Route 24.

Heavy rain in Lyman led to a canal breach. Water then flowed into the basement of a home, with water as deep as 8 feet. The basement was seriously damaged, and the personal property inside the basement was a total loss.
Rain over the Seeley Fire burn scar led to a few mudslides, with mud and debris crossing State Route 31. However, the flow was not enough to close the road.
Flash flooding was reported in Choprock Canyon after heavy rainfall.
A flash flood was reported along Wahweap Creek.
Flash flooding occurred in Hildale, with three feet of water on Canyon Street, making the road impassable.

Widespread flash flooding occurred across Zion National Park. Canyons that were flooded included Heath, Pine, Spry, and Keyhole. The Emerald Pools were also flooded, and the Scenic Road had three areas where sand covered the road, requiring plows to remove the sand.
Flash flooding occurred along North Creek, with the downstream river gauge at Virgin rising to 626 cfs.
Flash flooding occurred along the Paria River, with the gauge along the Paria River at Kanab rising from 0 cfs to 2648 cfs in two hours.
Flash flooding was reported along the Wahweap Creek and Warm Creek drainages.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Washington, resulting in the evacuation of two homes. The homes experienced minor damage from the flood waters, and most of the damage across town was to yards and other outdoor areas.

A fire started at a Salt Lake City green waste storage site, with lightning as the suspected cause of the fire. The fire was contained to a 200-by-300-foot pit where mulch was stored, and firefighters were able to extinguish the blaze before it spread to any adjacent buildings.

Lightning struck a cluster of oil storage tanks just outside Altamont, starting a fire at the facility. At least one of the tanks exploded, sending 50-foot-tall flames into the air, and creating a loud boom that woke people in Altamont. One tank was launched outside the containment berm around the well location, and two other storage tanks were engulfed in flames before firefighters reached the site. Once crews shut down the gas line that runs near the well, firefighters were able to put out the fire in less than two hours, and no injuries occurred due to the fire or explosion.

Heavy rain resulted in a large debris flow off the Seeley Fire burn scar, covering a 10-mile stretch of State Route 31 in water, mud, and debris. This flow caused extensive damage and undercutting in the Horse Canyon area, near milepost 31.

On the northeast end of the Seeley Fire burn scar, flash flooding plugged culverts after one round of heavy rain, and then a larger flash flood occurred after a second thunderstorm moved over the area. In contrast to the flash flooding that typically flows over State Route 31, this water moved eastward toward Price.

Flash flooding occurred in the town of Washington, with flooding beginning along Washington Drive and Interstate 15, and then spreading into the Coral Canyon subdivision. Two homes were especially impacted, with flood waters moving into their backyards. Using water pumps, the fire department was able to keep the flooding from entering one of the homes, but they were unable to keep waters from flowing into the second home. Water and mud as deep as two inches made it into the majority of the home, with interior damages estimated to be as high as $15,000.

Washington City once again experienced flash flooding, and again it was the Coral Canyon subdivision that was hit the hardest. At least 6 basements experienced flooding, with as much as six inches of water flowing into those homes. Homes in a nearby trailer park also experienced some exterior damage, as flood waters flowed along the outside of the homes, but no interior flooding occurred.

Significant flash flooding occurred in Cedar City and Enoch, following record rainfall. The Cedar City ASOS recorded 2.25 inches of precipitation for the day, breaking the previous one-day record precipitation for the site. In Cedar City, 30 to 40 homes, as well as one church, experienced flooding, primarily in basements. In addition, heavy rain caused the roof of the Metalcraft Technologies building to collapse, though no one was in the building at the time. In Enoch, two homes and one public works building had significant flooding resulting in damage. Despite all this property damage, no injuries were reported due to the flood waters.
Flash flooding occurred in the town of Hurricane after a heavy thunderstorm. Water was running through town along Gould Wash, and at least 10 homes were damaged due to flood waters.
Flash flooding was reported along Sulphur Creek in Capitol Reef National Park.

A microburst occurred near the intersection of Utah State Route 111 and New Bingham Highway in West Jordan, knocking over or snapping a series of power poles. Rocky Mountain Power reported that 37 large transmission poles and 4 smaller distribution poles were damaged and had to be replaced. This temporarily knocked out power to about 3,000 customers, as well as closing State Route 111 for several hours. The downed power lines also dragged a couple of metal poles supporting traffic signals to the ground. Despite the destruction, two sensors very close to the intersection (the SR-85 at Dannon Way sensor and the Trans-Jordan Landfill sensor) only recorded peak wind gusts of 45 mph and 42 mph respectively.
Flash flooding was reported along Capitol Gorge in Capitol Reef National Park.

A large flash flood was reported in Capitol Reef National Park and near the town of Cainville. Water flowed across State Route 24 near Cainville, and several drainages in Capitol Reef National Park experienced flash flooding. Downstream, the Fremont River rose 4 feet from all the additional water.

A large debris flow occurred off of the Seeley Fire burn scar, covering State Route 31 with trees, mud, and rocks, as much as 1-2 feet deep in some locations. The debris flow damaged State Route 31, and closed the entire canyon for several hours.

A large debris flow came off of the Wood Hollow Fire burn scar following heavy rainfall. The flow was generally 3 feet deep, and ran 4 miles out of the burn scar, but did not impact the town of Fountain Green.
An isolated microburst over the Salt Lake Valley knocked over a large cottonwood tree at Wheeler Historic Farm. The time is approximate.
Flash flooding occurred in Capitol Reef National Park, with rangers reporting more than a foot of water running down the Grand Wash. The flooding also resulted in the closing of the Scenic Drive.
Widespread flash flooding was reported along many normally dry washes and canyons, including Spooky Gulch, 25 Mile Wash, the Egypt 3 slot canyon, and several others.
Flash flooding was reported along the Upper Escalante drainage near State Route 12.
Flash flooding was reported in the Johnson Canyon area, as well as Lick Wash. In Lick Wash, hikers scrambled out of the wash for an hour and a half to get away from the flood waters.
Heavy rain caused a debris flow off the Seeley Fire burn scar, covering parts of State Route 32 with mud.

Heavy rain caused a flash flood on Huntington Creek and a debris flow off of the Seeley Fire burn scar. Flooding impacted the Huntington Power Plant, with water having to be diverted around the plant. Logs, mud, and rocks were in the river as it passed the power plant.

A debris flow occurred off of the Clay Springs Fire burn scar, with debris flowing out of the southwest aspect of the scar. Flood waters were as tall as four feet high as it ran toward US Route 50, but ran alongside the road rather than cross over it.

Multiple sensors in the Wendover area recorded severe wind gusts from a thunderstorm that passed through the area, including peak gusts of 76 mph at the Wendover AWOS, 63 mph at the Interstate 80 at Milepost 1 sensor, and 59 mph at Wendover Peak.
The Wendover AWOS recorded a peak wind gust of 79 mph.
Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down several trees on Fairfield Road in Layton.
Multiple members of the public reported nickel to quarter sized hail falling over Layton and Kaysville.
The West Salt Flat sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 64 mph.
The Diddle Knoll sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 64 mph.
A debris flow occurred off of the Seeley Fire burn scar, covering State Route 31 with mud, and producing significant rises on Huntington Creek.
Heavy rain over the Wood Hollow Fire burn scar resulted in a debris flow, with mud crossing over State Route 132 between Fountain Green and Moroni.
Significant flash flooding was reported across much of the western side of Zion National Park, including in the Subway area, in Kolob Terrace, and along Taylor Creek in the Kolob area.
Flash flooding was reported along Wahweap Creek.

Significant and widespread flash flooding was reported across Zion National Park after more than an inch of rain fell over the park. The heavy rain filled culverts, and large rocks were washed onto the main scenic drive, resulting in the road being closed down for a period of time. Many canyons were running very high with water, and the gauge on the North Fork of the Virgin River rose to 3159 cfs.
Small flash floods were reported in Capitol Reef National Park, but the Fremont River rose significantly when all of these washes combined into the main river as it flowed toward Caineville.
Heavy rain over a large area resulted in the flash flooding of many drainages in far southern Utah, including the Paria River and Wahweap Creek.
Widespread flash flooding was once again reported in Zion National Park. Most notably, the East Fork of the Virgin River rose to an estimated 5489 cfs.

Heavy rain over the Quail Fire burn scar near Alpine resulted in a debris flow and flash flooding. Mud flowed across several streets in Alpine, including Grove Drive, Box Elder Drive, and Moyle Drive. One home was flooded, with mud and water 18 inches deep flowing into the basement. One shopping center in the area also experienced some flooding as the water and mud flowed through town. Mud and debris took multiple days to clean up on many roads and lawns.||Associated with the same thunderstorm, flash flooding occurred along the Dry Creek Trail near American Fork Canyon, stranding two hikers for a couple hours before they could be rescued.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The Patch Springs Fire began due to a lightning strike on August 10, two miles from the community of Terra, Utah, which eventually received some damage as the fire spread. Property damage from this fire first occurred on August 17, and the fire eventually grew to 31,010 acres before being contained on August 24. ||The fire destroyed 5 trailer homes and significantly damaged 1 additional trailer home. In addition, 8 outbuildings and 1 commercial property were destroyed by the flames. Along Highway 199, 26 power poles were damaged or destroyed by the fire.

The Rockport Fire began due to a lightning strike on August 13 near Wanship, Utah and Rockport State Park, and spread quickly into nearby residences. The fire grew to 1,920 acres before being effectively contained on August 18. ||Eight homes were destroyed by the fire, three within the Rockport Ranches area and five within the Rockport Estates area. The estimated value of these 8 homes was $550,000. In addition, 20 outbuildings were destroyed by the flames, and several vehicles and boats were damaged or destroyed. Some infrastructure was also damaged, with repairs needed to culverts and power lines.
Flash flooding was reported along Wahweap Creek. The time listed is approximate.

Significant flash flooding was reported along Chalk Creek following a heavy thunderstorm. The dramatically increased flow damaged two campgrounds in the area, washed out one bridge, and knocked down several trees along the banks.
Flash flooding occurred in Croton Canyon, damaging one of the roads through that area.
Flash flooding was reported on both Clear Creek and the East Fork of the Virgin River, as well as several slot canyons in the area. The river gauge on the East Fork rose to 1795 cfs.

Flash flooding occurred in the southwest corner of Zion National Park, with the most dramatic rises along the Virgin River. The gauge on the Virgin River at Laverkin Creek rose from 92 cfs to 1084 cfs in one hour.

Flash flooding occurred in the Pine Valley area following a heavy thunderstorm. Five homes experienced basement flooding, with water as deep as 6 inches. Many roadways in the area had debris across the road, and a few roads sustained damage from the flood waters.
A large flash flood was reported in the Dry Valley drainage and its tributaries. This included along the Buckskin Wash, where the flood waters passed under State Route 89 around 6 pm MST.
A large debris flow occurred off of the Seeley Fire burn scar. Water and debris covered State Route 31, and the road was closed at both the top and bottom for several hours.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak wind gusts across the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet included 60 mph at the Causeway sensor, and 58 mph at both the North Salt Flats and Callao sensors.
The Wendover airport recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
The Horse Hollow RAWS recorded a peak wind gust of 65 mph.
The Hat Island sensor recorded a 60 mph wind gust.
A 65 mph wind gust was recorded at the Simpson Springs sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet.
A sensor in Syracuse, Utah recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.
Hail with a diameter of one inch was reported in Hurricane, and a police car was damaged by the hailstones.
Hail the size of hen's eggs, or approximately 2 inches in diameter, was reported in East Carbon, Utah.
Hail with a diameter of one inch was reported in Castle Dale.
Hailstones that were the size of golf balls, or approximately 1.75 inches in diameter, were reported in Duchesne.
The State Route 30 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 73 mph.
The Hat Island sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 73 mph.
A 60 mph wind gust was recorded by the Sherwood Hills sensor.
The Willard Point of Entry sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.
A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the Great Salt Lake Minerals sensor.

Park rangers reported flooding in the Capitol Gorge section of Capitol Reef National Park, with water a foot high flowing through the Gorge, leading them to temporarily close the area to visitors. Additional flooding was also reported in and around other portions of Capitol Reef National Park, including impassable roads in Cathedral Valley and along the |Notom-Bullfrog Road.
Flash flooding was reported along the Grand Wash, Sulphur Creek, and the Scenic Drive in Capitol Reef National Park.
Flash flooding was reported in the lower Escalante drainage, washing out some minor roads in the area.
A large flash flood was reported along Buckskin Gulch and Deer Spring Wash.

Heavy rain over the Clay Springs Fire burn scar caused significant debris flows out of both the Fool Creek and Oak Creek drainages. However, prior mitigation efforts in Oak City protected homes from damage and flooding.
A small debris flow was reported off the Seeley Fire burn scar, with mud moving past the Huntington Power Plant.
Park rangers in Zion National Park reported flash flooding in Clear Creek and Keyhole Canyon.

Flash flooding occurred along Wahweap Creek in the overnight hours, after afternoon rainfall had worked southward through the drainages. The flood was estimated to be 20 feet across and 2 to 3 feet deep at the peak flooding.
Flash flooding was reported in the town of Hildale, with some flood waters causing issues for four hours straight.
A large flash flood occurred along Deer Spring Wash and its drainages, including 4 feet of water coming out of some of the smaller washes.

Widespread flash flooding occurred once again across Wayne County due to heavy rainfall. State Route 24 was closed from Fruita to Hanksville, as flood waters flowed over the road. Capitol Reef National Park had flooding and debris along the Scenic Drive and the Grand Wash. Roads across the wide area again experienced damage due to the flood waters.

Widespread flooding occurred across Canyonlands National Park, including the far western portions of the park. Many roads were closed due to flooding, and the entire park was even closed for a period of time.
Flash flooding occurred along State Route 95, damaging portions of the road, especially near mile marker 31.

Significant flash flooding occurred in Herriman, South Jordan, and West Jordan. In Herriman, flood waters entered an apartment complex, impacting about 18 apartment units. In addition, minor flooding occurred at Herriman High School. In South Jordan, 11 homes in the Sunstone subdivision experienced basement flooding, with water several inches deep. In West Jordan, about 10 apartment units were flooded with water and mud, and portions of the Mountain View Corridor were closed so that the Utah Department of Transportation could drain retention ponds that had filled with the heavy rainfall.
Sulphur Creek in Capitol Reef National Park experienced flash flooding following heavy rainfall.
A funnel cloud was reported and photographed near Morgan, Utah. The time listed is approximate.

Significant long duration rainfall caused widespread flooding across Wayne County. State Route 24 was closed in several locations over the two day period, including between Caineville and Hanksville, as well as near Capitol Reef National Park, where the road was eroded due to the overflowing Fremont River. In addition, State Route 95 was damaged by flood waters and closed near Hanksville. Damage also occurred at Fish Creek Cove, where the road was cut off; this left about a dozen homes inaccessible, some of which were primary residences.||In Capitol Reef National Park, all of the streams and slot canyons were running high; the Scenic Drive was closed for an extended period of time, and many roads around the park sustained damage. Aside from roads, the most significant damage in Wayne County was at a diversion dam near Hanksville on the Fremont River, which will have to be completely rebuilt.

Heavy rainfall fell over a wide area, resulting in flash flooding over most of the washes and drainages within the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. There was also damage near the town of Escalante, as flood waters deposited rocks and mud on State Route 12, and some larger boulders also helped to damage the road.||Most local roads were closed for more than a day, and many of these roads sustained damage from flood waters, including significant damage to Hole-in-the-Rock Road. At least three culverts along Hole-in-the-Rock Road were damaged, and at least five culverts required extensive debris removal. By the end of September, road damage across all of Garfield County due to flooding was $320,000, most of which occurred in this event.

Significant flooding impacted Emery County over two days, particularly on the west side of the county. Road damage and high water levels caused multiple highways to close down. State Route 10 closed from Castle Dale to Emery, with many boulders moving onto the road, some as large as cars. State Route 29 closed from mile post 0 to 12, or approximately Orangeville to Joe's Valley Reservoir. State Route 31 was closed multiple times through the event, in part due to multiple debris flows coming off of the Seeley Fire burn scar. In addition to the major routes listed here, many more local roads were closed due to flood waters, including Cottonwood Canyon. Monetary damages to roads were estimated to be approximately $150,000.

Heavy rainfall fell over a wide area, resulting in widespread flash flooding. Similar to Garfield County, most of the washes and drainages within the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument experienced flooding, most local roads were closed for more than a day, and many of these roads sustained damage from flood waters, including significant damage to Hole-in-the-Rock Road.||In the central portion of Kane County, many drainages flooded, most notably along the Paria River. In addition, State Route 89 flooded from Kanab to Page.||On the far western part of Kane County, State Route 9 (also known as the Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway) was closed for an extended period of time at the east entrance of Zion National Park. Several sections of the road experienced flash flooding, including a ravine where flood waters blocked a road culvert and undercut the road. In total, road damage from this event in Kane County was approximately $185,000.

Long-duration heavy rainfall caused flooding in Washington County, particularly in Zion National Park and the town of Hurricane. Flooding in Zion National Park was widespread, impacting countless streams and washes. State Route 9 (also known as the Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway) was impacted on the Washington County side as well as in Kane County, and was closed all the way to the Canyon Junction, after debris and water damaged the road. ||In Hurricane, many roads across town experienced water and mud across the road, impairing traffic through the town. In addition, ten homes experienced some flooding; some had water flow into basements, while others simply had damage to lawns or garages.

Heavy rain over multiple days resulting in flooding in Duchesne County, mostly impacting the town of Duchesne and State Route 191. Several streets in Duchesne were flooded, including Main Street, with the worst flooding occurring through the day of September 14. Earlier in the event, on the morning of September 12, multiple mudslides occurred on State Route 191 between Duchesne and Helper. The mud across the road trapped several motorists for a few hours before the debris could be cleaned up, but no injuries occurred due to the slides.
A rope funnel cloud was spotted and photographed near Midway, Utah. The time listed is approximate.
Heavy rains caused flash flooding and a rockslide along State Route 143 between Parowan and Brian Head, with large boulders over the road.
Heavy rain over the Clay Springs Fire burn scar resulted in a debris flow along Fool Creek. Mud flowed out of the drainage, but did not cross the road.

In the morning hours of September 2, heavy rain over State Route 6 caused a mudslide approximately 10 miles southeast of Soldier Summit. The road was closed for about 8 hours as crews cleared away the mud, and the slide temporarily closed parts of a construction project in the area. The mudslide also caused some damage to a local farm on the other side of the road.

Heavy rain just northeast of Panguitch, Utah caused flash flooding in the Sand Wash and Lime Kiln parts of town. Flooding in the agricultural area was significant, causing thousands of dollars of damage to fields and yards; however, no damage was reported to homes, and no injuries were reported to people or livestock.
The Escalante River gauge near Escalante rose from near zero cfs to 2200 cfs in one hour.
Flash flooding was reported across the Notom Road and much of the southern half of Capitol Reef National Park.
Flash flooding was reported along Buckskin Gulch, as well as many other small streams and dry washes in the lower Paria drainage.
Flash flooding occurred in the town of Big Water following heavy rainfall.
A very large flash flood was reported in Wahweap Creek, Buckskin Gulch, and many other drainages in the area.
Flash flooding and large waterfalls were reported throughout much of Zion National Park. In addition, the East Fork Virgin River Near Springdale, UT gauge rose from 34 cfs to 1400 cfs in one hour.
Some smaller slot canyons in the northern portions of Zion National Park experienced flash flooding, and the North Fork Virgin River Near Springdale gauge went from near zero cfs to 415 cfs.
A large flash flood was reported on Wahweap Creek and the Paria River, as well as smaller drainages in the area.

A debris flow was reported off of the Dump Fire burn scar, but prior mitigation was successful, as retention ponds filled up, but debris did not flow into the towns of Eagle Mountain or Saratoga Springs.

Heavy rain over the Quail Hollow Fire burn scar caused a significant debris flow, with water and mud flowing down into the town of Alpine. About 100 residents were evacuated from their homes due to the imminent flooding. Roads across the area were inundated with mud, and 15 homes were damaged by the water and debris.

Strong thunderstorm winds developed in Provo, with the Provo airport AWOS recording a peak wind gust of 59 mph. The most significant wind damage was a roof that was torn off of an apartment building. In addition, some smaller trees were knocked down, and hundreds of tree branches were downed.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding across much of urban Utah County, with multiple locations recording 0.6-0.8 inches of rain in only 15 minutes. The most significant damage from flooding was reported in Provo, Orem, Payson, and Santaquin. Street flooding was widespread and some roads incurred major damage, with the worst damage occurring at 900 North and Grand Avenue in Provo, where water undercut and washed out a large portion of the asphalt road. Debris from the storm was scattered across most local roadways, taking several days to clean up, and even closed some roads for a period of time. Flowing water caused also caused significant damage to large concrete stairs at Lions Park in Provo. At University Mall in Orem, water quickly filled the parking lot, submerging many cars in more than a foot of water. ||Residential areas also received significant flood damage. In Provo, at least 25 homes had major damage, with more than 50 receiving minor damage. In Orem, approximately 30 homes received flood damage. In Santaquin, about 30 homes had flooding a foot deep or more, while about 30 other homes had flooding with less than a foot of water. Water wasn't the only problem in Santaquin, as the storm drainage system became overwhelmed, and raw sewage flowed into many homes. ||Finally, the flooding also impacted Timpanogos Cave National Monument, where heavy rain and associated debris stranded 150 hikers for several hours, before rangers were able to clear a path and rescue them. The Monument was closed for two full days while debris was cleaned up from both the hiking trails and nearby State Route 92.
A small tornado was spotted and recorded by a member of the public. The tornado removed a metal roof from a barn, and did minor damage to trees and other outbuildings in the area.
Peak wind gusts in west central Utah included 68 mph at the US-6 at Eureka sensor and 59 mph at the Oak City sensor.
The Evanston, Wyoming ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph with the passage of a cold front.
Peak recorded wind gusts in the mountains of central Utah included 78 mph at the Signal Peak RAWS and 76 mph at the Lost Creek RAWS.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Strong southerly winds developed across the Great Salt Lake Desert, with the highest winds recorded in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet. Peak wind gusts included 73 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 68 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 66 mph at Diddle Knoll, 62 mph at English Village, 60 mph at Gunnison Island, and 58 mph at Badger Island.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: The peak recorded wind gust in far southwest Utah was 53 mph in St. George. In addition, one tree was blown over on the campus of Dixie State University.

Strong south winds developed across southwest Utah, with the strongest winds in Cedar City. The Cedar City ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 71 mph, while the Milford ASOS recorded 64 mph. At least 15 large trees were knocked down by the winds; 10 of these trees were on the campus of Southern Utah University, one of which caused minor damage to a building. In addition, some roof damage was reported, including one barn that sustained significant roof damage from the strong winds.

The storm brought heavy snow to the Cottonwood Canyons, with Brighton Resort receiving 17 inches of new snow and Alta Ski Lifts recording 15 inches of new snow. Both of these resorts received most of this snow in a 12-hour period during the daytime hours of November 16.

Downslope winds were strongest in the northern Wasatch Front, with a peak recorded wind gust of 85 mph at a UDOT shed in Centerville. Other sensors in Centerville and Farmington also recorded 80 mph wind gusts. The wind knocked out power to more than 10,000 residents across the area. Included in these power outages were some traffic signal lights and street lights that were out; these outages, combined with the winds and blowing debris, were blamed for an auto-pedestrian accident in Ogden, which resulted in one injury and one fatality. ||Damage was less severe than other downslope windstorms in recent years, but was  still widespread. Several street signs were bent or knocked over, including four exit signs along Interstate 15. Numerous large trees were uprooted, and damage to fences and roofs was common. An RV in North Ogden was knocked over, and semitrailer traffic was stopped for a period of time along Interstate 15 and Legacy Highway. Other items that sustained damage or became airborne included trampolines, children's playground equipment, and garage doors.

Winds in the Salt Lake Valley were considerably weaker than further north, with a peak recorded wind gust of 62 mph at The University of Utah. Damage was also considerably less, with relatively minor damage reported to trees, fences, and playground equipment.

Escalante received 18.5 inches of snow over a 48-hour period. Since records began in Escalante in 1901, this was the thirteenth highest snow total over a 3 calendar day period, and the highest value ever recorded earlier in the season than January.
Capitol Reef National Park received a storm total of 9.9 inches of snow.
Storm totals in Utah's southern mountains included 22 inches of snow at Brian Head Resort and 19 inches at Eagle Point.

A storm total of 10 inches new snow fell across Bountiful, Bountiful Bench, and Centerville. The accumulating snow caused hazardous road conditions, with 62 accidents reported in Davis County on December 3. Davis County proved to be the northern edge of significant impacts with this storm, as the valleys of Weber County just to the north generally recorded 2 inches of snow or less.

Storm total snowfall across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 11.5 inches in Cottonwood Heights, 10 inches in Millcreek and Sandy, and 9 inches in Stansbury Park. The biggest impact to travel was on Tuesday, December 3, with more than 200 car accidents reported across Salt Lake County, including 20 reported injuries.
Storm total snowfall included 13 inches at Elk Ridge, 12 inches in Spanish Fork, and 11 inches in Springville and Provo. Utah County reported 75 car accidents, with seven injuries.
Storm totals in the Wasatch mountain valleys included 9 inches in Heber City, 8 inches at Deer Creek Dam, and 7 inches at Park City.

Storm total snowfall included 18 inches at both Deer Valley and Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort, 17 inches at both Alta Ski Lifts and Brighton Resort, and 16 inches at the summit of Park City Mountain Resort.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 1.30 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.
The Hans Flat Ranger Station received a storm total of 9.6 inches of snow.
Richfield received a storm total of 8 inches of snow.
Storm total snowfall in west central Utah included 14 inches of snow in Fillmore and 9 inches in Oak City.
Cedar City received a storm total of 12 inches of snow. Snow accumulation impaired travel on area roads, and there were 22 car accidents on Interstate 15 in Iron County, with no injuries reported.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: Springdale received 3 inches of snow, while St. George received 2 inches of snow. The rare snowfall caused at least 30 car accidents in Washington County, with one reported injury. A few of these automobile accidents caused  property damage, including a fire hydrant that was hit, and a tree branch that fell onto a vehicle.
The Pickle Keg SNOTEL received 0.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 15 inches of new snow, most of which fell in a short period on December 3.
The Kimberly Mine SNOTEL received 1.20 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 18 inches of new snow.

Lows near or below zero degrees Fahrenheit were common across the northern Wasatch Front, and freezing pipes and sprinkler systems caused flood damage in a couple different buildings. An overhead sprinkler froze at the Farmington courthouse, damaging the clerical area, including computers and copier machines. In Ogden, the Shepherd Union Building at Weber State University experienced flood damage after a portion of the fire sprinkler system froze. The broken pipe caused a section of ceiling to collapse above one of the student lounges, damaging some furniture and parts of the campus store. Other issues caused by cold across the area included school buses being unable to start, and the closure of Highland Junior High School in Ogden when the temperatures froze a boiler coil, disabling the heating system.
Kanab and Apple Valley both received 8.5 inches of snow from the storm.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: Unusually large amounts of snow fell in Utah's Dixie, with storm total snowfall of 14 inches at Zion National Park, 13 inches in Springdale, 8 inches in Ivins, 7 inches in La Verkin, and 6 inches in both St. George and Hurricane. The snow caused significant travel difficulties in the area, especially considering many cities do not own any snowplows. Interstate 15 was closed due to snowfall in the Virgin River Gorge just southwest of St. George, stranding about 300 people on the highway overnight in Arizona. In addition, a semitrailer traveling northbound on Interstate 15 jackknifed in snowy conditions, closing two lanes of the highway for a couple hours in the Black Ridge area of Washington County. Also, the St. George airport was closed for most of the day on December 7, as the long period of snowfall overwhelmed its single snow plow.
Heavy snow fell in localized spots in southwest Utah, with storm total snowfall of 17 inches in Paragonah and 10 inches in New Harmony. Meanwhile, Cedar City received only 0.5 inches of snow.
Evanston received 11 inches of new snow from the storm, while Mountain View received a storm total of 10 inches of snow.
Storm total snowfall across the northern Wasatch Front included 12 inches at Bountiful Bench, 10 inches in Centerville, 9 inches in Fruit Heights, and 8 inches in both Farmington and Clearfield.

Storm total snowfall in the Salt Lake Valley included 12 inches in Magna, 8.5 inches in  Millcreek, and 6 inches in West Valley City, South Salt Lake, and Sandy. Most of the snowfall in Magna occurred on the morning of December 8, as a lake effect snow band set up over the city for an extended period of time.
Storm total snowfall from the Wasatch mountain valleys included 12 inches at Deer Creek Dam and 8 inches at Heber City.
Snowbasin Resort received 18 inches of new snow. In addition, the Farmington Lower SNOTEL received 0.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.
Provo Canyon received a storm total of 18 inches new snow.
The Mammoth-Cottonwood SNOTEL received a storm total of 0.90 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.
The Pine Creek SNOTEL received 1.30 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow.
The Merchant Valley SNOTEL received 1.20 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 22 inches of new snow. In addition, Duck Creek Village reported 16 inches of new snow.

Freezing rain was less significant in the Cache Valley than other parts of the state, but snowfall was quite heavy on the morning of December 19. Storm total snowfall included 8 inches in Providence and 7 inches in Logan.

A combination of freezing rain and heavy snowfall caused slick roads in the northern Wasatch Front, with about 40 automobile accidents reported in Davis County. Snowfall was heavy on the morning of December 19, with generally about 7 inches of new snow reported across the area. Locations that reported 7 inches of snowfall included Clearfield, South Ogden, Centerville, Bountiful, and Bountiful Bench.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Heavy snowfall impacted travel across Utah's northwest desert. The Utah Test and Training Range received 3 inches of new snow, with more snowfall likely in the higher terrain of the area, and 30 slide-offs were reported along Interstate 80 in Tooele County.
Evanston received 8.5 inches of new snow, while Mountain View reported a storm total of 4 inches of snow.
Storm total snowfall from the Wasatch mountain valleys included 8 inches near Kamas and 6 inches of snow in Park City.
Storm totals from the northern Wasatch Mountains included 19 inches of snow at Snowbasin Resort and 17 inches of new snow at Powder Mountain.
Storm total snowfall included 16 inches at Brighton Resort, 13 inches at Alta Ski Lifts, and a foot of new snow at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort and Deer Valley.

The Salt Lake Valley was perhaps the hardest hit by the combination of freezing rain and heavy snowfall. Most of the freezing rain occurred during the early morning hours on December 19, before switching to all snow through the morning. Storm total snowfall across the valley included 10 inches in Herriman, 8 inches in Sandy, and 7 inches in West Valley City and Draper. ||Salt Lake City International Airport was shut down for a few hours in the morning, and over 200 flights were cancelled due to the slick runways. Travel by automobile was slow and hazardous, with over 450 accidents reported in the Salt Lake Valley, and 24 minor injuries from those accidents. Power outages were common, with over 14,000 customers losing power. Along State Route 201, a utility pole broke, with power lines falling across the roadway. These power lines shut down the road for several hours in both directions.

A 56-year-old woman and her husband were hiking the Brimhall Double Bridge Trail in Capitol Reef National Park on August 15, when the woman became ill. The man went to get help, but she had passed away by the time medical personnel arrived. The cause of death was heat exhaustion, with temperatures exceeding 90 degrees. The time listed is approximate.
In the Wasatch mountain valleys, snow was heaviest in the Ogden Valley, with 10 inches of snow in Liberty and 9 inches of snow in Eden.
Powder Mountain received 11 inches of new snow. In addition, the Ben Lomond Peak SNOTEL received 1.30 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 18 inches of new snow.
Storm total snowfall included 17 inches at Brighton Resort, 12 inches at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort and Alta Ski Lifts, and 11 inches of snow at Park City Mountain Resort.
The Tony Grove Lake SNOTEL received 1.60 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.

At approximately 2 pm MST, strong winds in Ferron pulled the roof off of the fire station in town, with only the roof's plywood substructure remaining. The maximum recorded wind gust in Ferron was 55 mph.
Peak recorded wind gusts in Uinta County, Wyoming included 61 mph at Fort Bridger, 58 mph at Church Butte, and 58 mph at the French sensor.
The Ben Lomond Peak SNOTEL received 3.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow.
The Strawberry Divide SNOTEL received 1.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 18 inches of new snow.
The Seeley Creek SNOTEL received 1.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 18 inches of new snow.
The Sanpete and Sevier Valleys received the most valley snowfall across the state, with storm total snowfall of 10 inches in Manti, 10 inches in Richfield, and 9 inches in Gunnison.

A group of six snowshoers were traveling just north of Tibble Fork Reservoir in American Fork Canyon when they triggered a small avalanche. One of the snowshoers, a 21-year-old female, was swept away and buried in the snow. While she was able to be resuscitated, she passed away the next day in an area hospital.

A group of four snowmobilers were recreating near the Left Fork Huntington Creek when one of them became stuck.  Another person, a 36-year-old male, circled uphill to come help; he triggered an avalanche that buried him but did not catch the stuck snowmobilers. The other snowmobilers began rescue efforts immediately, but the victim was buried 6-8 feet deep, and he passed away at the scene.
Storm total snowfall across the Cache Valley included 14.5 inches at Hyde Park, 12.5 inches in Richmond, and 12 inches of new snow at both Utah State University and North Logan.
Storm total snowfall in the valleys of the Wasatch Mountains included 16 inches in Eden and 10 inches at Deer Creek Dam.

Powder Mountain received a storm total of 36 inches new snow, while Snowbasin Resort received 28 inches of snow. Water totals in the northern Wasatch Mountains were very high; the highest was at the Tony Grove Lake SNOTEL, which reported liquid equivalent precipitation of 7.70 inches.
Storm total snowfall included 47 inches at Brighton Resort, 32 inches at Provo Canyon, and 28 inches at Alta Ski Lifts.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 3.90 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 35 inches of new snow.
Evanston received a storm total of 12 inches new snow.

Much of the precipitation remained as rain in Coalville, and two straight days of rain proved to be too much for one of the open culverts in the town. When that drainage system failed to handle the volume of water, four homes were flooded along 150 South in Coalville, with two of those homes experiencing extensive flooding. One of the significantly damaged homes was flooded with a couple feet of water, and the other had 6 inches of water.
The Tony Grove Lake SNOTEL received 4.60 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 30 inches of new snow during the warm, but moist, event.
A sensor in Saratoga Springs recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts across far northwest Utah included 63 mph at Promontory Point, 59 mph at the State Route 30 at Curlew sensor, and 58 mph at the Groome sensor.
The US-40 at Starvation sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
The Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded several strong wind gusts, reaching a peak speed of 65 mph.

A 60-year-old tree was knocked over in St. George by gusty winds. The tree fell onto the home, causing damage to the roof. There were no injuries associated with the event, as no one was home at the time. The peak recorded wind gust in the area during this time was 49 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Multiple hours of strong winds were recorded at the Badger Island sensor, with a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
Strong winds were recorded at several locations in the Uinta Mountains, including peak recorded wind gusts of 86 mph at Lofty Lake Peak, 84 mph at Windy Peak, and 76 mph at Dry Ridge.

The Ben Lomond Peak SNOTEL received 4.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 28 inches of new snow. Several other SNOTEL sites in the area also reported snow totals in the 18-24 inch range.
Peak recorded wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 73 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 61 mph at Vernon Hill, 60 mph at a sensor in Sandy, and 58 mph at Stockton Bar.
The Milford ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph.
Both the Muddy Creek sensor and the Leroy sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph.

Two brothers were snowmobiling in the Uinta Mountains, on a popular slope in Gold Hill Basin. One of them, a 39-year-old male, triggered an avalanche, which caught, carried, and buried him several feet deep in snow. The other brother was able to dig him out and attempt CPR, but the victim was pronounced dead at the scene.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Winds were strong across much of the west desert for a few hours, with more than a dozen sensors recording wind gusts greater than 58 mph. Peak recorded gusts included 68 mph at Wendover Peak and 66 mph at the Interstate 80 sensor in the Dugway mesonet.
The St. George AWOS recorded a wind gust of 68 mph.

Peak recorded wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 65 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 64 mph at Vernon Hill, 61 mph at Flight Park South, and 57 mph at both South Mountain and Olympus Hills.
The sensor in Saratoga Springs recorded strong winds both ahead of and behind the cold front, with a peak recorded gust of 60 mph.
Strong southwesterly winds occurred in Milford, with a peak recorded gust of 67 mph.
Several hours of strong west-southwesterly winds were recorded at the Bullfrog Marina sensor, with a peak wind gust of 70 mph.

A trampoline was blown out of a backyard and into some power lines in Minersville. Recorded wind gusts in the area at the time were relatively light, so it is likely that this was caused by a strong dust devil. Time listed is approximate.

Strong winds knocked over two hay barns in Lewiston, Utah. Both barns were 30 feet wide; one was 80 feet long and the other was 100 feet long. The barns were used to store hay, and the toppled hay buried about 20 calves, though none were injured. In addition to the barns, an empty semi-trailer in a parking lot in Logan was knocked over by the winds.
The Antelope Island sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph. In addition, some damage to shingles and siding was reported.

Peak wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 81 mph at Flight Park South, 70 mph at Vernon Hill, 67 mph in Grantsville, 63 mph at Point of the Mountain, and several other reports greater than 50 mph. Shingles were blown off of homes and other roof damage was reported in several locations, especially in the Magna and Grantsville areas. In addition, multiple large trees and traffic light poles were knocked down across the area.

Peak recorded wind gusts included 73 mph in Saratoga Springs and 60 mph recorded in Pleasant Grove, Orem, and at Pioneer Crossing. Damage across the area included multiple fences knocked down by the winds.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
