events.event_narrative: The Badger Spring RAWS recorded strong northeasterly wind gusts for several hours, including a peak gust of 69 mph. The White Reef RAWS also recorded a maximum gust of 66 mph.

Storm total snowfall reports from this relatively quick event included 10 inches in Tooele, Cottonwood Heights, and South Jordan, as well as 8.5 inches in Taylorsville, 8 inches in Kearns, and 7 inches in Sandy.
Storm totals from the southern Wasatch Front included 14 inches in SunCrest, 9 inches in Lehi and American Fork, and 8 inches in Nephi.

Sundance Mountain Resort received the most snow from this storm with a total of 19 new inches. Other snowfall reports included 13 inches in Provo Canyon and 12 inches at both Alta Ski Lifts and Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort.

Storm total snowfall in the northern Wasatch Front included 14 inches at both the Bountiful Bench and South Ogden, 13 inches at the Northeast Ogden Bench, and 12 inches in Bountiful and Centerville. Snow on transformers and power lines led to power outages for approximately 1,200 Rocky Mountain Power customers in Ogden and Riverdale on the 22nd.

Many locations in the Wasatch Mountain Valleys received a foot or more of snow from this storm, with reports of 18 inches of snow in Liberty, 15 inches in Eden, 14 inches in Heber City, 13 inches in Park City, and 12 inches at both Wanship Dam and Morgan.

Over 3 feet of snow fell across much of the northern Wasatch Mountains, including storm totals of 43 inches at Snowbasin Resort and 37 inches at Powder Mountain.  Travel was treacherous through the mountains routes and canyons, with snow-packed roads common across the area.

Snowfall totals in the Wasatch Mountains were impressive, with many locations reporting 3-4 feet of new snow. The highest total was at Brighton Resort, which received 76 inches of snow at its 9500 foot crest. Other large totals included 48 inches at Solitude Mountain Resort, 42 inches at Alta Ski Lifts, 41 inches at Park City Mountain Resort, and 38 inches at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort. Travel was treacherous through the mountains routes and canyons, especially in Parleys Canyon and the Cottonwood Canyons, and snow-packed roads were common across the area.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 2.90 inches of liquid water equivalent, or approximately 36 inches of new snow.
The Mammoth-Cottonwood SNOTEL received 3.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 35 inches of new snow.
The Buck Flat SNOTEL received 3.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 40 inches of new snow.

Most of Davis and Weber Counties received over a foot of snow, with storm total snow reports of 30 inches at Bountiful Bench, 25 inches in Centerville, 20 inches in Bountiful, 17 inches in Fruit Heights, 15 inches in both South Ogden and East Layton, and 13 inches on the Northeast Ogden Bench. Over 1,000 customers were without power at some point during the event, and there were at least 50 automobile accidents caused by the snow covered roads.

Most of the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys received over a foot of snow during the event, with storm totals of 23 inches in Sandy and Cottonwood Heights, 21 inches in Upper Millcreek, 18 inches in the Upper Avenues, 17 inches in Olympus Cove, and 15 inches in Draper and Tooele. Totals were often smaller toward the northern end of the Salt Lake Valley, with the Salt Lake International Airport receiving 9.5 inches of snow; however, this included 8.2 inches on the calendar day of December 14, which broke the old record for the date of 5.8 inches in 1922. Over 150 accidents or stranded motorists were reported in the Salt Lake Valley, and at least 1,500 customers were without power at some point during the event, with many of those in Bluffdale and Draper.

Storm total snow amounts in the southern Wasatch Front included 27 inches in Suncrest, 12 inches in Levan, and 9 inches in Spanish Fork, Alpine, and Lehi. At least 50 automobile accidents were reported during the storm, and power outages were significant in the area, with over 7,700 people losing power in the Eagle Mountain and Cedar Fort areas.
Storm total snowfall in in the northern Wasatch Mountains included 19 inches at Powder Mountain Resort and 17 inches at Snowbasin Resort.
Storm total snowfall reports included 34 inches at Alta Ski Area, 31 inches at Snowbird Ski Resort, 22 inches at Brighton Resort, and 20 inches at Solitude Mountain Ski Resort.
Storm total snowfall in west central Utah included 11.5 inches in Fillmore and 10.7 inches in Oak City.
Both Cedar City and New Harmony received about 8 inches of snow from the event.
The Pickle Keg SNOTEL received 2.30 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow.

Storm total snowfall in Utah's southern mountains included 20 inches at Eagle Point Ski Resort and 16.5 inches in Parowan. The Midway Valley SNOTEL received 2.40 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow. Road impacts were significant across the area; semitrailers were banned from State Route 14 between Cedar City and the Long Valley Junction with U.S. 89, and a 3-mile stretch of State Route 143 near Panguitch was completely closed down.

A group of skiers was skiing along Gobblers Knob, between Big Cottonwood and Millcreek Canyons, on the afternoon of January 21. An avalanche, about 600 feet wide, was triggered, and two of the skiers were caught. One skier was partially buried and sustained minor injuries. The other skier, a 49-year-old male, was fully buried by the avalanche. He did not have a pulse when others dug him out of the snow, and he was pronounced dead later that day when all attempts to resuscitate him proved unsuccessful.

A 50-year-old male skier went missing in the Park City area on the afternoon of January 31. After two days of searching, his body was eventually found along Rip's Ridge, where he apparently had triggered an avalanche, and had been buried and killed.
Storm total snowfall reports in the Cache Valley included 11 inches in Providence and Logan, as well as 10 inches in Millville.

Centerville, Bountiful Bench, and northeast Ogden Bench all received 7 inches of new snow from this storm, while many other places received 6 inches of snow including Brigham City, Kaysville, and South Ogden.

Storm total snowfall reports included 18 inches at Powder Mountain and 12 inches at Snowbasin Resort. In addition, the Ben Lomond Peak SNOTEL received 2.50 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of new snow.
Storm total snow reports included 18 inches at Brighton Resort, 14 inches at Alta Ski Lifts, an 13 inches at Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 1.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 24 inches of new snow.
Snow totals in the San Rafael Swell included 9 inches at the Hans Flat Ranger Station, 7 inches at Capitol Reef National Park and 5 inches at Hanksville. Note that this event continued into February.
Snow totals in the San Rafael Swell included 9 inches at the Hans Flat Ranger Station, 7 inches at Capitol Reef National Park and 5 inches at Hanksville. Note that this event began in January.
Richfield received a storm total of 11 inches of snow and Manti received 9 inches of snow. Note that this event continued into February.
Richfield received a storm total of 11 inches of snow and Manti received 9 inches of snow. Note that this event began in January.
Fillmore received a storm total of 16.5 inches of snow. The Millard County School District closed down on Monday, February 1 due to the heavy snow. Note that this event continued into February.

Snow accumulations were unusually heavy for south central Utah, with storm totals of 17.5 inches of snow in Escalante and 11 inches of snow at Kodachrome Basin State Park. Note that this event continued into February.

Snow accumulations were unusually heavy for south central Utah, with storm totals of 17.5 inches of snow in Escalante and 11 inches of snow at Kodachrome Basin State Park. Note that this event began in January.
The Coop station at Fremont Indian State Park recorded a storm total of 28 inches of snow. Note that this event continued into February.
The Coop station at Fremont Indian State Park recorded a storm total of 28 inches of snow. Note that this event began in January.

The Midway Valley SNOTEL received 3.10 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 40 inches of new snow. In addition, the Boulder Coop station reported a storm total of 24 inches of snow, and 12 inches of snow was reported at Loa. The heavy snow led to multiple road closures across the area, including State Route 143 from Brian Head to Mammoth Creek, State Route 14, and State Route 20. Note that this event continued into February.

The heavy snow led to multiple road closures across the area, including State Route 143 from Brian Head to Mammoth Creek, State Route 14, and State Route 20. Note that this event began in January.

Storm total snowfall was perhaps most impressive in southwest Utah, where storm totals included 28 inches in Enterprise, 20 inches in Milford, and 18 inches in Cedar City. Automobile incidents along Interstate 15 attributed to the snow included 2 injury accidents, 24 collisions, and 46 slide-offs. In addition, 20 semitrailers that had pulled over at a rest area near New Harmony became stuck after several of the semis were without snow chains and couldn���t get going again. School closures included the Iron County School District, the Beaver County School District, the Gateway Prep Academy in Enoch, and Southern Utah University. Notably, the Iron County School District closure was the first snow day for the district in 61 years. Note that this event continued into February.

Automobile incidents along Interstate 15 attributed to the snow included 2 injury accidents, 24 collisions, and 46 slide-offs. Peak wind gusts across the northern Wasatch Front included 64 mph at Bountiful Bench, 63 mph at the Legacy Parkway, and numerous gusts in the 50-55 mph range. Damage to trees, fences, and trampolines was reported across the area.

The strongest recorded wind gusts in the Salt Lake and Tooele valleys included 74 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 72 mph in Sandy, 71 mph in Tooele, 63 mph in Olympus Hills, 61 mph at the interchange of Interstate 15 and Interstate 215, and numerous gusts in the 50-60 mph range. UDOT periodically banned semitrailer rigs along Interstate 80, but one semitrailer was still knocked over by strong winds near Grantsville. In Salt Lake City, scaffolding collapsed on an assisted living center being built; no one was injured, but debris from the incident covered the road and forced the closure of the northbound lanes of Foothill Drive and Parleys Way during the morning commute. At Salt Lake City International Airport, winds caused some flight delays, and seven flights were diverted to other cities. Power outages were common across the area due to downed trees and power lines. The hardest hit area with regard to trees was the Tooele Cemetery, where several large 100-year-old  trees were blown over. Damage to fences, siding, and trampolines was also common across the area.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Winds were strong across Utah's northwest desert, particularly at the Dugway Proving Ground. The Proving Ground's mesonet recorded wind gusts of 75 mph at Romeo and Centerline, 72 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 69 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, and 66 mph at Target R. Other strong wind gusts across the area included 62 mph at Hat Island and 60 mph at Interstate 80 at Milepost 1. Numerous other gusts in the 50-60 mph range were reported.

The Heber City Municipal Airport - Russ McDonald Field AWOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph. The winds destroyed a barn in Wallsburg. Nearly 100 trees were downed in the community of Wolf Creek Ranch, and another 40 trees were reported toppled near Empire Pass.

The strongest recorded wind gusts in the northern Wasatch Mountains included 106 mph at Ogden Peak, 102 mph at the Snowbasin-Straw Top sensor, 88 mph at the State Route 65 at Big Mountain Pass sensor, and 84 mph at the Snowbasin - Wildcat sensor. The winds impacted several mountain resorts, which either had to shut down some of their lifts or close early.

Peak recorded wind gusts in the Wasatch Mountains south of Interstate 80 included 94 mph at the Arrowhead Summit sensor at Sundance Mountain Resort, 89 mph at the Park City - Jupiter sensor, 84 mph at Reynolds Peak, 81 mph at Mt. Baldy, 80 mph at the Dreamscape Study Plot, and 79 mph at the Torpedo Hill - Big Cottonwood Canyon sensor. The winds impacted several mountain resorts, which either had to shut down some of their lifts or close early. Several downed trees were reported across the area, particularly at Brighton Resort.
The strongest recorded wind gusts in the Uinta Mountains included 122 mph at Windy Peak and 113 mph at Lofty Lake Peak.
The US-6 at Eureka sensor recorded strong winds for several hours, including a peak gust of 71 mph.

The Cedar City Airport ASOS recorded strong, gusty winds for several hours, including a peak gust of 70 mph. Multiple trees were knocked down and landed across State Route 14 east of Cedar City, forcing the highway to shut down for a period of time. A large tree also fell onto a building on the campus of Southern Utah University.

The automated sensor 2 miles south of Brian Head recorded strong winds for several hours, including a peak gust of 87 mph. Approximately 30 trees snapped and fell on runs at Brian Head Resort, and 20 trees fell on runs at Eagle Point. Both mountain resorts were closed at the time.
Peak recorded wind gusts in the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 61 mph at Vernon Hill and 59 mph in Draper.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts included 68 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 65 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 61 mph at the I-80 at Grassey sensor, 61 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 60 mph at Hat Island, and many other recorded gusts in the 50-60 mph range.
The US-6 at Eureka sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph, while the Fillmore Airport reported a maximum gust of 60 mph.
A maximum wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the Bullfrog Marina.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The strongest winds in Utah's northwest desert occurred behind the cold front, with a maximum recorded gust of 65 mph at Promontory Point. Peak gusts in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet included 62 mph at Camel Back Mountain and 58 mph at Causeway.

The Tony Grove Lake SNOTEL received 2.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 27 inches of snow. Powder Mountain received 18 inches of new snow. In addition, winds were strong on March 14, with a maximum wind gust of 90 mph on Ogden Peak.
Storm total snowfall included 29 inches at Brighton Resort and 20 inches at Alta Ski Lifts.
The Hewinta SNOTEL received 1.70 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of new snow.
The Bullfrog Marina sensor recorded several hours of gusty winds both ahead of and behind the cold front, including a peak gust of 68 mph recorded with the frontal passage.

A period of snowfall, with minor accumulations, led to slick roads along Interstate 15 in southern Utah in the early morning hours of March 26. These slick roads were a factor in several accidents near Beaver, Utah, including a rollover accident that led to two injuries and one fatality. The victim who passed away was a 48-year-old female who was not wearing a seatbelt, and was subsequently ejected from her vehicle.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: The strongest winds in Utah's northwest desert developed ahead of the cold front, with peak recorded gusts of 67 mph at the Groome sensor, 66 mph at Wig Mountain, 62 mph at Camel Back Mountain, and 59 mph at both Playa Station and the Wendover Point of Entry. In addition, strong post-frontal winds developed near the Utah/Idaho border, with a peak wind gust of 59 mph at the Interstate 80 at Milepost 1 sensor.
The Fish Springs sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.
The Brimstone Reservoir RAWS recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.

A strong thunderstorm moved over Interstate 15 near mile post 100, dropping heavy rain and significant, accumulating small hail. This storm led to a large pileup accident involving 4 semitrucks and one passenger vehicle. Interstate 15 was shut down in both directions for about 2 hours, and three people (one semitruck driver and two people from the passenger vehicle) were injured.

Damage from the downslope wind storm was widespread across Davis and Weber Counties, as well as parts of Box Elder County, with the strongest observed winds occurring in Centerville and Farmington. Peak recorded wind gusts from the event included 91 mph at the US-89 at Park Lane sensor, 87 mph in Farmington, 81 mph in Centerville, 74 mph at the Brigham City Airport, 70 mph in South Ogden, and many other reports in the 55-70 mph range.||There was one wind-related fatality, when strong winds pushed a pickup truck onto the shoulder of Interstate 15, where it it had been traveling near Parrish Lane. The pickup crashed into the back of a semitruck, which had pulled over to the side of the road because of the winds. The driver of the pickup, a 61-year-old male, was transported to the hospital, where he passed away.||Hundreds of large trees were knocked over by the wind, including several that fell onto houses and cars. The wind damaged many fences and roofs, and countless personal items, such as lawn furniture and trampolines, were scattered across towns. In Honeyville, the wind overturned a 32-foot-long sheep shearing trailer, killing 11 sheep. The wind caused damage to power lines and power poles, with over 39,000 customers impacted by power outages. Three semitrucks were toppled along Interstate 15 near Corinne, and portions of the Interstate were prohibited for high profile vehicles during the event. In Centerville alone, an estimated $500,000 of damage was done to private property, with an additional $20,000 of damage to city property. About 20% of the single family dwellings in Centerville (about 1000 homes) received at least minor damage. In Ogden, the culinary water system went off-line for an extended period of time, and the city was operating on reserve storage. The biggest problem for multiple cities was debris removal, with cities, individuals, and green waste sites working around the clock to remove and process all of the downed trees. Note that this event began in April.

An arsonist intentionally set fire to a field in Tooele on the night of July 19. The fire spread quickly into a nearby neighborhood due to gusty winds, with gusts generally in the 25-35 mph range. By the time firefighters had controlled the blaze by the morning of July 20, the fire had destroyed 10 homes and caused significant damage to 8 other homes. In addition, about eight cars and at least five outbuildings were destroyed. The fire also consumed trees and vinyl fences. Ten people were treated at the hospital for smoke inhalation, and at least three of those were first responders. One person was treated for a head injury from a fall related to the fire.

The Tokewanna Fire was discovered on the afternoon of July 28, about 15 miles south of Mountain View, Wyoming. The fire burned approximately 1,300 acres and destroyed 8 structures in the Tokewanna Estates Subdivision. The fire forced the evacuation of 140 homes and the Uinta County Youth Camp, and also closed portions of Highways 271 and 410. One firefighter on the wildfire suffered burns from the fire. The fire was 100% contained as of 6 p.m. MDT Saturday, August 6.

A tornado touched down in Riverdale in Weber County. The tornado moved rapidly to the northeast, but was not consistently on the ground. It skipped on several occasions in Riverdale, producing primarily EF0 damage to trees and a several homes. The tornado then produced a more continuous swath of damage through Washington Terrace producing EF1 damage to numerous homes, structures, as well as many trees. Finally, the tornado skipped briefly into South Ogden producing EF0 damage before dissipating. One person suffered a head injury and took private transportation to a hospital. A few others were cut by flying glass, but were not hospitalized. The many downed trees across the area caused widespread power outages, with over 37,000 customers impacted. Approximately 12 homes in Washington Terrace were so damaged that they were deemed uninhabitable until repaired, and a total of about 30 homes were damaged across Weber County.

A tornado touched down in Panguitch, producing an intermittent damage path|which included EF1 damage to a business in town and EF0 damage to several homes and numerous trees. The most significant damage occurred to a business located at 609 North Main Street, where the tornado took off the roof of a building. The tornado also caused significant damage to numerous vehicles in the area and knocked down multiple power lines, leaving much of the community without power. No injuries were reported across the area.
Strong thunderstorm winds in Logan knocked over a tree that was a foot in diameter and approximately 50 feet tall. This tree fell onto a house and knocked out power in a 3 block radius.

Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall brought widespread flooding to Carbon County. Significant flooding occurred in Wellington near 100 East, and severe damage was reported to approximately 10 homes. In Carbonville, the Pilling Trailer Park received extensive flooding, forcing the evacuation of 80 different mobile homes. Flooding also occurred in Sunnyside, with widespread street flooding causing manhole covers to pop up across the city. The Price River also experienced significant flooding, with flow along the river jumping from the normal flow of less than 10 cfs to greater than 8,000 cfs. In total across the county, flooding damaged over 140 private homes, several businesses, and many local roads. County officials reported uninsured damages of $1,602,000 to infrastructure, $971,000 in damage to businesses, and $1,071,000 to private property.

Heavy rain caused widespread flash flooding across Washington County, including the town of Hildale. The gauge of the Virgin River at Virgin reported an increase from the normal flow of under 100 cfs to nearly 3300 cfs by late morning on September 22. Storm total snowfall included 15 inches in Garland, 11 inches in Thatcher, and 8 inches in North Ogden and Brigham City.
Liberty received 27 inches of snow, while Kamas reported 15 inches and Park City reported 13 inches of snow.

Snowbasin Resort received 28 inches of snow for the storm. In addition, winds were strong in the beginning of the storm, with peak wind gusts of 76 mph at the Snowbasin Resort Snowbasin-Straw Top sensor and 74 mph at Ogden Peak.

Storm total snow reports included 43 inches at Brighton Resort, 33 inches at Alta Ski Area, and 27 inches at Snowbird Ski & Summer Resort. In addition, winds were strong at the beginning of the storm, with a peak wind gust of 86 mph recorded at Cardiff Peak.
The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 2.20 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of snow.
The Timberline SNOTEL received 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 22 inches of snow.
Heavy snow fell in the Uintah Basin, with Altamont receiving 14 inches of snow and Duchesne receiving 10 inches of snow.
The Webster Flat SNOTEL received 2.20 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 25 inches of snow.
Peak wind gusts across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys included 67 mph at Stockton Bar, 62 mph at the SR-201 at I-80 sensor, and 58 mph at Vernon Hill.

Powder Mountain received 17 inches of new snow. In addition, winds were strong through the storm, with peak recorded wind gusts of 101 mph at Logan Summit, 94 mph at Ogden Peak, 90 mph at the Snowbasin Resort Snowbasin-Straw Top sensor, and 89 mph at the Powder Mountain sensor.

Brighton Resort received 17 inches of snow. In addition, winds were strong through the storm, with peak recorded gusts of 76 mph at Alta Ski Area Alta - MT Baldy sensor and 73 mph at the Sundance Moutain Resort Arrowhead Summit sensor.

The Trial Lake SNOTEL received 2.40 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 20 inches of snow. In addition, winds were strong through the event, with peak recorded gusts of 101 mph at the Chepeta RAWS, 88 mph at Windy Peak, and 80 mph at Lofty Lake Peak.
Peak recorded wind gusts included 64 mph at the US-6 at Eureka sensor and 60 mph at the Black Rock sensor.
Peak recorded wind gusts in Uinta County, Wyoming included 62 mph at the Evanston-Uinta County Airport - Burns Field ASOS and 59 mph at the Church Butte WYDOT sensor.

Significant rainfall and snowmelt caused main stem river flooding along the Bear River, and also overwhelmed drainage systems away from the river across much of Cache County. Many roads were flooded and structurally compromised, with over $2.5 million worth of damage reported to roads alone. Debris and flood waters also caused significant damage to sewage and water control systems. Dozens of homes experienced basement flooding, particularly in Wellsville, Hyrum, and Mendon.

Significant rainfall and snowmelt led to main stem river flooding along the Bear River, and also produced widespread flooding away from the river across Box Elder County, with one estimate from the County Commissioner saying that 90% of communities in the county had been affected. Approximately 60 to 100 homes experienced basement flooding, especially in Bothwell, Garland, and Tremonton. Flooding also impacted many businesses and churches. Damage to roadways was also widespread, with over $3.1 million in road damage alone.

Heavy rain and snowmelt overwhelmed drainage systems in portions of Rich County. A 10 to 15 foot section of a canal was breached near Garden City, leading to flooding in several homes. Eleven homes were also flooded in Laketown, and water flowed over multiple area roadways, including State Route 16 between Randolph and Woodruff.
Heavy rain and snowmelt led to residential basement flooding across portions of Weber County, with damage reported in Farr West, Plain City, and across parts of the Ogden Valley.

Thunderstorms along the cold front produced strong winds across the Cache Valley, with a peak recorded gust of 53 mph at the Logan-Cache Airport ASOS. Several damage reports were received across the valley, including nine power poles that were knocked down in Wellsville and two power poles that were knocked over in Amalga. In addition, a 50-foot tree was knocked over and fell onto a mobile home in Smithfield.

Winds across the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys were strong both ahead of and behind the cold front, with peak recorded gusts of 69 mph at the Olympus Hills - MSI sensor, 69 mph at the SR-201 at I-80 sensor, 68 mph at both Vernon Hill and Stockton Bar, 67 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 66 mph in Sandy, and 58 mph at the South Valley Regional Airport.
Storm total snowfall in the Salt Lake Valley included 15 inches in Cottonwood Heights, 10 inches in Sandy, 8 inches at Upper Millcreek and the University of Utah, and 7 inches in Taylorsville.
Storm total snowfall included 16 inches at the Spanish Fork Power House, 15 inches in Springville, and 11 inches in Alpine.
Storm total snowfall reports in the Wasatch mountain valleys included 16 inches in Heber City, 13 inches in both Eden and Park City, 11 inches in Kamas, and 10 inches at the Deer Creek Dam.

Powder Mountain received 34 inches of snow for the event. In addition, winds were strong through the storm, with peak wind gusts of 90 mph at Ogden Peak, 81 mph at Sherwood Hills, 77 mph at Powder Mountain, and 76 mph at the SR-65 at Big Mountain Pass sensor.

Storm total snowfall reports included 47 inches at Brighton Resort, 45 inches at Alta Ski Area, and 42 inches at Snowbird Ski & Summer Resort. In addition, winds were strong through the event, with peak recorded wind gusts of 86 mph at the Sundance Mountain Resort Arrowhead Summit sensor and 72 mph at Park City Mountain Resort Park City - Jupiter sensor.

The Chalk Creek #1 SNOTEL received 2.00 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 30 inches of snow. In addition, Windy Peak recorded a maximum wind gust of 79 mph, while the Chepeta RAWS recorded a peak gust of 77 mph.
Storm total snowfall in the Cache Valley included 12 inches in Logan, 9 inches in Smithfield, and 8 inches in Providence.
Spanish Fork received 12 inches of snow from the storm.

Brighton Resort received 26 inches of new snow from the storm, including 16 inches during the daytime hours of February 27. Other storm totals included 22 inches at Alta Ski Area and 21 inches at Snowbird Ski & Summer Resort.
Eight inches of snow was reported in both Smithfield and Wellsville.

The Parrish Creek SNOTEL received 1.50 inches liquid equivalent precipitation, or approximately 16 inches of snow. In addition, winds were strong ahead of the cold front, with peak recorded gusts of 96 mph at the SR-65 at Big Mountain Pass sensor, 89 mph at Ogden Peak, and 82 mph at the Snowbasin Resort Snowbasin-Straw Top sensor.

Alta Ski Area received 15 inches of snow, while Park City Mountain Resort received 14 inches of snow. In addition, winds were strong ahead of the cold front, with peak recorded gusts of 110 mph at the Sundance Mountain Resort Arrowhead Summit sensor, 96 mph at Dear Valley DV - Mount Baldy sensor, 82 mph at the Deer Valley DV - Bald Eagle sensor, and 82 mph at the Dreamscape Study Plot sensor, as well as numerous reports in the 70-79 mph range.

Peak recorded wind gusts included 59 mph at the Ogden-Hinckley Airport ASOS and 58 mph at the Fremont Island - Miller Hill sensor. In addition, roof damage was reported in parts of the area, including West Haven.

Peak recorded wind gusts included 77 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 76 mph in Tooele, 72 mph at the Olympus Hills sensor, 68 mph at Draper, and dozens of reports in the 55-65 mph range. Tree damage was widespread across both the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys, with many trees uprooted. Damage was also reported to roofs, carports, and fences.

Maximum recorded wind gusts included 66 mph at the Pioneer Crossing sensor, 63 mph in Pleasant Grove, and 58 mph in Lehi. The most significant damage across the area was reported in Eagle Mountain, where multiple fences were blown down, a trampoline became airborne and landed on a car, and miscellaneous roof and siding damage was reported.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts included 71 mph at Camel Back Mountain, 70 mph at Lakeside Mountain, 66 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, and 64 mph at the Salt Flats sensor. In addition, an empty semitrailer was blown over by the winds on Interstate 80 near milepost 79; the driver of the semi was not injured.

Peak recorded wind gusts included 80 mph at the US-40 Mayflower Summit sensor, 69 mph at SR-248, 64 mph at the US-40 Heber sensor, 62 mph at the Heber City Municipal Airport - Russ McDonald Field AWOS, and 60 mph at Morgan.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 64 mph at the Interstate 15 at Sevier River sensor, 62 mph at Interstate 70 at Salina, and 62 mph at the Sevier Reservoir sensor.

Peak recorded wind gusts in west central Utah included 69 mph at the Clearspot sensor, 68 mph at Black Rock, 65 mph in Oak City, 62 mph at Delta Municipal Airport, 61 mph at the Oasis sensor, and 61 mph at Fish Springs. In addition, some trees were blown over in Oak City, including one large pine tree that fell onto two vehicles.

Maximum recorded wind gusts included 70 mph at the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field ASOS, 67 mph at the Cedar City Regional Airport ASOS, 65 mph at Enterprise, and 65 mph at Brimstone Reservoir. Tree and fence damage was reported at multiple locations, including Enoch, Fillmore, and Cedar City. In addition, the winds and low visibility due to blowing dust were both significant factors in multiple car accidents along State Route 21 near Milford, which was closed for a period of time between mileposts 78 and 90. The reduced visibility led to a three-vehicle pileup, involving a semitrailer, an SUV, and a pickup truck pulling a trailer, which resulted in several serious injuries. Another three-vehicle accident was caused by windblown debris in the middle of the roadway, also involving two passenger cars and a semitrailer, with injuries sustained in that accident as well. Also along this part of State Route 21, the roof of a barn was blown off and became caught in power lines, causing them to crash down to the ground.
The Little Bear River reached flood stage at multiple gauges in the Cache Valley. This included the Little Bear - Paradise river gauge, which reached a peak flow of 1340 cfs on March 23.

Heavy rain fell across the Salt Lake Valley on March 23. At the Sunnyvale Apartments on 3940 South 764 West, two families had to evacuate their apartments due to flooding. Relatively close by at the Salt Lake City International Airport, 1.97 inches of rainfall was recorded; this was the wettest day on record for the month of March, and the 6th wettest day since records began in 1874.

The St George Regional Airport AWOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. In addition, multiple large utility poles were knocked down due to strong winds on River Road, causing power outages and forcing traffic to be diverted around the area.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Ibapah received 10 inches of snow. In addition, winds were strong along the cold front on the afternoon of March 30, with peak wind gusts of 65 mph at the 	|I-80 @ mp 1 sensor, 61 mph at SR-30 at Curlew, and 58 mph at the Interstate 80 sensor. With these strong winds, a semitrailer was blown over on Interstate 80 near milepost 1.
Enterprise received 9 inches of snow, while Cedar City received 6 inches of snow.

Strong easterly downslope winds developed in the northern Wasatch Front late on March 31. Peak recorded wind gusts included 68 mph at the US-89 at Park Lane sensor, 62 mph in Farmington, and 61 mph in Centerville. Note that this event continued into April.
The sensor at the University of Utah William Browning Building recorded a maximum wind gust of 58 mph.

Strong easterly downslope winds developed in the northern Wasatch Front late on March 31. Peak recorded wind gusts included 68 mph at the US-89 at Park Lane sensor, 62 mph in Farmington, and 61 mph in Centerville. Note that this event began in March.
Multiple people in Davis County reported approximately quarter-sized hail.
A CWOP station in South Weber recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Winds were strong behind the cold front, with peak recorded wind gusts of 59 mph at Callao in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet and 58 mph at the I-80 @ mp 1 sensor.

Storm total snowfall included 26 inches at Alta Ski Area, 18 inches at Snowbird Ski & Summer Resort, and 17 inches at Brighton Resort. Winds were also strong, particularly early in the event, with peak recorded gusts of 87 mph at the Sundance Mountain Resort Arrowhead Summit sensor, 80 mph at the Brighton Resort Brighton Crest sensor, and 77 mph at the Dreamscape Study Plot.
Southwesterly winds were strong ahead of the front, with a peak recorded gust of 64 mph at the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field ASOS.
The Logan-Cache Airport ASOS recorded a maximum wind gust of 66 mph. In addition, winds caused a power outage in Hyde Park and Smithfield, with over 3,000 customers losing power.
A maximum wind gust of 60 mph was reported in South Ogden, and approximately 3,000 customers lost power in Roy and Riverdale.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts included 76 mph at the I-80 @ mp 1 sensor, 70 mph at the V-Grid sensor in the Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, 69 mph at both Lakeside Mountain and the Wendover Airport AWOS, and numerous other gusts in the 60-67 mph range. Three semitrailers were blown over by the strong winds on Interstate 80 between Wendover and Tooele; one of the trucks was blown over near milepost 77, west of Grantsville, while the other two were blown over near milepost 40.

A peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at Lehi. Wind damage was widespread across Lehi, including multiple trampolines that were damaged or became airborne, a large digital road construction sign that was damaged, a car window that was blown out, significant damage to homes under construction, damaged playground equipment, several damaged fences, and a set of baseball bleachers that was blown onto the adjacent backstop. In Eagle Mountain City, power lines were knocked down, closing the Pony Express Parkway at Porter's Crossing.

Maximum recorded wind gusts included 82 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 78 mph at SR-201 at I-80, 75 mph at the Point of the Mountain sensor, 73 mph at Vernon Hill, 71 mph at Flight Park South, 69 mph at the University of Utah, and numerous other reports in the 50-64 mph range. Large trees were knocked over and fell onto houses in Murray and Magna, and fence damage was also reported across the area. A trampoline became airborne in South Jordan and landed in an adjacent street. About 7,300 homes in the Salt Lake Valley lost power. At the Salt Lake City International Airport, more than two dozen flights were diverted to other airports across the region due to the strong winds. The Great Salt Lake Marina was also temporarily closed down due to safety concerns with the winds.
The U.S. 6 at Eureka sensor reported a peak wind gust of 65 mph, while the Clearspot sensor recorded a maximum gust of 60 mph.

The ASOS at the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph, with other reports in the area of 60 mph at the Murdock sensor and 59 mph at the Brimstone Reservoir RAWS.
The Causeway sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
Storm total snowfall included 26 inches at Alta Ski Area and 20 inches at Snowbird Ski & Summer Resort.
The Interstate 70 at Salina sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 62 mph.
The ASOS at the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
Strong thunderstorm winds at Antelope Island State Park caused significant damage, including damaging multiple pavilions and breaking several windows across the park.
The Lake Point I-80 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 63 mph.
The I-15 at Beer Creek sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph.
A maximum wind gust of 66 mph was recorded in Syracuse.
The Fremont Island - Miller Hill sensor recorded a very strong wind gust of 91 mph.
The Pleasant Grove RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 68 mph.
A peak wind gust of 67 mph was recorded at the Great Salt Lake Minerals sensor.
The I-80 at Grassey sensor reported a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
A 59 mph wind gust was recorded at the I-15 at Tremonton sensor.
The I-15 at Plymouth sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 64 mph.
Nickel-sized hail was reported along Interstate 80 near the Utah/Wyoming border.

Strong thunderstorm winds caused significant damage to several outbuildings at the Wight Fresh Turkey Farm. Some of the structures were blown down completely, while others sustained major damage to support posts and tin roofs. Damage across the entire farm was estimated at $60,000.

Extensive snowmelt caused the South Fork of the Ogden River to exceed flood stage east of the Pineview Reservoir and the town of Huntsville, with flows at the Pineview Reservoir gauge peaking near 1200 cfs. Much of the flooding was mitigated by sandbagging efforts, but minor damage was reported to cabins and lawns near the river.

The Provo River exceeded flood stage after a planned release from Deer Creek Dam, which was necessary to make space in the upstream reservoir in anticipation of spring snow melt. Flows peaked at 1905 cfs on May 17, before gradually decreasing through the week. The flood waters undercut the Provo River Trail near Canyon Glen Park, causing the Utah County Sheriff to close the trail, but otherwise damage was minimal due to planning and mitigation.

A strong thunderstorm went through the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, producing maximum recorded wind gusts of 73 mph at the Salt Flats sensor, 69 mph at the Target R sensor, 62 mph at North Salt Flats, and 59 mph at Causeway. A 68 mph wind gust was also recorded at the UDOT I-80 @ mp 78 sensor.
The Callao Gate sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 70 mph.
The Center Tailings sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 65 mph.
The UDOT I15/I215 SB sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph.
The SR-201 at I-80 sensor recorded a wind gust of 59 mph.
The UDOT I-80 @ mp 78 sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 75 mph.

The Logan River exceeded flood stage several times through the first two weeks of June, with the gauge near Logan peaking at 1450 cfs on the morning of June 6. The flooding resulted in the closure of multiple campgrounds and other recreation areas in Logan Canyon, but otherwise mitigation and sandbagging helped prevent further damages.
Rangers at Capitol Reef National Park reported flash flooding in Grand Wash.
Strong winds from a dry microburst knocked over a section of fence and caused damage to large tree limbs in Clearfield. In addition, a 64 mph wind gust was recorded at Hill Air Force Base.

Strong winds caused damage in parts of Davis County, including knocking off roof shingles, uprooting multiple trees, and knocking over a mailbox. In addition, over 1,000 customers lost power in Davis and Weber counties. Peak recorded wind gusts included 82 mph at the Fremont Island - Miller Hill sensor, 68 mph at Hill Air Force Base, 61 mph in South Ogden, and 58 mph at the Great Salt Lake Minerals sensor.

Peak recorded wind gusts included 77 mph at the SR-201 at I-80 sensor, 74 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 71 mph at the Center Tailings sensor, 67 mph at Vernon Hill, 62 mph at Stockton Bar, and 60 mph at both the UDOT I-80 @ mp 78 sensor and the Salt Lake City International Airport SLC Airport Wind 3 sensor. In addition, a secondary weather sensor at the Great Salt Lake Marina recorded a gust of 90 mph. The most significant damage across the area occurred at the Great Salt Lake Marina, where several sailboats were damaged by the winds. In addition, tree limbs were damaged across the Salt Lake Valley, including a large branch that fell onto and damaged a home in Holladay. As many as 8,500 Rocky Mountain Power customers were without power at one point on June 12, with the majority of outages occurring in Rose Park, Glendale, and South Salt Lake.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: Peak recorded wind gusts included 76 mph at Hat Island, 65 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 59 mph at Gunnison Island, and dozens of wind gust reports between 50 mph and 57 mph. Four semitrailers were knocked over by the high winds along Interstate 80, closing the highway for a period of time on the morning of June 12, and causing delays in both directions. One of these accidents resulted in minor injuries for the semitruck driver.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 61 mph at Hanksville and 60 mph at Torrey.
Maximum recorded wind gusts included 63 mph at Church Butte and 60 mph at Fort Bridger.
The ASOS at the Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
A peak wind gust of 59 mph was recorded at the Chaulk Hill sensor.
The Vernon Hill sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 80 mph.
The sensor at US-189 at Deer Creek Dam reported a peak wind gust of 64 mph.
A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was recorded at the Roosevelt Municipal Airport AWOS.
The Callao sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.

Many sensors in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded strong winds from a thunderstorm, including 73 mph at Causeway, 63 mph at Upper Cedar Mountain, 62 mph at the APG sensor, 61 mph at Playa Station and V-Grid, 60 mph at the Salt Flats sensor, and 58 mph at Wig Mountain.
Multiple sensors along Interstate 80 recorded strong wind gusts, including 59 mph at the      U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground Interstate 80 sensor and 58 mph at the I-80 @ mp 29 sensor.
A maximum wind gust of 93 mph was recorded by the I-80 @ mp 29 sensor. The Utah Department of Transportation reported that a variable message sign at milepost 29 was blown down.

A maximum wind gust of 45 mph was recorded at the Bear Lake sensor. Wind damage was reported near Bear Lake and in Garden City, including large tree limbs that were damaged and roof shingles that were blown off of a house.

The Brianhead Fire started on June 17, when a man used a weed torch at his Brian Head area cabin, and the fire became out of control. The fire burned 71,675 acres, with most of the growth in the first two weeks of the fire. The Brianhead Fire destroyed 13 homes and 13 minor structures. A priority sage grouse habitat was also impacted east of the fire perimeter in the Panguitch watershed area. Costs associated with the fire were approximately $36.6 million, with rehabilitation efforts projected to cost double or triple that amount. At the height of the fire, approximately 1,831 personnel were fighting to contain the wildfire, and 1,562 people were evacuated from 11 communities in Iron and Garfield counties. The fire was contained on July 28. Note that this event continued into July.

The Brianhead Fire started on June 17, when a man used a weed torch at his Brian Head area cabin, and the fire became out of control. The fire burned 71,672 acres, with most of the growth in the first two weeks of the fire. The Brianhead Fire destroyed 13 homes and 13 minor structures. A priority sage grouse habitat was also impacted east of the fire perimeter in the Panguitch watershed area. Costs associated with the fire were approximately $36.6 million, with rehabilitation efforts projected to cost double or triple that amount. At the height of the fire, approximately 1,831 personnel were fighting to contain the wildfire, and 1,562 people were evacuated from 11 communities in Iron and Garfield counties. The fire was contained on July 28. Note that this event began in June.
The US-40 at Starvation sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
The UDOT sensor at Kimball Junction and I-80 recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in portions of Capitol Reef National Park, including Cohab Canyon, Sulphur Creek, and Grand Wash.

Heavy rainfall on the Brianhead burn scar caused flash flooding near Panguitch Lake. The flooding was most significant along the Clear Creek drainage, with water overwhelming the culverts and side roads.

The Utah Department of Transportation reported a flash flood and debris flow in Paragonah after heavy rain fell over the Brianhead burn scar. The flood waters came down Red Creek Canyon and reached all the way down to Main Street/State Route 271 in Paragonah.

Heavy rain over Kanab produced widespread flash flooding across the town. Multiple businesses suffered flood damage and approximately 20 homes had some mud or water in their basements. Many roads were flooded, and one drainage canal suffered damage.
A member of the public spotted and took a picture of a tornado east of Panguitch Lake. No damage was reported or found.
A member of the public observed and photographed a tornado east of St. George. No damage was reported or found.

A line of thunderstorms produced several severe wind gusts across Interstate 80 and the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet, with peak recorded gusts of 65 mph at the Interstate 80 sensor, 64 mph at the I-80 @ mp 29 sensor, 62 mph at the Salt Flats sensor, 60 mph at Wig Mountain, and 59 mph at Playa Station.
A 59 mph wind gust was recorded at the Fremont Island - Miller Hill sensor.
The Salt Flats sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
Heavy rain south of Scipio caused flash flooding along US-50, temporarily closing the roadway.
Heavy rain north of Capitol Reef National Park, with radar estimates of over 3 inches of rain, caused flash flooding along State Route 72.
Widespread heavy rain across Capitol Reef National Park caused flash flooding in many drainages, particularly in Cathedral Valley and along Sulphur Creek.

Heavy rain caused widespread street and residential flooding in Salem, with 139 homes damaged. This damaged varied widely; most homes experienced only minor yard or basement flooding, while 3-5 homes experienced significant basement damage. One person sustained a major leg injury that required stitches, after a window was blown out and glass cut her leg. At least one other person sustained minor injuries related to the flooding.
Flash flooding was reported in Centerfield, particularly over Clarion Road, with flowing water temporarily making the road impassible.
Heavy rain caused multiple mudslides across Nine Mile Canyon Road, temporarily shutting down the roadway.
Widespread flash flooding was reported across south central Utah, including in Croton Canyon, Spooky Canyon, the Egypt 3 slot canyon, Coyote Gulch, and Last Chance Creek.

Flash flooding was reported in several drainages, including Cottonwood Creek, the Paria River, Buckskin Gulch, and Wahweap Creek. Flood waters caused damage to House Rock Road and Cottonwood Road, temporarily stranding multiple groups of people.

Heavy rain over the Brianhead Fire burn scar caused widespread flash flooding and debris flows. On the south side of the burn near Panguitch Lake, multiple roads were washed out along Clear Creek. On the north end of the burn scar, flooded roads were reported both east and west of the ridgeline.
Flash flooding occurred along the headwaters of the Escalante River, including along Birch Creek and Upper Valley Creek.
Flash flooding was reported in Sheep Creek, Yellow Creek, and Willis Creek.
Flash flooding was reported along the Paria River and Buckskin Gulch.
Minor flash flooding was reported along Wahweap Creek.
Widespread flash flooding was reported in the upper drainages of the Escalante River.
Flash flooding occurred along the Escalante River, with the river gauge on the Escalante rising from 0 cfs to 1549 cfs in one hour.
Flash flooding was reported along Wahweap Creek during the overnight hours.
A large flash flood was reported southeast of Bryce Canyon, including along Sheep Creek, Yellow Creek, and Willis Creek.

Heavy rain caused a significant flash flood in Buckskin Gulch. This flood impacted a group of approximately 8 hikers who had set up camp along the gulch; most of the hikers put their tents above the gulch in a safe area, but two people set up their tent upstream in the gulch alone. Shortly after falling asleep, the flood waters reached their tent; while both adults were able to exit the tent, they were carried several hundred feet before coming to a stop on the bank. Another hiker tried to get down to the gulch to save the family members from the flood, and broke both feet in the process due to the rough terrain and drops into the gulch. Eventually the group was able to get assistance for the injured members of the party, and some of them were airlifted from the scene.

Heavy rain led to a flash flood in the Narrows section of Zion National Park, which was observed and video taped by hikers in the park. Most of the floodwater appeared to be about 2-3 feet high, and carried typical debris of sticks, logs, and rocks. No injuries were reported due to the flooding.
A large flash flood was reported in Johnson Canyon, particularly in the upper drainage portion of the canyon.
The Fish Springs sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 58 mph.

Two girls, ages 8 and 16, were camping with relatives near Big Flat in the Beaver Mountains. The girls were by themselves, accompanied by a family dog, when they were both struck by lightning. The dog returned to camp to alert the rest of the family, and the family found the girls unconscious. Both girls were flown via helicopter to the hospital, and both survived, despite suffering significant injuries.

Thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall moved into the Salt Lake Valley in the early morning hours of July 26 and generally persisted for 3-4 hours, producing widespread flash flooding. The highest reported rainfall totals included 2.40 inches in Sugarhouse near Parleys Way, and many locations on the east side of the Salt Lake Valley reported 1.00 to 1.60 rain. The most significant damage occurred at East High School, where flooding caused $2.5 million in damage, with the largest percentage of the damage impacting the athletics department. Flooding was also reported at other Salt Lake City schools including Highland High School, Emerson Elementary, and the Salt Lake Center of Science Education. Another building that was damaged significantly was the Sprague Library, where water poured into the library's basement, damaging books, computers, furniture, and walls. Damage to the Sprague Library totaled $1.5 million. The train track for the TRAX light rail was under a foot of water on 200 West at 1100 South, causing significant delays and forcing UTA to use a bus bridge between stops. Street flooding was also reported at several locations across the city, including major thoroughfares such as Foothill Drive and 3300 South. Temporary power outages impacted about 4,200 customers across the metro area. Damage was reported at 172 total homes across the area. These private damages were primarily minor basement flooding, but 26 homes experienced damage due to overflowing sewer lines, and 3 homes experienced major damage of approximately $35,000 at each of these 3 houses. In total, private damages were estimated to be $1.75 million, while public damages were estimated at $7 million.
The I-80 @ mp 29 sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
The Interstate 80 sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 60 mph.
The Henry Mountain RAWS recorded a peak wind gust of 70 mph.
The Bullfrog Marina automated weather station reported a peak wind gust of 73 mph.
Flash flooding was reported in multiple slot canyons in Zion National Park.
Widespread flash flooding was reported across Capitol Reef National Park.
A large flash flood was reported in Buckskin Wash and some surrounding drainages.
Flash flooding was reported across many tributaries of the Escalante River.
Heavy rain caused flood damage to the Salt Lake City Justice Court and to a nearby Crossfit gym.
Flash flooding was reported on Pleasant Creek in Capitol Reef National Park.
A flash flood was reported in Buckskin Wash.

Thunderstorms moving over the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area produced severe microburst winds in the Padre Canyon, Sand King, Lone Rock, and Gunsight areas of the park. Several boats were overturned, including a 75 foot houseboat carrying 14 people. Aboard the large houseboat in Padre Canyon, the arm of an 80-year-old woman was severed, and a 57-year-old woman suffered head and hip injuries. Another person near Gunsight suffered a dislocated shoulder.
The Brimstone Reservoir RAWS recorded a maximum wind gust of 72 mph.
The Callao sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
A peak wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at the Causeway sensor in the U.S. Army Dugway Proving Ground mesonet.
A 62 mph wind gust was recorded at the Bullfrog Marina sensor.
A member of the public reported dime-sized hail near Interstate 15 and 7200 South.
Nickel-sized hail was reported near Price.
Quarter-sized hail was reported across Herriman, with a picture of the hail also provided.

Flash flooding was reported in Capitol Reef National Park, with 4 to 6 inches of flowing water reported in Capitol Gorge. This water damaged the dirt road that provides access to the Capitol Gorge area.
Heavy rain led to flash flooding across the southern half of Zion National Park, including along Pine Creek. In addition, street flooding was reported in the towns of Springdale and Rockville.
Flash flooding was reported along Coyote Creek, which is a tributary of Wahweap Creek.
The Paria River rose from 7 cfs to 1240 cfs, or an increase of approximately 3 feet.
Flash flooding along Parowan Creek spilled over onto Interstate 15, temporarily closing the right-hand lane of northbound Interstate 15.

The Uintah Fire started on September 5 near the mouth of Weber Canyon. The fire was sparked by a downed power line and spread rapidly due to strong easterly canyon winds in the area, eventually burning 619 acres. More than 900 people were evacuated from their homes in the cities of Uintah and South Weber on September 5 before being allowed to return by September 7. The fire destroyed three homes and damaged two other homes and a mixed-use property. In total, the fire destroyed or damaged 18 structures. The estimated damage was $849,000, with operational costs to fight the fire at around $273,000. The fire was contained on September 10.
An outflow from a thunderstorm south of St. George caused damage near the Red Cliffs Mall. Eight trees, 5 to 12 inches in diameter, were uprooted by these strong winds.
Heavy rain over the Brianhead Fire burn scar caused flash flooding along State Routes 143 and 271, temporarily closing these routes due to debris on the roadways.

Heavy rain on the Brianhead Fire burn scar once again caused flooding and debris along State Route 143, this time near the White Bridge Campground in the Panguitch Creek Drainage. A front loader was needed to remove the boulders from the road.

Multiple rounds of heavy rain over the Brianhead Fire burn scar produced both flash flooding and debris flows. This debris and water first inundated State Route 143, ultimately closing portions of the roadway for multiple days. A second round of rain in the early evening hours flowed into Parowan Creek and ran into the town of Parowan, with water 6-8 feet above normal stage during the event. This later flooding damaged four homes in Parowan, primarily basements. In addition, flood damage occurred along Old United States Highway 91, as well as northbound lanes of Interstate 15 between milepost 73 and Parowan. The debris field along Interstate 15 was approximately an eighth of a mile long, and forced the closure of the roadway for several hours.

Strong westerly downslope winds developed in Castle Country, with peak recorded wind gusts of 71 mph at the I-70 at Fremont Junction sensor, 70 mph at the SR-72 at Hogan Pass sensor, 62 mph in Orangeville, and 58 mph in Ferron.
A peak wind gust of 59 mph was recorded at the I-15 at Beaver sensor.

The strong winds with the cold front led to significantly reduced visibility across the valley in blowing dust. In addition, the high winds knocked down power lines in Midvale, with over 2,000 customers losing power. A 60-year-old tree in Sugarhouse was also blown down by the winds.

A maximum wind gust of 68 mph was recorded in Lehi after the cold frontal passage. Strong winds were also likely a factor when a semitrailer knocked down four power poles in Provo, disrupting power for about 100 customers. In addition to the poles, underground wiring and transformers also suffered damage from the collision.
Peak recorded wind gusts included 64 mph at the SR-201 at I-80 sensor, 61 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, and 58 mph at Flight Park South.

Damages also included many fences that were blown down, whole sides of houses that were missing siding, shingles blown off, and portions of roofs missing. The city of Tooele submitted about $50,000 worth of damage, including damages sustained at the golf course, cemetery, and various city buildings. The Dollar Ridge Fire was a human caused wildfire that began during the afternoon of July 1. The fire burned 68,869 acres and destroyed 363 structures, including 74 homes. Initially only about 20 acres, it experienced exceptional growth on September 12 due to high winds and low relative humidity, and eventually burned 18,620 acres. Though the Salt Lake Valley received the lighter precipitation from this event than surrounding valleys, some areas still accumulated large amounts of snow. Brighton Crest received the most snow in the state, with 22 inches storm total. Other totals from the area included 20 inches at Alta Collins and 19 inches at Park City Jupiter Peak. This snowfall was accompanied by strong winds, with the strongest recorded gust being 76 mph at Mt. Baldy.

Several sections of Interstate 15 in Box Elder, Weber and Davis counties were closed throughout portions of the evening.

Heavy snow in the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys was accompanied by strong winds, including a 59 mph wind gust at the University of Utah. These white-out conditions had a major impact on the afternoon commute on the 13th and the morning commute on the 14th. Snow totals in the Salt Lake Valley included 10 inches at Upper Millcreek, 8 inches in the Upper Avenues, 8 inches in Sandy, and 6 inches at the Salt Lake Airport. In addition to all this, the storm stalled over the Tooele Valley for several hours on the morning of the 14th, resulting in a storm total for Tooele of 21 inches of snow.

Impact-wise, the southern Wasatch Front was hit the hardest by this storm. Woodland Hills and Payson both received a foot of new snow for the storm, but the real story was the effect on afternoon and evening travel.  With the heavy snowfall, this area received the strongest winds for the state in a valley location, with the strongest recorded gusts being 70 mph in Alpine and 69 mph in Lehi. This led to white-out conditions and high impacts to the afternoon commute. Over 200 students were stranded at 3 elementary schools, and ten buses with 60 to 70 students each were stranded because of road closures or weather conditions, most later returning to their schools until parents could get them. Numerous roads were closed down, including U.S. Highway 6 in Utah county east of Spanish Fork, and all of Redwood Road in Utah county. Many motorists were forced to abandon their cars and come back on Valentine's Day, only to find them buried in snow drifts, some as high as 10 feet. Many of these motorists spent the night in gas stations and grocery stores, and reports indicated that these stranded people numbered in the hundreds. Accidents with this storm included a 12-car pileup at Redwood Road and Lehi Main in Saratoga Springs, two jack-knifed semitrailers blocking several northbound lanes of I-15 near Point of the Mountain, a seven-car accident near American Fork, and 16 vehicles involved in a massive pile-up on Highway 73 in Saratoga Springs.

During the late evening and early nighttime hours, intense rainfall was observed in St. George. The St. George, UT Coop observer reported 2.00 inches of rainfall in two hours, corresponding to a recurrence interval of approximately 200 years. The Santa Clara River at St. George rose from 3 cfs to 1,586 cfs in 3 hours. Interstate 15 was closed in both directions, with five to six feet of water reported across roadways in the area producing additional road closures, including the Red Hills Parkway. Many cars were stalled and stranded, several sink holes were reported, and power outages occurred.  St. George Rehabilitation was partially evacuated. Flood damage was reported in apartment complexes and basements. Monetary damage to public infrastructure was $3,082,501, with an additional $2,302,000 in damage to private property.
A peak wind gust of 60 mph was recorded by the Badger Spring sensor.

A peak wind gust of 68 mph was recorded at the Logan-Cache Airport. Widespread power outages were reported, with Rocky Mountain Power reporting 13,000 customers lost power. Numerous large trees were downed, including a tree estimated at 140 years old.

A historic downslope wind event unfolded along the Northern Wasatch Front. The peak wind gust for the event, not only in this zone, but across the state, was a 99 mph peak wind gust recorded by the US-89 at Park Lane sensor.   Other notable peak wind gusts included 97 mph at Farmington, 84 mph at Hill Air Force Base, 82 mph in North Brigham City, 75 mph at Brigham City Regional Airport, 75 mph at Centerville, and 64 mph at Ogden-Hinckley Airport. Extensive wind damage was reported along the entire Wasatch Front, with widespread downed trees, damaged roofs and power outages. Transportation was heavily impacted with all major north-south (Interstate 15, Interstate 84, and U.S. Highway 89) routes closed or restricted at times through the event.  At least 50 semitrailers were overturned, with four truck drivers with injuries taken to  hospitals. Over 180,000 power outages were reported along the Wasatch Front, with some locations taking days to around a week to have power restored due to the extensive damage. All school districts were closed Tuesday, with some closures continuing into Wednesday. Two Ogden hospitals reported significant damaged, and an Intermountain Life Flight helicopter was severely damaged. At least 20 manufactured homes were heavily damaged in Box Elder County, requiring residents to be transferred to shelters.  Damage and cleanup costs for the event tallied $4.3 million.

A historic downslope wind event impacted the Salt Lake and Tooele Valleys, with the most extensive damage observed across the Salt Lake Valley. A peak wind gust of 89 mph was recorded at The University of Utah Browning Building. Other notable peak wind gusts recorded included 77 mph at Salt Lake City International Airport, 68 mph at the Great Salt Lake Marina, 68 mph in the Salt Lake City Avenues, 67 mph by the Baccus Highway sensor, 67 mph by the I-215 at Olympus Cove sensor, and 59 mph by the Foothill Dr at Mario Capecchi Dr. sensor.  Widespread wind damage, downed trees, and power outages were reported. The Salt Lake Forester estimated more than 1500 trees fell on public land alone, not including private property, during the event.  Many of the trees were 60 to 100 years old. Liberty Park lost 69 trees, and the City Cemetery lost 255 trees. Over 180,000 power outages were reported along the Wasatch Front, with some locations taking days to around a week to have power restored due to the extensive damage. Salt Lake City schools were closed Tuesday through Thursday. The Capitol Complex was closed due to extensive tree damage, as were numerous parks, golf courses and recreation areas. Many COVID-19 testing sites were damaged and had to close, including all University of Utah testing sites. The only know fatality for the event occurred in South Salt Lake, when a 61-year-old truck driver unloading his truck was blown over by the wind, striking his head. In addition, Intermountain Healthcare  reported that 12 patients were treated for wind-related injuries. Damage and cleanup costs for the event tallied $4.3 million.

The Forest Service Utah Avalanche Center reported that two groups, totaling eight people, were backcountry skiing at Wilson Glade in Millcreek Canyon, when an avalanche was triggered. The avalanche caught and buried six of the people, leading to four fatalities, while two survived, one with injuries. The avalanche occurred in terrain that was rated for High avalanche danger that day. The weather the day of the avalanche was sunny and fair. However, two storm systems the week prior to the avalanche brought roughly 20 inches of snow and winds 15-30 mph, with gusts up to 45 mph.
A peak wind gust of 76 mph was recorded by the Ogden Peak sensor.
The Lofty Lake Peak sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 77 mph. Other peak wind gusts recorded included 66 mph by the Windy Peak sensor and 62 mph by the Chepeta sensor.

Storm total snowfall reports included 17 inches in Milford and 6.5 inches in Beaver. The Interstate 15 northbound lanes were closed at milepost 109.

events.event_narrative: A storm total snowfall report of 4 inches was received for a location 5 miles north-northeast of Santa Clara.
The Interstate 15 at Milepost 369 sensor, north of North Brigham City, recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph.
The United States 89 at Weber Canyon Tripod sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 74 mph, and the United States 89 at Park Lane sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 72 mph.

Downslope peak wind gusts along the Northern Wasatch Front included 86 mph recorded by the United States 89 at Weber Canyon Tripod sensor and 79 mph recorded by the United States 89 at Park Lane sensor.  Other reports included 65 mph in Farmington and Bountiful, 60 mph in Ogden, and 59 mph at Hill Air Force Base.

Peak wind gusts included 60 mph at Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field,  59 mph at Brimstone Reservoir, and 58 mph at Cedar City Regional Airport. In addition, the Utah Department of Transportation reported a semitrailer was blown over on Interstate 15 south of Cedar City.

The Wasatch Mountains north of I-80 received a wide variety of snowfall amounts, with generally 6 to 12 inches of snow falling in an 8 hour period. The highest amounts of about 12 inches were at Parley's Summit and Louis Meadow. There was also a large impact on the commute on I-80, as the heaviest snow fell between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m. local time.

Including some pre-frontal snow showers, Alta received a storm total of 20 inches of new snow, while The Canyons received 13 new inches. The heaviest snow fell on the morning of April 7th, with reports of 4 inches of snow per hour at The Canyons.

Alta received 12 inches of new snow in 12 hours during the overnight hours of April 9th into April 10th. The storm total snowfall for Alta was 17 inches, while Brighton Crest and Snowbird received 15 inches and 13 inches respectively.
The Cardiff Peak sensor, located at an elevation of 10,059 feet MSL, recorded a maximum wind gust of 77 mph.
The Snowbasin Straw Top sensor, located at 8,999 feet elevation, recorded a maximum wind gust of 93 mph. In addition, the Snowbasin Wildcat sensor, located at 7,703 feet elevation, gusted to 91 mph.

High winds were observed in southwest Utah, including peak wind gusts of 62 mph at Milford Municipal Airport/Ben and Judy Briscoe Field, 59 mph recorded at the Interstate 15 at Milepost 62.5 sensor, and 58 mph recorded by the Interstate 15 at Paragonah sensor.
The Signal Peak RAWS had a maximum wind gust of 82 mph.
Several sensors in Tooele valley had strong wind gusts, the strongest of which was a 72 mph gust at Vernon Hill. Other wind gusts included 65 mph at South Mountain and 61 mph at Stockton Bar.

The sensor at Vernon Hill recorded very gusty winds for a period of several hours, with the maximum gust being 67 mph. Wind gusts of 61 mph were also recorded at the sensors at Stockton Bar and South Mountain.

events.event_narrative: The Tower Grid sensor in the Tooele mesonet recorded multiple wind gusts of 58 mph over the course of a few hours.
Alta Collins received 14 inches of new snow, while Spruces UDOT received 13 inches, both of which occurred in less than 12 hours.

events.cz_name: UTAHS DIXIE AND ZION NATIONAL PARK
events.event_narrative: The St. George AWOS recorded several strong wind gusts on the afternoon of April 30th, the strongest of which was 60 mph.

Snowbird received 23 new inches of snow for the storm total, while Alta received 22 inches. Both of these sites received 12 to 15 inches of new snow in a 12 hour period. Note that this event continued into May.

Flash flooding was observed at the state Route 12 overpass of the Escalante River. Additional reports of flash flooding were observed upstream, including in Escalante River Canyon and at Death Hollow. The Escalante River gauge climbed from no flow to 400 CFS.
Hildale Fire Department personnel reported multiple road closures in town, multiple flooded residences, and several stranded motorists due to flash flooding in the area.
Significant flash flooding occurred from the entrance of Zion National Park, across the eastern portions of the park. State Route 9 within the park closed due to flooding and debris on the roadway.

Widespread flash flooding occurred from Wire Pass to the mouth of Buckskin Gulch. Several hikers were stranded between Wire Pass and the entrance to Buckskin Gulch, with muddy water levels rising to waist deep. Another group was trapped within Buckskin Gulch overnight due to Flash Flooding. The group was able to climb onto narrow ledges above the flood waters, where they remained overnight, then evacuated the next day.
A peak wind gust of 65 mph was recorded by the U.S. Highway 189 at Deer Creek Dam sensor.
A peak wind gust of 58 mph was recorded by the state Route 72 at Hogan Pass sensor.

An unusually early heat wave developed, including the earliest 100 degree day on record, June 4, occurring at Salt Lake City International Airport.  Daily average temperatures for the period were 15 to 16 degrees above average. Cooling centers were opened in Salt Lake County and Utah Department of Transportation road crews adjusted working hours to avoid peak heating hours.
An unusually early heat wave developed, with daily average temperatures running 13 degrees above average during the period.
An unusually early heat wave developed, with daily average temperatures running up to 19 degrees above average during the period.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: An unusually early heat wave developed, with daily average temperatures running 19 degrees above average during the period.
An unusually early heat wave developed, with daily high temperatures up to 105 degrees at St. George, and warm overnight temperatures in the 70s.
An unusually early heat wave developed, including a daily high temperature of 102 degrees at Big Water.
A prolonged heat event occurred with daytime high temperatures as high as 114 degrees  at St George, and little overnight relief, with low temperatures in the 70s to as warm as 80 degrees.

events.cz_name: GREAT SALT LAKE DESERT AND MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: A two-day stretch of abnormally hot temperatures occurred, with daily average temperatures running as high as 16 degrees above average.
Excessively hot temperatures included a daytime of 104 degrees at Tooele, with a nighttime low of only 80 degrees, and a daily average temperature nearly 24 degrees above normal.
Excessive heat conditions included a daily high temperature of 106 degrees at Ogden, and nighttime lows in the 70s. This pushed daily temperature average to 20 degrees above normal.

On June 15, the temperature at Salt Lake City International Airport reached 107 degrees, tying the all time highest temperature ever recorded at the site. This combined with nighttime lows in the 70s, resulted in daily average temperatures of 20 degrees above normal.
Temperatures up to 105 degrees were recorded at the Provo BYU COOP station.
The temperature at the Myton COOP station reached 101 degrees for three days in a row.
The temperature at Price reached 101 degrees two days in a row, followed by a night with the low temperature in the 70s.

The temperature reached at least 107 degrees five days in a row at Hanksville, including a 109 degree reading on one day. In addition, low temperatures remained in the 70s for the second half of the event.
High temperatures up to 114 degrees were recorded, including many days above 105 degrees. Nighttime low temperatures remained in the 70s.
Temperatures reached 100 degrees or warmer at Kanab during the period, including a day up to 106 degrees.  Overnight lows were in the 70s some nights.

events.cz_name: CAPITOL REEF NATIONAL PARK AND VICINITY
events.event_narrative: Daily temperatures reached as high as 101 degrees at Capitol Reef National Park.  Nighttime lows were in the 70s.
Daily high temperatures were in the upper 90s at Hans Flat Ranger Station, with nighttime lows in the 70s.

A prolonged period of high temperatures over 100 degrees, with low temperatures above 70, occurred at Big Water.  Daily high temperatures including 107, recorded twice.  Overnight lows temperatures were as warm as 84 degrees.

Capitol Reef National Park rangers report 4 to 5 inches of water flowing across Scenic Drive at the first wash crossing. Water 6 to 7 inches deep was reported at the State Route 24 bridge crossing the Grand Wash. Waterfalls were also observed in the park, and debris was flowing down the Fremont River.

Capitol Reef National Park officials reported flash flooding in a dry wash leading into Sulphur Creek from upstream heavy rainfall. The water level on Sulphur Creek near the Visitor center rose 2 feet.
Nine homes were damaged from flooding and debris flows due to heavy rain in the Enoch and Summit areas.

Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument officials reported flash flooding occurred on Calf Creek, with significant debris washed over the waterfalls. Flash flooding was also reported on Egypt Road and in the Egypt slot canyons along Hole-In-The-Rock Road.

Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument officials reported flash flooding on Harris Wash. The flooding occurred later as peak flow worked around from Alvy Wash into Harris Wash. Also, the Escalante River gauge near Escalante indicated a 702 CFS flood wave, with a time above 300 CFS from 1845 MDT to 2015 MDT.

Flash flooding near Lund derailed a Union Pacific Railroad train, forcing 14 cars off of the tracks. Train tracks were determined to be washed out at a small bridge crossing over a normally dry wash. After the train derailed, injured train operators were trapped on top of the overturned train as flood waters continued to rise. In addition, emergency responders were washed off of the road to the crash site by the flood waters, delaying response to the injured train operators.
Kodachrome Basin State Park officials reported brief flash flooding of washes within the Park, including at the campground at the north end of the park.
The North Fork of the Virgin River jumped to 180 CFS, a rise of 1.5 feet, after heavy rainfall over the headwaters overnight.

Water and debris flowed across State Route 21.
Flash flooding washed out the main access road to Old Irontown from State Route 56. Emergency managers stated the road was closed until repaired.
Urban flash flooding was reported in Cedar City.  A video received via social media showing water flowing down streets near the Ashdown Subdivision.
Zion National Park officials reported flash flooding in both the main canyon and in tributaries feeding the canyon from the east.
Flash flooding occurred in a tributary of Shoal Creek. An abandoned pickup truck was observed submerged in the water.
Capitol Reef National Park officials reported flash flooding in Sulphur Creek, with water running 6-12 inches high. Also flash flooding occurred in the Fremont River and Grand Wash.
A Capitol Reef National Park official shared a video of flash flooding in Sulphur Creek.
A weather spotter reported water running down streets in Tropic.

Beaver County dispatch and emergency management personnel reported street flooding in Milford with water 3 feet deep. In addition, debris from flooding was reported on State Route 21 near Milford. The Milford automated weather station recorded 1.10 inches of rain in one hour.
